closest.title: Read, Grep, and Synthesize: Diagnosing Cross-Domain Seed Exposure for LLM Research Ideation (PaperGym, arXiv 2605.11532)
closest.overlap: Closest single design. It retrieves grounded seeds across seven ML domains, synthesizes methods, and compares against no-retrieval, same-domain and random-diverse-seed controls. Cross-domain beats no-retrieval and same-domain on pairwise novelty but does not beat random diverse seeds. Differences from the proposal: the seeds stay inside ML (roughly the proposal's B1/B2 only), outcomes are rubric/LLM-judged rather than executed, and there is no graded distance ladder or single-facet graft. The proposal's R arm deliberately reuses this null.

closest.title: Cross-domain mapping and creativity in humans and LLMs (arXiv 2603.19087)
closest.overlap: Not in the proposal's prior-art list and should be added. It manipulates source-target semantic distance as an independent variable for both humans and LLMs. More distant pairings give more original ideas; humans benefit at nearly any distance, while only the highest-rated LLMs benefit, and only when the source is sufficiently remote. LLMs transfer structural and functional properties. Differences: the outcome is originality ratings on product-design tasks, not executed gains, and there is no ML-training target.

closest.title: Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning (Shen, Druckmann, Zou, arXiv 2605.11258)
closest.overlap: Supplies the structured relational-mapping step (the source of the 21.6% to 50.4% novel-solution lift) and runs four computational case studies with coding agents on public benchmarks, all in biomedicine. Domain distance is measured afterwards by an LLM judge, not manipulated, and analogies are generated rather than retrieved from an index.

closest.title: Same Problem, Different Field: Cross-Domain Solution Import via Domain-Stripped Computational Fingerprints (Kulikowski, arXiv 2609.07595, JCDL 2026)
closest.overlap: The source of the proposal's graft-library format (mechanism skeleton plus computational facets with domain and method names removed). Benchmark: 18 method families across 109 papers; average precision rises from 0.222 (abstract) to 0.513 (skeleton) and 0.557 (full fingerprint). Retrieval only: no generation, no execution, no distance bands.

closest.title: Scideator: Human-LLM Scientific Ideation through Facet Recombination (arXiv 2409.14634)
closest.overlap: Retrieves facets at controlled distances, from the same topic to entirely different areas, and recombines them. Evaluated by a user study of creativity support; nothing is executed.

closest.title: Guiding Data-Driven Design Ideation by Knowledge Distance (InnoGPS, arXiv 2210.10104)
closest.overlap: A pre-LLM patent-network system that uses knowledge distance between technology classes to retrieve near-field and far-field stimuli. This is prior art for distance-banded sources defined by a classification hierarchy rather than embeddings, which is the proposal's OpenAlex-band idea. Evaluated only with two case studies; no execution.

closest.title: ERA: LLM recombination of published methods (Aygun et al., arXiv 2509.06503)
closest.overlap: Executed recombination of two same-field parent methods: 24 of 55 recombinations beat both parents. The operator is a symmetric two-parent blend within one field. There is no distance variable and no conventional-core-plus-one-graft asymmetry.

closest.title: DeepEvolve: Scientific Algorithm Discovery by Augmenting AlphaEvolve with Deep Research (arXiv 2510.06056)
closest.overlap: Shows under execution that adding external literature retrieval to LLM program evolution beats evolution that relies only on the model's internal knowledge. Retrieval is topical, and source distance is neither banded nor tested as a variable.

closest.title: Prime Intellect autonomous nanoGPT speedrun and METR's NanoGPT provenance note
closest.overlap: Executed LM-training loops in which progress comes from imported external ideas (upstream PRs and the literature); a novelty-gated phase with no imports could not improve the baseline. METR's note (metr.org/notes/2026-04-21-ai-rd-nanogpt-progress) supplies the imported/adapted/invented provenance labels that the proposal's backtest reuses. Neither varies the field distance of the source.

closest.title: AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration (arXiv 2605.27905)
closest.overlap: A 219,655-idea study reporting that AI-generated ideas explore more locally than follow-on human papers (search snippet: exploration distance 0.322 vs 0.410). It is a descriptive motivation for forcing distance and includes no intervention and no execution.

art.to_make_novel:
What already exists: every component has prior art. Distance-controlled source retrieval is in Scideator and InnoGPS (2210.10104, which also defines distance by a classification hierarchy rather than embeddings). The domain-stripped mechanism index is Kulikowski 2609.07595. Structure-mapping analogy is Shen AR 2605.11258. Cross-domain seeds against a random-diverse-seed control is PaperGym 2605.11532. Executed retrieval-augmented evolution is DeepEvolve and the autoresearch/nanoGPT loops. Manipulated source distance, judged only by ratings, is arXiv 2603.19087, which finds LLMs benefit only from remote sources. That last paper is missing from the proposal and directly bears on the H2 prediction. Its product-design, originality-rated result is a different task and outcome from executed training gains, so it is suggestive rather than contradictory.

What no located work does: treat source field distance as a manipulated, pre-registered independent variable with executed outcomes. None of them run a distance ladder (B1-B4) against paired-seed training results, with random-seed and free-synthesis controls and a check that a far graft has not collapsed into a known method after mapping. That combination, applied to LM training efficiency, is the novel contribution.

What would make it cleanly novel:
(1) Claim only the executed distance dose-response and the collapse-to-known correction as new, and credit the components to the works above.
(2) Keep the R and F arms exactly as specified, since PaperGym's null is the strongest threat.
(3) Make the Uzzi-profile-predicts-executed-gain test a primary, adequately powered analysis rather than an exploratory one; nothing found tests bibliometric atypicality on machine-generated ideas against executed outcomes.
(4) Add 2603.19087 and InnoGPS to the prior-art section and state H2 against their findings.

Caveat on search coverage: this session hit its shared cap of 200 web searches after about 8 searches of mine. I then used the arXiv API and fetched pages directly, but Semantic Scholar, GitHub and lab blogs were only partly covered. A closer 2026 match may exist, and a follow-up search with a higher budget is advisable before relying on the novelty claim.

feas.will_it_work:
It will partly work. The pipeline is buildable, but as specified it will probably not answer its own questions.

What should work:
- Every step can be built with current tools: domain-stripped skeletons as in Kulikowski (AP 0.557 for full fingerprints vs 0.222 for abstracts, on a single-author benchmark of 109 papers), a structure-mapping table, a one-facet diff, and a Claude Code implementation on a calibrated proxy.
- Making field distance an executed, controlled variable, with PaperGym's random-diverse-seed null and a free-synthesis arm, is the right test of IDEAS_FACTORY.md's central claim. PaperGym found that targeted cross-domain seeds were no better than random diverse seeds, but only under an LLM judge; this proposal would test that under execution.

Where it breaks mechanically:
1. **The incumbent R\* does not exist yet.** results holds only the 12-run M1 grid (1-epoch vs 4-epoch). The stacked, regularized recipe is SWARM.md Phase A (about $500), not yet run, and the 1.11x noise floor was measured on the 1-epoch M1 setup, not on a regularized multi-epoch core.
2. **Hits will be rare.** Against a tuned, stacked core, one-facet changes at 7M parameters and 1-4M tokens will rarely clear 1.11x. For comparison, most NanoGPT-speedrun records are a few percent each.
3. **The B1 arm is known by construction.** B1 skeletons come from the B1 corpus, which is the same corpus the collapse-to-known check searches. So B1 means "re-apply a recent known lever": higher hit rate, near-zero novelty value.
4. **Distance is confounded with implementability and with Opus's mapping quality.** B4 grafts will fail more often to implement, break the one-facet rule, or collapse to known. A B4 deficit would therefore not isolate the value of distance.
5. **The METR backtest adds almost nothing.** I checked the CSV (metr.org/assets/data/ai-rd-nanogpt-progress/classifications.csv): 22 Imported, 34 Adapted, 20 Invented. Every imported or adapted record comes from ML or systems/HPC (FlexAttention, QK-norm, reduce_scatter, Polar Express, Cautious Weight Decay), and Muon is labelled Invented. So there are about 0 B4 imports. The result will reflect what speedrunners read (an availability confound), in a wall-clock domain, with labels from a single analyst.
feas.eval_issues:
What is sound:
- The evaluation is non-circular: only executed outcomes count, with no LLM novelty or quality scores.
- Paired seeds, an 8-seed confirmation, a second independent implementation, tier-2 replication and a corpus frozen before the run are all good.
- These choices guard against Goodhart and contamination about as well as proxy work can.

What is broken is the statistics and the arm definitions.

1) **H1 is badly underpowered, and failing it triggers a kill.** I simulated the pre-registered rule (128 pooled graft ideas vs max(R,F) with 32 per arm; graft rate at least 2x control; Fisher one-sided p<0.1). Power to detect a true doubling:
- 3% vs 6%: 4%
- 5% vs 10%: 6%
- 2% vs 8%: 17%
- 5% vs 15%: 32%
- 10% vs 20%: 23%

So the H1 test will almost certainly "kill" the retrieval-and-mapping machinery even when it truly doubles the hit rate. A false kill of the factory's core hypothesis is the main hazard. Taking max(R,F) inflates the control further.

2) **H2 is also weak.** For 64 vs 64 ideas, power is 29% at 5% vs 10%, 61% at 5% vs 15% and 54% at 10% vs 20%.

3) **The screen will surface many noise candidates.** A one-sided p<0.1 screen on 192 ideas yields about 19 false candidates under the null. The confirmation step handles them, but its $60 budget covers only about 25 candidates.

4) **Relabeling collapsed ideas as B1 is an as-treated reassignment.** It biases the band comparison. The analysis must be intention-to-treat by the band that was sampled.

5) **Hit rate treats a re-applied known B1 lever the same as a novel B4 import.** The outcome is not value-weighted.

6) **Small-scale proxy error applies.** DataDecide (data-recipe choices only, up to 1B parameters) finds single small-scale rankings correct on about 80% of 1B pairwise calls. Fantastic Optimizers finds optimizer speedups shrink from 1.4x at 0.1B to 1.1x at 1.2B once the baseline is tuned. Far-band gains may be the most scale-fragile, and tier 2 only partly covers this.

7) **The Uzzi-profile analysis is exploratory with near-zero power.** The proposal says so honestly. Its premise comes from correlational citation data, not executed gains.
feas.cost_realistic:
The core estimate is roughly realistic but leaves items out. A realistic all-in figure is about $800-1,000, which still fits the under-$2k-per-POC budget.

What checks out:
- 576 proxy runs at about $0.25 each is plausible for a 7M-parameter model. Multi-epoch R\* multiplies the tokens per run, but runs stay minutes long on a rented GPU.
- $0.08 per idea to generate and $0.4 per idea to implement are plausible, and are largely absorbed by the Max subscription (with rate limits).

What is low or missing:
- **Index.** $35 for 2,000 skeletons is about $0.02 per paper, which means distilling from abstract-length input. Full-text distillation would cost several times more, though still well under $200.
- **Building R\*** (SWARM.md Phase A, about $300 of LLM plus about $200 of GPU) is not in the budget.
- **Confirmation** is budgeted at about 25 candidates, but about 19 false candidates are expected under the null, so more money is likely needed.
- Human audit time and the OpenAlex degree-preserving null computation are also not costed.

Steady state at $1.2-2.5 per executed graft is credible.
feas.biggest_risk:
The most likely outcome is either an inconclusive result or a false negative that wrongly kills the knowledge-base graft machinery.

- The binary confirmed-hit endpoint against a strong stacked core makes this likely: at realistic hit rates of 2-10%, the H1 test has only about 4-32% power.
- Distance is also confounded with implementability and mapping quality.
- The team would then drop the cross-domain knowledge base, which is the factory's main claimed point of difference, on evidence that cannot distinguish "no effect" from "no power".
feas.fix:
Replace the binary hit-rate kill rule with a continuous, intention-to-treat primary endpoint, and kill only on an equivalence bound.

1. **Primary endpoint.** Use each idea's paired log data-efficiency multiplier vs R\*, analysed by the band that was sampled, with implementation failures and collapsed ideas scored as 0 rather than relabelled. Fit an arm-level mixed model, and add a tail metric (the expected best of k ideas per arm, by bootstrap). The tail is what matters for a factory that promotes only its best.
2. **Kill rule.** Kill the graft machinery only if the upper confidence bound on (graft minus random-seed control) falls below a pre-set margin, not merely because p>0.1.
3. **Controls.** Compare against R and F separately, not max(R,F). Rebalance from 6 arms of 32 to about 48 ideas in each control arm, for example by merging B1 and B2.
4. **Weight by novelty.** Report "novel confirmed hits" (post-freeze collision check passed) as the value-weighted outcome, so B1 re-applications of known levers cannot win by construction.
5. **Order of work.** Run SWARM.md Phase A first so R\* exists. Re-measure the noise floor on R\* before fixing the sample sizes.
feas.general_factory_value:
Moderate to high.

What carries over to other domains:
- The domain-stripped skeleton index, the "tuned incumbent plus exactly one graft" operator, the band posterior with random-seed and free-synthesis controls, and the collapse-to-known check are all domain-agnostic.
- They plug into any domain pack that has an incumbent protocol with separable facets and an executable verifier (materials screening, forecasting models, solvers, assay protocols).
- The experiment answers the question that decides whether the "polymath knowledge base" is worth building at all: does structured cross-field import beat diverse seeds once ideas are executed? LLM-efficiency is the right cheap place to ask it.

What does not carry over:
- The distance-shape finding itself may be domain-specific. Luo & Evans report that gap-filling behaves differently in formal and design fields than elsewhere, and Shi & Evans found the premium for distant "expeditions" in MEDLINE but not in patents. So a B1/B2 win in ML efficiency should not set the default band for bio or materials packs. Each domain pack needs its own band posterior.
- The facet decomposition assumes a well-defined incumbent recipe, which open-ended domains may lack.

closest.title: CausalEvolve: Towards Open-Ended Discovery with Causal Scratchpad (Chen, Liu, Chen, Liu, Han, Zhang; arXiv 2603.14575, Mar 2026)
closest.overlap: The closest match, and it is missing from the proposal's own prior-art list. It is an AlphaEvolve/ShinkaEvolve-style evolve loop that detects 'surprise patterns' after the fact: sign inversions and significant shifts in the estimated treatment effects of solution factors. It then uses abductive reasoning to hypothesize new factors that 'better explain all the observed patterns', and those factors steer the next generation. So 'surprise -> abduction -> explanation seeds generation' already exists. Differences, checked against the HTML: (a) there is no pre-registered outcome forecast; surprise is measured against estimated causal effects, not against the model's own prediction. (b) It has no calibration step and no noise gate across seeds. (c) Hypotheses are not adjudicated by dedicated discriminating probes before use; they are 'suggested to evaluate in future experiments'. (d) The tasks are math and algorithm problems (Hadamard n=29, autocorrelation inequality, circle packing N=26, AIME), not ML-training efficiency. (e) Nothing is reserved for harness bugs.

closest.title: Model Discovery Agent: LLM-assisted Bayesian experiment design for data-efficient discovery of mechanistic world models (arXiv 2608.09696, Aug 2026; attributed to Kevin Murphy on alphaXiv, co-authors not verified)
closest.overlap: Very close on the prediction-failure -> abduction -> discriminating-experiment core. When the best model fails an out-of-sample predictive check, the LLM proposes new mechanisms. Experiments are then chosen by expected information gain to discriminate among competing models, and a posterior over model structures is kept with nested SMC. This is a more rigorous version of the proposal's steps 3-4 (EIG plus a full posterior rather than hand-designed probes and a heuristic posterior). The difference is the goal and domain. Its goal is to recover a mechanistic world model (physics, chemistry, NeuronBench biology), not to use verified laws to generate new efficiency interventions. Its 'forecast' is a fitted model's prediction, not an LLM's pre-registered effect forecast about its own ideas.

closest.title: Heuresis: Search Strategies for Autonomous AI Research Agents (Antoniades et al., arXiv 2606.25198, Jun 2026), Curiosity strategy
closest.overlap: The in-domain baseline, already cited by the proposal. On nanoGPT, the ideator emits y_hat before execution, surprise is |y - y_hat|/sigma_M, anchors are weighted by learning progress, and the operator is predict-then-improve. Verified from the HTML: no strategy asks why a prediction failed. The authors report that surprise is uncorrelated with quality (r = -0.11) and that 'the ideator's weak predictor turns prediction error into noise'. This supports the proposal's recalibration and noise-gate steps and leaves the 'why' step open in this domain.

closest.title: AutoDiscovery: Open-ended Scientific Discovery via Bayesian Surprise (Agarwal et al., arXiv 2507.00310, NeurIPS 2025)
closest.overlap: Measures surprise as the shift from the LLM's prior to its posterior belief after executed tests on 21 real datasets, and uses it as the MCTS reward. Surprise is the thing being maximized, not a trigger for explanation and then intervention generation. The proposal describes this correctly.

closest.title: The Little Scientist: LLM Agent-Driven Discovery via the Scientific Method (Travis Smith, arXiv 2608.16951, Aug 2026)
closest.overlap: The agent must predict each experiment's outcome in advance. A 'reconciliation' worksheet then makes it confront the gap between its prediction and the result, and that gap drives the next hypothesis. A separate Kuhn agent injects paradigm-shifting conjectures when progress plateaus. Domains are protein fitness (first on ProteinGym) and DNA motif discovery. This covers 'forecast -> mismatch -> explanation -> next idea' as a prompting workflow, without noise gating, calibration, competing explanations or discriminating probes.

closest.title: Popper: Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications (Huang, Jin, Li, Li, Candes, Leskovec; arXiv 2502.09858, Feb 2025)
closest.overlap: LLM agents design and run falsification experiments, with sequential testing and Type-I error control. This is prior art for 'hypotheses adjudicated by executed tests with code-owned statistics', which is the proposal's step 4 guard. It validates given hypotheses rather than generating them from surprises, and it does not feed survivors into an efficiency-idea generator.

closest.title: DeepScientist (Weng et al., arXiv 2509.26603, ICLR 2026)
closest.overlap: A 'hypothesize, verify, analyze' loop framed as Bayesian optimization, with a cumulative Findings Memory of all successes and failures that conditions later ideation, on frontier AI tasks. It overlaps with steps 5-6 (accumulated local findings re-conditioning the generator). It is performance-driven, not residual- or surprise-driven, and has no competing-explanation adjudication.

closest.title: HypoAgents (arXiv 2508.01746), Hypothesis Evolution Protocol (Takahara & Mizoguchi, arXiv 2607.09195), and HypoGeniC/HypoRefine
closest.overlap: General hypothesis-test-evidence-belief loops with Bayesian or entropy belief tracking (HEP in materials science; HypoAgents on ICLR research questions). They overlap with the law/scope/evidence bookkeeping and posterior updates, but none are triggered by calibrated forecast residuals or aimed at generating executed efficiency interventions.

art.to_make_novel: The core loop has been published. 'Surprise -> abductive hypotheses -> they steer the next generation' appears in CausalEvolve (Mar 2026). 'Prediction failure -> LLM proposes competing mechanisms -> EIG-chosen discriminating experiments -> posterior' appears in Model Discovery Agent (Aug 2026). Pre-execution forecasting with a mismatch-reconciliation step appears in The Little Scientist. So the proposal's why_novel claim that prior surprise-driven loops never ask WHY is false, and the proposal must cite CausalEvolve and MDA; its own prior-art note admits web search was exhausted before it looked beyond Heuresis. What remains defensible, and should be the stated contribution: (1) Surprise is computed against the LLM's own pre-registered, recalibrated effect forecasts, with a multi-seed noise gate. Heuresis shows that raw prediction error is noise (r = -0.11 with quality), and neither CausalEvolve nor MDA calibrates. (2) Competing explanations are adjudicated by executed discriminating probes before any idea is generated. CausalEvolve feeds unverified factors straight into evolution, so the S-vs-C arm comparison should add a 'CausalEvolve-style abduction without probes' arm; it is the real ablation that isolates the probe step. (3) An explicit harness-bug explanation class. (4) The first application to ML training data, compute and energy efficiency, with execution-only confirmation and novelty checked by collision against a frozen corpus. (5) Optional: adopt MDA's EIG probe selection instead of hand-designed probes, and credit it. Framed as 'calibrated, noise-gated, probe-verified abduction for ML-efficiency research, benchmarked against CausalEvolve and Heuresis-Curiosity', it is a legitimate incremental combination rather than a new paradigm. Caveat: the session-wide WebSearch cap (200 calls) was hit after 8 searches in this task, so the remaining coverage came from direct fetches and arXiv API queries. GitHub and lab blogs were not searched beyond Heuresis, which leaves some residual risk of unfound work.

feas.will_it_work:
Probably not as a generator of novel, winning ideas at proxy scale, though parts of it will pay off. The loop runs: forecast, recalibrate, find noise-gated residuals, write competing explanations, run discriminating probes, record a law, then seed new ideas from it. That loop only works if the forecaster's residuals are structured, meaning they point at real mechanisms the literature does not predict. The closest in-domain evidence says they are not. Heuresis (arXiv 2606.25198, nanoGPT val_bpb on ClimbMix, Gemini-3.1-Pro ideator) computes the same surprise, |y - y_hat| / sigma_M. The paper itself says prediction error became "noise rather than a refinement cue" because the LLM predictors were weak. SciPredict points the same way, though it covers natural-science outcome prediction rather than ML multipliers, so it only suggests the problem. Three mechanistic problems follow.

(1) Most residuals will come from forecaster ignorance, implementation bugs and dead interventions, not from anomalies. The 3-extra-seed gate removes seed noise only. A mis-implemented idea is deterministic, so it reproduces perfectly and passes the gate. So the kill condition "more than half of puzzles are harness bugs" is fairly likely to fire.

(2) Surprises are asymmetric. Most interventions land near 1.0x or hurt. Large reproducible residuals will mostly be negative breakages. Positive "why did this work better than expected" puzzles, the only ones that seed good ideas, will be rare among 100 ideas.

(3) Laws found on a 7M-parameter model trained on 1-4M BabyLM tokens are likely to be small-data or tokenizer artefacts. They may already be known in the BabyLM and small-data regularization literature. Tier-2 replication is correctly made mandatory.

Two things are likely to work: the pre-registered forecast ledger with recalibration, which yields a calibrated selector, and the reserved bug slot, which yields a harness-audit tool. Both are real dividends even if the novelty hypothesis fails. Heuresis also shows why selecting on surprise is risky: Curiosity scored 1.298 val_bpb vs Greedy's 0.957 on nanoGPT, and all 20 of its NS=2 ideas targeted residual-stream geometry. Novelty there was bought with quality, and "novel" was graded by an LLM agent on the Gupta & Pruthi rubric, not by an executed result.
feas.eval_issues:
Several design choices are good: blind forecasts, cross-fitted recalibration, code-owned statistics, no LLM novelty scores, human audit of hits, a replica control of Heuresis Curiosity (arm C), and pre-registered kill conditions. Five problems remain.

(a) Confounded arms. Only arm S's generator must propose ideas for which "literature retrieval finds no precedent". Arms C and P get "improve this" with no novelty filter. The headline metric counts novel hits, so S can win purely from the retrieval filter, with no help from abduction. The kill test (novel hits in S no greater than in C) is biased the same way. Every arm needs the same retrieval novelty filter, or an extra arm C+filter.

(b) Severely underpowered. At a matched 150 runs, S gets only about 28 ideas (64 runs go to probes) vs 50 for C and P. Novel confirmed hits per arm will realistically be 0-3, given Heuresis's frontier and Prime Intellect's result that the novelty-gated phase could not improve the baseline. A Poisson comparison of such counts against "S >= P+2" has little power and a non-trivial false-positive rate. The proposal concedes it detects only a large effect, but the rule is still likely to return noise.

(c) Probes are underpowered. They get 1-2 runs each (about 2 per explanation), while the proxy needs 3 seeds just to detect 1.11x (pooled seed sd 0.015 held-out loss). A posterior above 0.6 will then mostly reflect Opus's prior. The mechanism check ("50% of probes confirm the explanation predicted to win, vs 25% chance") is partly circular: Opus both designs the probes and predicts which explanation wins, and the 25% baseline assumes explanations are equally likely and truly exclusive.

(d) Winner's curse in the noise gate. Taking the top 12 by |z| and then judging "still |z| > 2" on the pooled 6 seeds carries the selection bias forward. The z-score has to be recomputed on the fresh seeds only.

(e) Multiple comparisons. Diagnostic-signature mismatches across per-bucket losses (rare vs frequent tokens, CHILDES vs BNC, early vs late training) and across gradient or curve shape need a correction, or noise will manufacture "puzzles".

Two things are sound. Contamination risk is low, since the forecasts are blind. Goodhart resistance is reasonable, since no LLM grades anything.

Several cited numbers come from other tasks and are weak support here:
- AutoDiscovery's 0.67 is crowd-rated surprise from Prolific STEM annotators.
- Theorizer's 61% vs 34% is LLM-judged support.
- The 0.56x shrinkage from Hewitt/Ashokkumar is GPT-4 simulating survey treatment effects in social science. It does not transfer to Opus forecasting ML data-efficiency multipliers.
- The METR 33% figure is irrelevant.
feas.biggest_risk: The residuals are forecaster noise plus deterministic implementation or harness bugs, not mechanistic anomalies. Heuresis already reported that LLM prediction error in the same kind of loop is "noise rather than a refinement cue". If so, too few genuine positive puzzles survive, the probes are too weak to separate the explanations, and the laws that come out are proxy-scale artefacts. The loop would then produce well-documented bug reports and small-data folklore rather than novel efficiency ideas.
feas.fix: Make puzzle status depend on a second, independent implementation reproducing the residual, not just extra seeds, and keep only positive-sign surprises for the idea-seeding path. Negative ones go to the harness-audit queue. At the same time, give every arm the same literature-no-precedent filter and power the probes at 3 or more fresh seeds (paired seeds) each. Pay for this by cutting the 8 puzzles to the 4-5 best. Together these remove deterministic bugs from the puzzle pool, stop the novelty-filter confound, and make the posterior mean something.
feas.general_factory_value:
Moderate, and higher for its by-products than for its headline claim.

Domain-general parts:
- The pre-registered forecast ledger with calibration tracking plugs straight into the factory's outcome ledger and gives it a calibrated selector or abstain signal in any domain.
- Code-owned statistics in place of self-graded analysis addresses the analysis-layer inflation seen in Robin: its agent reported 7.5-fold, human re-analysis found 1.75-fold on the same data.
- The reserved bug explanation class works as a harness audit for every domain pack.

Where the full loop can work: it needs a cheap, repeatable, high-throughput verifier with a known noise model. That covers ML proxies and simulation-verified packs such as DFT or docking screens, solver and compiler benchmarks, and computational maths checks. It is weak in the high-value slow-verifier domains, like wet-lab, prizes and grants, where OptiLex wants money quickly: there, too few executed outcomes exist to yield noise-gated puzzles.

The first experiment tests only the LM-training calibration domain. A win would not show the abduction step transfers.

closest.title: LLaMEA-HPO: In-the-loop Hyper-Parameter Optimization for LLM-Based Automated Design of Heuristics (van Stein, Vermetten, Baeck, 2024)
closest.overlap: Closest match to mechanism steps 2-3 (verified from the HTML). The LLM outputs each candidate algorithm together with its own configuration space, which corresponds to the proposal's 'cheap call names idea-specific knobs'. SMAC then tunes every generated candidate, and the tuned score is fed back as fitness inside the evolutionary loop. Selection on tuned rather than first-shot performance, with per-idea knobs, therefore already exists in LLM-driven algorithm discovery. Differences: the domain is combinatorial and black-box heuristics, not ML training-recipe research. It has no expected-max tuning curve or UCB on a tuned gap, no novelty-scaled tuning budget, no separate re-tuning of an incumbent or co-adaptation model, no clade credit and no headroom predictor.

closest.title: LLM-Driven Evolutionary Generation of Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization Algorithms (Laskaris, van Stein, Baeck et al., 2026)
closest.overlap: Same lab, 2026: SMAC hyperparameter optimization runs inside the LLM-evolution loop for every generated candidate (abstract verified). This confirms in-loop per-candidate tuning as an active pattern in 2026. It shares LLaMEA-HPO's gaps: no novelty subsidy, no expected-max selection, no lineage credit, and not ML research ideas.

closest.title: irace-evo: Automatic Algorithm Configuration Extended With LLM-Based Code Evolution (2025)
closest.overlap: Jointly explores parameter space (irace racing, which is successive-elimination style) and LLM code edits. It is close to an 'idea-level racing ladder' over code variants. The abstract does not say whether each variant is raced separately before comparison (not verified beyond the abstract). The domain is algorithm configuration, not research-idea search.

closest.title: Beyond the Node: Clade-level Selection for Efficient MCTS in Automatic Heuristic Design (Clade-AHD, 2026)
closest.overlap: Applies HGM-style clade credit (descendant evaluations aggregated into Beta posteriors, Thompson sampling for parent selection) to LLM-driven algorithm/heuristic discovery, not only to coding-agent self-modification (abstract verified). This undercuts the proposal's claim that clade credit is applied to idea lineages 'for the first time'. What remains new is applying it to ML-research idea lineages scored on tuned results.

closest.title: Huxley-Godel Machine (Clade-Metaproductivity), 2025
closest.overlap: Source of component 6: Thompson-sampled Clade-Metaproductivity for parent selection. It covers self-modifying coding agents only. The Semantic Scholar citation list (about 40 citers) shows no follow-up applying CMP to research-idea search, apart from Clade-AHD for heuristics.

closest.title: Heuresis: Search Strategies for Autonomous AI Research Agents (2026)
closest.overlap: States the problem explicitly: 'under-optimization on first attempt is a property of novelty itself'. It names predicting expected quality after further optimization as future work, and all six of its strategies select on a single first execution (verified). It motivates the proposal but provides no mechanism.

closest.title: Symbolic Discovery of Optimization Algorithms (Lion; Chen et al., 2023)
closest.overlap: Program search for ML training algorithms, verified from the PDF. Hyperparameters are mutable constants that evolve with each program, so tuning is folded into the search rather than done by a per-candidate ladder. The AdamW incumbent was given a 4x-compute tuning baseline, and funnel selection is a multi-fidelity promotion ladder on meta-validation tasks. This is partial prior art for 'tune the incumbent' and 'staged-fidelity promotion', but not for equal per-idea ladders or novelty subsidies.

closest.title: Show Your Work (Dodge et al., 2019), Show Your Work with Confidence (Tang et al., 2023), and Optimizer Benchmarking Needs to Account for Hyperparameter Tuning (Sivaprasad et al., 2020)
closest.overlap: Expected-max performance vs tuning budget, confidence bands on those curves, and 'tunability' as a comparison criterion. All three are reporting or evaluation protocols, not a selection signal inside a generative search loop. Tang et al. 2023 (arXiv 2311.09480) already gives the interval estimate the proposal plans to bootstrap. The Sivaprasad citation is from memory and was not re-verified this session.

closest.title: Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them (Wen et al., 2025), plus the fair-baseline tuning literature (e.g. Tune It or Don't Use It, 2108.13122; HPO Is Deceiving Us, 2102.03034)
closest.overlap: Establishes that unequal tuning flips conclusions and that baselines must be tuned with a matched budget. This is the equal-tuning principle, used as an evaluation protocol rather than an in-loop selection mechanism.

closest.title: AI Scientist-v2 (Sakana, 2025); Recovering Wasted Compute in Autoresearch Agents (2026)
closest.overlap: AI Scientist-v2 has an explicit 'hyperparameter tuning' stage, but it tunes the baseline before tree search, not each idea with an equal ladder. The 2026 wasted-compute paper documents that autoresearch agents 'often fail to tune hyperparameters' even with budget left, which supports the gap. Its fixes are agent and prompt design, not equal-tuning selection.

closest.title: AutoLLMResearch: Learning from Cheap, Optimizing Expensive (2026), and learning-curve extrapolation (Domhan et al. 2015; LC-PFN)
closest.overlap: Prior art for component 7 (the headroom predictor). Agents learn from low-fidelity runs and extrapolate to expensive configurations, and learning-curve extrapolation predicts final performance from early rungs. Neither targets an idea-level 'tuned gap vs a re-tuned incumbent' trained on the search engine's own ladders.

art.to_make_novel: The building blocks all exist separately: in-loop per-candidate HPO with LLM-named knobs (LLaMEA-HPO, LLaMEA-MOBO, irace-evo), clade credit in LLM algorithm discovery (HGM, Clade-AHD), expected-max tuning curves with confidence bands (Dodge, Tang), equal-tuning evaluation (Fantastic Optimizers, Lion's tuned AdamW baseline), and cheap-to-expensive extrapolation (AutoLLMResearch, LC extrapolation). Do not claim 'first in-loop tuning' or 'first clade credit on idea lineages'. The defensible novelty lies in three places. (1) The co-adaptation bias model: the incumbent is re-tuned with the same ladder, the tuning budget is scaled by an idea's distance from the incumbent's mechanism family, and there is a pre-registered test of whether rescue rates differ between novel ideas and known recipes. No found work measures or corrects this; Heuresis names it as future work. (2) Selection on a UCB of the expected-max tuned gap vs a re-tuned incumbent inside ML-research idea search (as opposed to heuristic-design search, where LLaMEA-HPO simply uses the tuned max). (3) An idea-level headroom predictor trained on the engine's own ladders, charged against compute and energy on the joint frontier. The first experiment ('does equal tuning reorder ideas?', including the novel-vs-known rescue asymmetry) appears unrun for ML training-recipe ideas and is the most publishable, lowest-cost piece. The proposal should cite LLaMEA-HPO and Clade-AHD as the direct precedents and position clade credit as a transfer to ML-research lineages scored on tuned, test-split results.

feas.will_it_work:
Partly. The core premise holds up mechanistically. Hyperparameters co-adapt with the incumbent, and optimal learning rate and weight decay shift when a method changes the data mix, the objective or the number of epochs. Equal tuning is also known to reverse conclusions. In Wen et al., Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers (arXiv 2509.02046), claimed 1.4-2x optimizer speedups fall to 1.4x at 0.1B and 1.1x at 1.2B parameters once AdamW is tuned properly. That study measured the opposite bias (under-tuned baselines), but the symmetry argument is fair.

Heuresis (arXiv 2606.25198, section 5.1) does say that "under-optimization on first attempt is a property of novelty itself". Section 5.1/6.1 names a signal of "expected quality after additional optimization" as the missing capability. I checked this against the paper's HTML. It is a hypothesis in that paper, not a measured effect, so the proposal rests on a stated rationale rather than evidence that rescues exist.

Three mechanistic reasons to expect a modest payoff:
1. Implementation choice dominates the variance the ladder cannot touch. The Implementation Lottery (arXiv 2607.26587, 13 tabular tasks) finds implementation explains 33-45% of within-task variance, against 4-6% for same-artifact reruns. A 3x3 hyperparameter grid does not fix a weak implementation.
2. For data-efficiency ideas, running a rung at 1/3 budget is not neutral. The effect of the idea interacts with the data and token budget, which is exactly what is being measured. Wen et al. also show that rankings flip before learning-rate decay finishes, so the successive-halving promotions can be systematically wrong.
3. The Heuresis data are equally consistent with novel ideas simply being weak (0 of 3,222 runs rated "Original"; 1 novel idea in the top 10). The rescue rate may be close to zero.

The expected-max curve (Dodge et al. 2019) extrapolated from 3 trials, the Clade-Metaproductivity (CMP) credit and the headroom predictor all sit on top of this uncertain base. The HGM result behind CMP is 60-task SWE-Verified-60 subsets, single runs, coding agents only (Pearson 0.778 vs 0.285 on SWE-Verified-60). The predictor will have fewer than 100 labelled ladders for a long time.

Novelty claim is overstated. It misses the closest prior art: AutoML's CASH problem (combined algorithm selection and hyperparameter optimization; Auto-WEKA, auto-sklearn, BOHB). CASH already treats "which method" as a variable, gives each method its own tuning budget, and races methods with successive halving. It also misses learning-curve extrapolation (freeze-thaw BO, LC-PFN), which is what the headroom predictor is. What is genuinely new is putting this inside an LLM idea-search loop, adding a subsidy that grows with novelty, and applying lineage credit to research ideas.

The question it asks, whether first-shot selection mis-ranks ideas at the proxy, is worth $250 to answer. The full engine (subsidy, clade credit, predictor) is unlikely to repay its 7-20x compute multiplier unless the first experiment shows large rescue rates.
feas.eval_issues:
1. No noise ceiling, so the proceed rule is nearly guaranteed. The first shot is a single seed. Proxy seed sd is 0.015 nats (FEASIBILITY.md, 7M model on M1). A 1.11x multiplier is only about 0.045 nats, so it is about 2 sd of a single-run difference. Seed noise alone will push the Spearman correlation between first-shot and tuned multipliers below 1. For a plausible spread of true effects, my back-of-envelope ceiling is about 0.8-0.9. So criterion (a), Spearman below 0.7, can be met by noise with no tuning effect at all.

2. False wins are confounded with regression to the mean. A single-seed win of 1.11x or more will often shrink at 5 seeds even against the un-retuned incumbent. The protocol never separates "vanished because of re-seeding" from "vanished because the incumbent was re-tuned". It needs an arm that re-seeds without tuning.

3. The kill criterion is practically unreachable. Killing requires all three of: Spearman of 0.85 or more (near or above the noise ceiling), zero rescues, and false wins under 10%. The pre-registration is asymmetric toward continuing.

4. The held-out selection/test split only removes eval-sample noise. Seed noise is shared across the two splits because the same trained model is scored on both. What actually protects against the winner's curse is re-confirming at 3 fresh seeds, which is good. Picking the best of 9 configurations at 2 seeds still inflates the UCB/headroom score used for selection.

5. There is no matched-compute control. Giving each idea 21 runs of any kind, such as 3 re-implementations or more seeds, might rescue as many ideas as tuning does. The Implementation Lottery says implementation variance is larger than hyperparameter variance, so this control is essential.

6. The novel-vs-known comparison, test (d), is heavily underpowered: 20 novel vs 10 known ideas, with rescues expected at 0-3. Most outcomes will not be statistically distinguishable.

7. The clade-credit test is one lineage search per arm, and success is judged on the best confirmed multiplier. That is n=1 per arm, essentially a coin flip. The HGM evidence it cites has the same single-run weakness.

8. The confounds and Goodhart risk are otherwise handled reasonably: prospective scoring of the predictor, charging ladder compute to each idea, re-tuning at scale rather than transferring hyperparameters, and a hacker-fixer audit. Contamination is not an issue for executed loss.
feas.biggest_risk: The first experiment cannot distinguish tuning headroom from seed noise and implementation variance. With single-seed first shots, no test-retest ceiling, no matched-compute re-seed or re-implement arm, and a kill rule that is nearly impossible to trigger, it will almost certainly report "proceed". That would commit OptiLex to a steady-state 7-20x GPU multiplier per promoted idea, about $40-120 a day, which works against its own compute-and-energy efficiency goal, on the strength of what may be noise.
feas.fix:
Add a matched-compute control with a noise ceiling to the $250 experiment. For every idea and for the incumbent:
- Run a second, independent 3-seed first shot at the incumbent's hyperparameters, with no tuning. This gives a test-retest Spearman and a regression-to-the-mean baseline for false wins.
- Spend the same roughly 21-run budget on 2 fresh re-implementations plus seeds, with no tuning.

Then pre-register the proceed criteria relative to these controls. Tuning must reorder ideas beyond the test-retest ceiling, and it must rescue more ideas than the re-implementation arm at equal compute.

Rebalance the kill criterion so it can actually fire. For example: kill if tuned-vs-first-shot Spearman is within 0.05 of the test-retest ceiling, or if tuning's rescues are no more than the re-implementation arm's.

This costs roughly an extra $100-150 and turns an experiment that confirms itself into one that is actually informative. It also decides whether the factory's generic "second-chance" budget should go to tuning or to re-implementation, which is a design choice that applies across domains.
feas.general_factory_value:
Low-to-moderate. The general principle carries across domains: compare candidates at equal optimization effort, give novel candidates a second chance before discarding them, credit stepping stones by what their descendants achieve, and learn a first-attempt-to-final-result predictor from the outcome ledger. It applies to any computational domain pack whose candidates have free parameters and a cheap verifier, for example heuristic and solver design, kernel or compiler tuning, simulation-based materials screening, and prize problems with executable scoring. Clade credit and the headroom predictor are domain-agnostic components of the engine.

However, the 7-20x evaluation multiplier makes the method unaffordable exactly where the factory wants to make money: prizes, bounties, licensing and grants, where verification is expensive or slow (wet lab, expert review, long simulations). The first experiment is entirely inside the LLM-training calibration domain, and its answer, whether proxy first-shot rankings are wrong, may not transfer to other verifiers.

Its real general value is as a cheap calibration study that decides the engine's second-chance policy. As a standing engine component it is mostly useful for cheap-verifier domains.
feas.cost_realistic:
Roughly realistic for the GPU runs, but it leaves out prerequisites. SWARM.md estimates tier 1 at 0.1-0.3 H100-hours per idea, about $0.03-0.09 per single run at $2.69/h. So 650 runs at the proposal's roughly $0.25 per run is plausible and even conservative, although tier-1 GPU cost has not been measured yet because the Phase 0 CUDA port has not happened.

What is not in the $200-250:
1. The 30 "already-implemented" ideas do not exist. The repo has only generated ideas in factory_pilot/ideas.jsonl, no implementations. IDEAS_FACTORY.md estimates about $30-45 of LLM spend per 20-30 implementations, plus $15 for the knob-parametrization edits, which is likely too low.
2. A meaningful incumbent needs the stacked baseline from Phase A, about $500. Against the 1-epoch pilot baseline, repetition alone gives a 3.4x "free" win and tuning results would be meaningless.
3. My recommended controls add about $100-150.

Realistic total for an informative first experiment: about $350-450 on top of Phase 0/A. The clade follow-up at $400-800 is affordable but, as designed, statistically uninformative. The steady-state $40-120 a day is the real cost concern.

closest.title: NewtonBench: Benchmarking Generalizable Scientific Law Discovery in LLM Agents (arXiv 2510.07172, Oct 2025)
closest.overlap: This is the closest match on the design principle. It generates 324 memorization-resistant discovery tasks through 'counterfactual law shifts' (systematically altered canonical laws), and agents must probe simulated systems interactively to recover the hidden law. That is the same logic as PMW's 'the answer exists in no literature, so success is not recall', plus scalable procedural generation. The difference is the domain: physics law fitting, not a training-efficiency intervention in a neural-network training run. It also has no measured headroom multiplier, no null tasks and no enumerative-library control.

closest.title: Propose, Don't Judge: An Anytime-Valid Referee for LLM Agents That Mine Investment Factors (arXiv 2609.27051, 22 Sep 2026)
closest.overlap: Already covers PMW's evaluation layer: a synthetic world with planted true factors, a frozen referee the agent cannot touch, false-discovery control by betting (e-values) at every stopping time, and a scripted/bandit proposer compared against the LLM. The domain is finance factors, not LM training. PMW's steps 5 and 6 (frozen e-value gate, false-discovery rate on null worlds) are a port of this, which the proposal already acknowledges.

closest.title: Library Reachability in LSR-Synth (arXiv 2607.28684, Jul 2026) and Dictionaries, Not Darwin (arXiv 2607.04108, Jul 2026)
closest.overlap: These supply PMW's 'mandatory enumerative-library control'. A semantics-free fixed vocabulary is run under matched budget to test whether planted anti-memorization tasks actually require LLM priors. They find the library covers most LSR-Synth tasks. PMW's NEAR/ALIEN label is this idea turned into a construction-time filter. That is a new use of it, but not a new idea.

closest.title: DiscoveryWorld (2406.06769), BoxingGym (2501.01540), SciGym systems-biology dry lab (2507.02083), DiscoveryBench synthetic split (2407.01725)
closest.overlap: Planted-truth discovery gyms. Agents run experiments against a hidden generative model: 120 parametric text-simulation tasks, 10 generative-model environments, 350 SBML biological systems, and 903 synthetic tasks with planted hypotheses. Scoring is by recovery of the hidden structure, which corresponds to PMW's structure-identification ARI. None of them plants the structure in the data-generating process of an actual neural-network training run or scores a realized training-efficiency multiplier.

closest.title: AuditBench (arXiv 2602.22755, Feb 2026), Auditing LMs for hidden objectives (2503.10965), InterpBench (2407.14494)
closest.overlap: Nearest precedent for planting a known truth inside trained neural networks and then scoring an investigator agent on recovering it: 56 models with implanted hidden behaviors in AuditBench, and transformers with known circuits in InterpBench. This undercuts PMW's claim that no prior work plants the answer in a neural-network training setting. It does not undercut the narrower claim: in those works the target is a behavior or circuit, not a data-efficiency intervention with known headroom.

closest.title: Automated LLM Speedrunning Benchmark (2506.22419), Progress over Points / NanoGPT-speedrun environment (2512.11183), 1GC-7RC (2605.17046), MLGym (2502.14499), MLRC-Bench (2504.09702), NanoGPT-Bench
closest.overlap: Same target capability and harness shape as PMW: agents edit a training script under a fixed compute budget and are scored on loss or efficiency by execution. MLRC-Bench explicitly separates LLM-judged innovation from measured performance. All of these use real tasks with unknown or public optima, so they cannot separate recall from invention and they are contaminable. That is the gap PMW targets.

closest.title: SynthWorlds (arXiv 2510.24427) and gg-bench (arXiv 2505.07215)
closest.overlap: SynthWorlds builds parallel real-mapped and synthetic-mapped worlds to measure a 'knowledge advantage gap', which is the recall-vs-reasoning separation PMW's NEAR/ALIEN split is after. gg-bench is a benchmark that is itself a data-generating process with fresh instances on demand, which is PMW's 'infinite procedural refresh'. Neither is about ML research.

closest.title: MAD: Mechanistic Design and Scaling of Hybrid Architectures (2403.17844) and Skill-it! (2307.14430)
closest.overlap: Precedents for PMW's substrate and validity bridge. MAD uses synthetic token tasks as proxies for architecture discovery and validates them against real scaling laws (the same move as PMW's Spearman >= 0.6 gate). Skill-it plants compositional skill dependencies in synthetic LM training data and shows that ordered data yields data-efficiency gains, which is essentially PMW's 'compositional skill dependency' primitive. Neither is used as an agent benchmark.

closest.title: Classical automated solvers for PMW primitives: Augerino (2010.11882), LieGAN (2302.00236), OpenDataVal planted-noise data valuation (2306.10577)
closest.overlap: Not benchmarks, but they bear on the ALIEN label. Learned-invariance and symmetry-discovery methods automatically recover hidden augmentation groups (the orbit-symmetry primitive). Data-valuation benchmarks plant corrupted or noisy sources and score detection (the latent clean-source primitive). Unsupervised segmentation such as BPE or Morfessor targets the hidden-segmentation primitive. A world that beats the proposed 40-intervention library can still sit squarely inside the published literature.

art.to_make_novel:
Nothing found combines three things: planted structure in the data-generating process of a real LM training run; per-world, execution-measured effective-data multiplier headroom (1.3-3x) used as the score; and an execution-defined NEAR/ALIEN/NULL distance label. That combination is the defensible novelty. Almost every other element has direct precedent: counterfactual or anti-memorization task generation (NewtonBench, LSR-Synth, SynthWorlds), procedural refresh (gg-bench), planted-truth discovery gyms (DiscoveryWorld, BoxingGym, SciGym), a frozen anytime-valid e-value referee on planted synthetic worlds with scripted/bandit baselines (2609.27051, POPPER 2502.09858), the fixed-library control (2607.28684, 2607.04108), planting truth in trained networks for investigator agents (AuditBench, InterpBench), and synthetic-proxy-to-real validation (MAD). To keep the novelty claim honest:
(1) Stop claiming the oracle interventions 'exist in no literature'. The primitives map onto known method families: learned invariance/symmetry discovery, data valuation and mixture reweighting, unsupervised segmentation, and skill curricula (Skill-it). What is novel is the specific instance, not the intervention class.
(2) Define ALIEN against a library that includes these classical automated solvers (for example Augerino/LieGAN-style augmentation search, clustering plus DoReMi- or data-valuation-style reweighting, BPE/Morfessor re-segmentation), not only ~40 generic interventions. Otherwise ALIEN measures distance to a hand-picked library rather than distance to the literature, and the recall-vs-invention split is not established.
(3) Make the headroom-multiplier score and the external-validity gate (alien-world HR vs real post-cutoff gains) the headline contribution. That link to real training-efficiency progress is the part no found benchmark has.
(4) Add composed or held-out primitive families so that alien worlds need interventions outside any single known method family. Otherwise a strong agent could solve them by recognizing the family.
Search caveat: the WebSearch budget was already exhausted, DuckDuckGo returned a CAPTCHA (not bypassed), and Semantic Scholar was rate-limited. Coverage therefore comes from roughly 30 arXiv API queries, arXiv abstract pages, OpenAlex, and GitHub repository search. Google Scholar-style and lab-blog coverage is thin, so 'not found' means 'not found by these channels'.

feas.will_it_work:
Partly. It will very likely produce a working gym: worlds that pass acceptance and an execution-only score. It will probably not measure what it claims to measure, which is invention as opposed to recall. There are five mechanistic problems.

(1) The planted intervention classes are textbook: symmetry augmentation, clean-source reweighting, re-segmentation or tokenization, and channel inversion. Only the secret parameters are new. So an ALIEN world means "a 40-item library with no structure-identification step fails". It does not mean "unknown to the literature". What gets scored is exploratory data analysis and system identification on a synthetic corpus (find the orbit partition, find the clean source), picked from a menu the designers wrote. Opus 5.5, handed a corpus and told to improve data efficiency, will do exactly this. The likely outcomes are bimodal: a ceiling when the structure is statistically detectable, and a floor when it is not. That is the failure mode the kill criteria anticipate.

(2) The claim of "known headroom" is wrong. I* is a lower bound on the achievable gain, not the optimum. For a small PCFG or HMM with a 2-4k vocabulary, the dominant strategy is to fit the generator (EM or spectral HMM, or grammar induction), then sample unlimited synthetic data or distill from it. That can push HR well above 1 on every world, including NULL worlds. So "M* = 1 by construction" on null worlds is false. A real gain there is not a false discovery, which makes the null-world FDR metric ill-posed as written.

(3) The noise-floor evidence does not carry over. The proxy's 1.11x MDE (3 seeds; 1.07x with 5) was calibrated in FEASIBILITY.md on natural text: 6.9M params, 8k BPE, 16.9M tokens from 6 sources. A synthetic PCFG/HMM with a 2-4k vocabulary has different loss variance and saturates at a known entropy floor, so the MDE must be re-measured per world family.

(4) The re-segmentation worlds change the loss units. Scoring has to be in bits per underlying symbol, otherwise patches can game the loss through tokenization.

(5) Patches can change epochs, model size or compute. "Data-efficiency multiplier" needs a hard compute cap in the frozen evaluator, or the gains are not comparable.
feas.eval_issues:
Non-circularity is only partial. The same team designs the primitive grammar and the engine, and the ALIEN label is set against a deliberately weak library. With no structure-inference baseline, ALIEN can be manufactured.

Goodhart: generator-fitting and distillation exploits (see will_it_work). Tokenization-unit gaming. Compute not held fixed. Structural overfitting to a small family grammar; the held-out-family mitigation is only promised.

The null-world design conflates "false structure claim" with "real generic gain". FDR should be scored on DSL structure claims, not on loss gains.

Power, at stated n. I assumed a per-world log-multiplier SE of about 0.03 at 5 seeds, back-derived from the 1.07x MDE on natural text (valid only if it carries over to synthetic data). On that assumption, a world with M* = 1.3 (log M* = 0.26) has a per-world HR SE of roughly 0.15. Averaged over only 6 alien worlds, and with between-world heterogeneity probably dominating, the pre-registered contrasts of 0.20-0.25 HR sit at about 1-1.5 SE. Instrument criteria (2) and (3) can therefore pass or fail by chance.

The e-value gate risks the opposite failure. Anytime-valid betting tests are conservative: in arXiv 2609.27051, approved true factors were delayed about 500 days. With only 5 fresh seeds it may never admit even I* on 1.3x worlds, so criterion (4) passes trivially. The proposal needs a power check of the gate on oracle submissions.

The external-validity gate is unpowered. For Spearman >= 0.6 across 5 harness variants, the exact permutation probability under zero true correlation is 21/120 = 17.5%. It also inherits all of CHSP's own noise and depends on CHSP existing.

Internal cost inconsistency: best-of-40 library interventions at 5 paired seeds needs about 200 runs per candidate world, not the stated about 24.

Contamination-free-by-refresh holds for the world instances, but not for the family grammar once it is published or reused.
feas.biggest_risk: Construct validity. PMW rewards finding a designer-planted, statistically detectable structure in a toy corpus and then applying a textbook intervention; it does not reward generating a new idea. So HR on "alien" worlds may have little relation to the factory's real bottleneck, which is fundamentally new methods. The evidence for that bottleneck is Heuresis (0 of 3,222 executed runs rated Original), Prime Intellect's "no fundamentally new method" result, and NanoGPT-Bench, where agents recovered 9.3% of human progress. The gym is also highly exposed to a generic fit-the-generator exploit. Optimising the engine against PMW (Goodhart) would then tune it toward synthetic-data detective work and generator-fitting tricks that do not exist for natural text, let alone for non-ML domains. The validity bridge that is meant to catch this is itself unpowered (17.5% chance pass under zero true correlation).
feas.fix:
Replace the weak enumerative library with a strong automated baseline, and anchor headroom to the true Bayes floor.

(a) For every world, compute the exact entropy rate or held-out cross-entropy of P. This is tractable for HMMs and PCFGs. Score gap-closed toward that floor, and hold compute fixed, rather than using the "known" M* of a designer-chosen I*.

(b) Make the ALIEN label require that BOTH the 40-item library AND a scripted structure-inference pipeline fail to recover more than 20% of the headroom. That pipeline would include invariance/co-occurrence probes, mixture/cluster fits, generator fitting plus synthetic sampling, and entropy-based segmentation.

(c) Score null worlds on false DSL structure claims, not on loss gains.

(d) Hold out whole primitive families for every test round.

This converts "beats a dumb library" into "beats competent automated EDA", which is the only version where alien-world success could plausibly indicate invention. It also closes the generator-fitting Goodhart path. Run it before spending on agent campaigns: if competent automated EDA already solves most worlds (the LSR-Synth lesson), stop at about $100 instead of about $400.
feas.cost_realistic:
Dollar cost is roughly right in order of magnitude for the GPU. It is materially understated for world construction and engineering.

GPU: 7M-param runs on 1-4M tokens take about 8 minutes on the M1 (FEASIBILITY.md) and seconds to a minute on a rented GPU. $0.013-0.08 per run is plausible but unmeasured.

World construction: best-of-40 library at 5 seeds is about 200 runs per candidate; add 3-budget curve fits and proxy recalibration on synthetic data. Across about 25 candidates that is roughly 5-6k runs, not about 850, so about $70-450 of GPU for construction alone.

Agent campaigns: at API prices, headless Claude Code campaigns with corpus analysis plus 20 training runs are more likely $10-40 each than $6. Under Claude Max this becomes a rate-limit and time cost rather than cash.

Engineering: "$40 to build the generator" ignores the real cost. That includes 3 primitive families with guaranteed P-invariance, a separate-machine secret store and sandbox, a claim DSL with a matcher, a frozen e-value evaluator, and per-world headroom validation, which I estimate at 1-3 weeks of engineer-plus-Claude time.

Realistic first experiment: about $500-900 cash plus 1-3 weeks. The full 60-world library plus 5 harness comparisons: about $3-5k. That exceeds the roughly $2k-per-POC envelope for an instrument that produces no sellable idea itself.

closest.title: Towards Execution-Grounded Automated AI Research (Si, Hashimoto et al., arXiv 2601.14525, ICLR/ICML 2026)
closest.overlap: This is the closest in mechanism. An automated executor turns natural-language ideas into code and runs them on nanoGPT pretraining and GRPO post-training environments, then reports each idea's benchmark score. Humans enter only as reference numbers from the nanoGPT speedrun leaderboard and the Stanford CS336 class leaderboard. Human ideas are not run through the same executor, there is no source blinding and no equal tuning budget, and it does not say whether any idea gets more than one implementation. It is an asymmetric comparison with a human ceiling, not a human control arm.

closest.title: The Ideation-Execution Gap (Si, Hashimoto, Yang, arXiv 2506.20803, ICLR 2026)
closest.overlap: This is the closest in design: a randomized, blind comparison of LLM-written and expert-written ideas, each actually executed and then reviewed. It differs from CHSP in four ways. The ideas were commissioned, not drawn from a natural post-cutoff stream. Humans executed them at about 100 h per idea. Outcomes are review scores after execution, not an automated metric. And it was a one-off NLP-prompting study with no replication across implementations and no frozen critic ledger.

closest.title: NanoGPT-Bench (Intology) and The Automated LLM Speedrunning Benchmark (arXiv 2506.22419); METR note on AI R&D progress from NanoGPT (Apr 2026)
closest.overlap: Both use later human speedrun records as ground truth, scoring agents on how much of the human progress they recover or reproduce. That is a match-target, conformity-rewarding design, which CHSP explicitly argues against. METR classified human and agent contributions to the speedrun but did not re-execute human ideas under a shared protocol.

closest.title: MLRC-Bench (arXiv 2504.09702, NeurIPS 2025 D&B)
closest.overlap: Agents propose and implement ideas on recent competition tasks. They are scored against a baseline and the top human solution, and the benchmark reports that judged innovativeness is uncorrelated with effectiveness. The human side is a single top leaderboard number, not a sampled distribution of human ideas re-executed by the same agent.

closest.title: HindSight (arXiv 2603.15164) and Reconstruction (arXiv 2608.16645, Aug 2026)
closest.overlap: Both use time splits: generated ideas are matched, by embedding or by an LLM judge, against papers published after a cutoff. Reconstruction uses papers first published after 2026-03-22 and reports post-cutoff match rates. Neither executes anything. CHSP's step 8 (recall discontinuity) is essentially this matching idea applied as a contamination audit.

closest.title: Temporal Leakage in LLM Backtesting (Zhang & Stadie, arXiv 2608.02985, Aug 2026)
closest.overlap: This directly undermines CHSP's step 8 as written. The paper shows that comparing scores before and after the cutoff is not an informative contamination check, because models legitimately know more about the period near their cutoff, so recency mimics leakage. It proposes a matched clean-control estimator instead. The recall-discontinuity design should adopt that estimator or it will confound recall with recency.

closest.title: Comment on arXiv:2607.01233: Survivorship Bias in Published-Paper Baselines (Dahl, arXiv 2609.15996), on Chen, Zhao & Cohan's 'Measuring the Gap Between Human and LLM Research Ideas' (arXiv 2607.01233)
closest.overlap: The Chen et al. paper compares a distribution of human paper ideas with LLM ideas generated from the same prior-work context. It uses a taxonomy only and executes nothing. The comment argues that a baseline of published papers against one-shot LLM proposals is confounded by survivorship. That is exactly CHSP's risk 1, and it has already been raised publicly, so CHSP needs an explicit correction or reframing, for example 'probability of beating the published, surviving stream'.

closest.title: One Run Is Not an Idea: The Implementation Lottery (arXiv 2607.26587)
closest.overlap: This paper already establishes the case for several implementations per idea and for reporting idea ICC. CHSP borrows the component; it is not new there.

closest.title: Wen et al., Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes (arXiv 2506.00794); Mule et al., Teaching LMs to Forecast Research Success (arXiv 2605.21491, ACL Findings 2026)
closest.overlap: Both train and test predictors of research outcomes, using labels taken from published benchmark numbers, and Wen et al. include a small prospective set. CHSP's frozen critic ledger and outcome-predictor training extend this line; they are not a new concept.

closest.title: ForecastBench (Forecasting Research Institute, arXiv 2409.19839 plus 2025-26 updates)
closest.overlap: This is the analogue from another field. It is a continuously refreshed, contamination-free benchmark in which LLMs are scored against contemporaneous human comparison groups (superforecasters and the public) on questions that resolve after the cutoff. It already argues that static post-cutoff sets go stale, which motivates continuous refresh. It shows the 'live human control arm' framing is established in forecasting, though not for executed research ideas.

closest.title: Paper-replication pipelines: PaperBench (2504.01848), RECLAIM (2609.28850), Coding-agents replicate SciML papers (2607.02134), AutoSOTA (2604.05550)
closest.overlap: Agents automatically re-implement recent human papers from their text. This covers CHSP's byproduct, the replication rate of recent human claims at proxy scale. It does not cover a results-stripped, source-blind head-to-head against AI ideas.

art.to_make_novel:
No paper found runs an uncurated, randomly sampled stream of post-cutoff human papers through the same automated executor as AI ideas, with results stripped, source blinded, and equal implementation and tuning budgets, to report P(AI idea > contemporaneous human idea). That core is the novel contribution. The other components are prior art, so frame them as borrowed: multiple implementations and ICC (2607.26587), outcome predictors (Wen, Mule), time-split matching (HindSight, Reconstruction), the live human comparison group (ForecastBench analogue) and automated paper replication (PaperBench, RECLAIM).

To make the novelty claim defensible:

1. **Redesign the recall-discontinuity step (8).** Replace the raw pre-cutoff vs post-cutoff jump with the matched clean-control estimator of Zhang & Stadie (2608.02985). Their paper shows the naive discontinuity confounds recall with recency.

2. **Handle survivorship bias head-on (Dahl, 2609.15996).** Either relabel the estimand as 'probability of beating the published, surviving human stream', or add a pre-filter arm. One option is to also sample human ideas from workshop and rejected submissions, or from pre-publication PR proposals that were not merged. Another is to apply the eligibility and card filter symmetrically, so AI ideas face the same survivorship screen.

3. **Show the claim experimentally.** Demonstrate that source-blind, equal-effort execution changes conclusions relative to the asymmetric baselines above: 2601.14525's human leaderboard ceiling, and match-target scoring as in NanoGPT-Bench or HindSight.

Caveat on search coverage: the WebSearch budget was already spent. Searches went through the arXiv API, which hit a rate limit (HTTP 429), arXiv's own search via WebFetch, and DuckDuckGo. GitHub and lab-blog coverage is therefore thinner than planned.

feas.will_it_work:
Partly. The pipeline will run, but the pilot will mostly return nulls.

What works mechanistically:
- Post-cutoff arXiv v1 papers (Jul-Sep 2026) really are unseen by Opus 5.5, so results-stripped human cards are a fair, uncurated comparison arm.
- Three implementations per idea is the right answer to the implementation lottery (arXiv 2607.26587: implementation explains 33-45% of within-task variance versus 4-6% for reruns, idea ICC 0.51-0.61). Caveat: that is 13 OpenML tabular tasks with a DeepSeek v4 implementer, not LM pretraining.
- Hashing the critic predictions before execution is sound and nearly free.

Why it will mostly return nulls:
1) Low base rate. Published efficiency claims rarely survive fair re-tuning against a strong baseline. Kaddour et al. (arXiv 2307.06440) tested layer stacking/dropping, selective backprop, RHO-loss, Lion and Sophia on BERT and T5 at fixed compute. They found the gains 'vanish compared to a baseline with a fully-decayed learning rate'. The paper is from 2023, but the mechanism (baseline tuning) does not depend on model generation, so it still applies. The proposal also cites optimizer gains shrinking from 1.4x to 1.1x under fair tuning. On top of that, most human ideas are shown at more than 100M parameters and then ported to 7-20M. My estimate is that H2 (25% or more of human cards beat 1.11x) fails, with a realistic rate of 0-15%. The proposal's own branch for that outcome is 'the eligibility filter fails, redesign'.
2) Asymmetric fidelity. Human ideas are compressed from 10-30 page papers into cards by an LLM distiller, while AI ideas are written as cards to begin with. Canonicalization hides the source but does not restore lost detail. The Opus implementers also share priors with the AI arms. Both effects push P(AI > human) upward for reasons unrelated to idea quality.
3) The 1.11x detectable effect is per implementation with 3 seeds. Choosing the best of 2 configs on the same seeds adds a winner's-curse bias unless confirmation seeds are held out.
feas.eval_issues:
Sound on circularity and contamination, weak on power.

Sound:
- No LLM judge decides any outcome. The evaluator is frozen and code-owned, and the critic ledger is hashed before execution.
- Post-cutoff human cards cannot be recalled by the generator.

Problems:
1) Underpowered for every inferential claim except H1.
   - P(superiority) with 15 vs 15 ideas has a bootstrap CI roughly +/-0.2. The proposal concedes this ('calibration, not a verdict').
   - H3 (critic AUC of 0.60 or less versus 0.70 or more) needs positives. At a realistic 2-5 of 45 cards beating 1.11x, the AUC CI is about +/-0.2-0.3, so H3 cannot be decided.
   - The top-decile share is 4-5 ideas.
   - H1 (ICC lower 90% bound above 0.3 with 45 ideas x 3 implementations) is roughly adequate if the true ICC is about 0.55. But if nearly every idea has a true effect near 1.0, between-idea variance collapses. ICC then comes out low for a floor-effect reason, not because of implementation noise, and the proposal would wrongly conclude that 'single-implementation labels are invalid'.
2) Floor effect. With most log-multipliers near 0, arm comparisons measure noise.
3) Selection-best-of-2-configs bias. There are no held-out confirmation seeds.
4) Arm asymmetry. Distillation loss affects only the human arm, and the implementer shares priors with the AI arms.
5) The recall-discontinuity test is confounded and small.
   - Topic drift between Mar-May and Jul-Sep 2026 changes match rates regardless of recall.
   - The cutoff is 'about June' and not verified from a primary source.
   - Pretraining data just before a cutoff is thin, which blurs any jump.
   - 30 cards per side at low match rates cannot resolve a discontinuity.
6) Weak Goodhart exposure. Engine ideas could be tuned toward what the fixed proxy rewards, such as short-horizon loss tricks. The proposal's own DataDecide figure is about 80% agreement between proxy rankings and 1B-scale rankings.
7) The Wen et al. context the proposal cites checks out, with one clarification. The fine-tuned predictor scored 64.4% in NLP (humans 48.9%), 77% on the full test set, and 63.6% on unpublished ideas, where o3 was near chance. That is pairwise benchmark prediction, a different task from pretraining-efficiency execution. The n=33 for the unpublished set is the proposal's own figure; the abstract I read did not state it.
feas.cost_realistic:
Mostly realistic for compute, but it leaves out human time and exceeds the per-POC cap.

Compute: 810 proxy runs of a 7M-parameter model on 1-4M tokens take minutes each on one GPU, so $0.08-0.25 per run is plausible (the proposal flags this as an estimate).

Implementation: 135 fresh Claude Code sessions at about $1.25 each. Under a Max subscription the binding cost is rate-limit time, not dollars, so expect days of wall-clock time.

Human time not costed:
- the eligibility spot-check;
- a 20% card-fidelity review, which means reading the source papers;
- the human check of recall matches;
- the optional check with authors.
That is realistically 15-30 hours for the pilot.

Budget cap: the steady state of $2.5-3.5k over 3 months is above the roughly $2k-per-POC guideline. It produces outcome labels, not a product, prize or licence.

Pilot: $260-400 is credible.
feas.fix:
Restructure around positives, and make the critic-validity ledger the headline instead of arm parity.

1) Run a sequential screen. Put about 150 cards (human stream plus engine plus bare Opus) through 1 implementation x 3 seeds, which costs about the same as the planned 45 x 3.
2) Confirm with 3 implementations and fresh held-out seeds only on:
   - the top about 20% of the screen;
   - a random 15% subsample, so hit rates and AUC stay unbiased by inverse-probability weighting.
3) Add 5-10 positive-control cards: known-effective pre-cutoff recipes with results stripped, for example known data-repetition or curriculum levers. These prove the executor and proxy can detect a real 1.11x+ effect through the card pipeline.
4) Correct for distillation loss by having an implementer also work from the full paper for a subset of human cards.

This gives enough positives to decide H3 (whether a cheap Opus judge can filter). That is the one output that transfers to other domains.

closest.title: Gao, Schulman & Hilton, Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization (2022)
closest.overlap: Defines the core object. Gao's best-of-n axis is the same thing as COC's selection-pressure axis: top-q selection = BoN with n = 1/q. Its RL axis is the analogue of COC's substance-Goodhart rounds, and the gold-versus-proxy hump gives k*. What differs: Gao uses a synthetic gold RM on chat outputs, not executed research ideas. The proposal already cites this paper.

closest.title: Khalaf et al., Inference-Time Reward Hacking in Large Language Models (2025)
closest.overlap: Characterizes the hump-shaped true reward as best-of-n / selection pressure increases on an imperfect reward model, and proposes hedging to choose the optimal amount of selection pressure. That is conceptually COC's V_E(q) curve plus the 'hill-climb up to k*' license. The domain is LLM alignment RMs, not research-idea critics with executed outcomes. The proposal does not cite it.

closest.title: Karwowski et al., Goodhart's Law in Reinforcement Learning (2023)
closest.overlap: Formalizes the critical point beyond which optimizing a proxy lowers the true objective, and gives an early-stopping rule. This is COC's k*, in generic RL. Not cited.

closest.title: Wen et al., Rethinking Reward Model Evaluation: Are We Barking up the Wrong Tree? (2024), and Frick et al., How to Evaluate Reward Models for RLHF (PPE, 2024)
closest.overlap: Both argue COC's central 'why novel' thesis directly: accuracy on a fixed pool is the wrong quantity for an evaluator that will be optimized against. Wen et al. relate RM accuracy to overoptimization outcomes. PPE (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14872) scores reward models by downstream post-optimization performance. The reframing is therefore prior art. Only its application to research-idea critics with executed outcomes is new. Neither is cited.

closest.title: Coste et al., Reward Model Ensembles Help Mitigate Overoptimization (2023)
closest.overlap: Overoptimization curves compared across several reward models and ensembles against a gold RM, which amounts to a per-evaluator comparison of hill-climbability. It is set in RLHF, not executed science.

closest.title: SciStyleBench: Style Wins, Substance Loses, a diagnosis of LLM-as-Judge in idea generation (2026)
closest.overlap: Applies controlled style perturbations to fixed-substance scientific ideas (600 ideas × 15 variants) and measures Top-K membership change and adversarial win rate. This largely pre-empts COC step 5, the presentation-Goodhart test, and prediction P3's 'share crossing top cutoff' metric.
