Remaining differences: COC uses an adaptive optimizer agent for 4 rounds against the judge (rather than fixed style variants), a patch-locked executable, and Opus judges. Already cited by the proposal.

closest.title: BadScientist (2025); Ye et al., Are We There Yet? Risks of LLMs in Peer Review (2024); One Token to Fool LLM-as-a-Judge (2025)
closest.overlap: These show that presentation manipulation, fabricated but convincing papers, injected text and 'master key' tokens inflate LLM reviewer and judge scores without any change in substance. That is prior evidence for the gameability measurement in COC step 5 (Ye et al.: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01708; One Token: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08794). They do not tie score changes to executed ground truth.

closest.title: Wen, Si et al., Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models (2025)
closest.overlap: An outcome predictor for research ideas, validated on real experimental results. It includes human-written and LM-designed stress tests of sensitivity to superficial features, which is a weak form of the gameability test. Evaluation is on a fixed pool of pairs. There is no selection or optimization curve.

closest.title: Si, Hashimoto, Yang: The Ideation-Execution Gap (2025), and Towards Execution-Grounded Automated AI Research (2026)
closest.overlap: Executes LLM-generated and human ideas and shows that pre-execution judged scores fail to track execution outcomes. The 2026 paper (2601.14525) does RL and evolutionary search on true execution reward. Together these supply the executed-ground-truth idea audit, but without per-evaluator curves as selection or optimization pressure rises.

closest.title: Ning et al., One Run Is Not an Idea: The Implementation Lottery in Automated Research (2026)
closest.overlap: Idea-level audit with multiple independent implementations per idea and idea-level selection regret. It notes that automated loops apply selection pressure precisely when candidates are close. This overlaps COC's ground-truth design (2 implementations × seeds) and its selection framing. It does not compare cheap critics or trace optimization curves.

closest.title: Prediction-powered evaluation machinery: Stratified PPI (2024), Active Statistical Inference (2024), MultiPPI (2026), PPSR 'Which Metrics Save the Most Human Annotation?' (2026), AutoEval Done Right (2024)
closest.overlap: All of COC's statistical design is prior art. Stratified sampling with known inclusion probabilities plus PPI is Active Statistical Inference (2403.03208) and Stratified PPI (2406.04291). One labeled sample serving many cheap predictors at once is MultiPPI (2603.27414). Ranking automatic metrics by how much gold labeling they save under PPI is PPSR (2608.26638), which is essentially COC's 'method success criterion'. AutoEval (2403.07008) applies PPI to autorater evaluation. None of them apply it to executed research-idea outcomes or to top-q selection value.

closest.title: Debate as Reward (2026) and ReviewGuard (2026)
closest.overlap: Both acknowledge reward hacking and over-optimization of LLM idea and review judges used as RL rewards. They mitigate it through judge precision, multi-agent deliberation or KL penalties, but never measure a Goodhart curve against executed truth. This supports COC's claimed gap.

closest.title: Cross-field analogues: q-error vs plan regret (2026); open-loop vs closed-loop driving metrics (2026); regressional/extremal Goodhart taxonomy (Manheim & Garrabrant 2018)
closest.overlap: The same question, 'does proxy accuracy predict value when the proxy is used to select or argmin?', answered by measurement in other fields. Examples: q-error is near-uninformative for plan regret (rho ~0.05); open-loop driving metrics show ranking inversions against closed-loop scores (2605.00066). These support the framing but are not prior art for idea critics.

art.to_make_novel:
What is already done:
- The conceptual core is prior art in RLHF: overoptimization curves against a gold signal as selection pressure (BoN) and optimization steps rise, an optimal stopping point k*, and the argument that fixed-pool accuracy is the wrong way to evaluate an optimized-against evaluator. Sources: Gao 2022; Khalaf 2025 inference-time reward hacking; Karwowski 2023; Wen 2024 and PPE 2024 on RM evaluation.
- The statistical engine is prior art: stratified or active sampling with inclusion probabilities plus PPI, many predictors against one gold sample, and metrics ranked by annotation saved (Active Statistical Inference, Stratified PPI, MultiPPI, PPSR).
- Presentation gameability of idea judges is largely shown already: SciStyleBench's Top-K churn under fixed substance, plus BadScientist and One-Token.

What appears unclaimed (under the search limits below):
- (a) Selection-validity and overoptimization curves for research-idea critics measured against executed outcomes, specifically: Opus rubric, BT tournament, trained predictor, time-split match, novelty distance.
- (b) Substance-Goodhart curves, where an optimizer edits the idea itself against a critic and the trajectory is executed.
- (c) A measured false-zero rate for time-split/future-paper matching metrics among ideas that actually win.
- (d) An adaptive optimizer rewriting against the judge under a byte-locked executable. This is stronger than SciStyleBench's fixed style variants.

To make the claim clearly novel:
1. Drop 'first to measure X under selection and optimization pressure' as a general claim. Cite Gao, Khalaf, Karwowski and Wen/PPE as the established framework and claim only the domain transfer with executed truth.
2. Move at least one substance-Goodhart curve (E1 or E4, rounds 0/3/6/9) into phase 1. It is the part with no precedent. Phase 1 as currently scoped (selection curves plus presentation rewrites) is mostly a re-run of known methods in a new domain.
3. Present the false-zero audit (P2) as a standalone headline contribution.
4. Head-to-head on the same ideas: SciStyleBench-style fixed perturbations versus the adaptive optimizer, to show that adaptive gaming is larger.
5. Test whether RLHF-derived remedies transfer to idea critics: Khalaf's hedging or pessimism for choosing q, and Coste-style ensembles of E1+E2+E4.
6. Use MultiPPI or active inference and report PPSR rather than presenting the PPI design as a contribution.

Search caveat: WebSearch budget was exhausted, and arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were heavily rate-limited. Coverage came from arXiv id lookups, two combined arXiv API queries and a local cache of about 60 papers. GitHub and lab blogs were not searched. A 2026 paper doing exactly this could have been missed, but none surfaced in the cached critic literature (2601–2609).

feas.will_it_work:
Partly. The three parts differ a lot in how likely they are to work.

(a) The patch-locked presentation-Goodhart test (step 5) will almost certainly work and give a clear answer for about $15. Opus rewrites of a card whose executable patch is locked byte-for-byte isolate gameability with no confound. The literature (laundering rewrites +0.45, style changing top-30 membership by 15.9%) makes it very likely that E1 moves while E2 on canonicalized cards moves less. This is the most reliable and most transferable output.

(b) The selection-validity curves V_E(q) are sound in principle. The target is well defined, and Horvitz-Thompson (HT) weighting with non-zero inclusion probabilities is valid. But the curves will be badly underpowered:
- 60 executed ideas spread over 18 strata (E1 tertile x E2 tertile x E6 match/no-match) is about 3 per stratum.
- The top-1/8 set of any evaluator contains roughly 7-15 sampled ideas, and with the proposal's own estimate of 10-20% positives that is only about 1-3 winners.
- The HT weights are uneven, which inflates variance further.
- E7 is not a stratification variable, so its top-1/8 cell gets the fewest samples.
- For most evaluators, expect CIs of about +/-0.1-0.2 on the log-multiplier scale. That is as wide as the effect itself: log(1.11) = 0.104.

(c) The prediction-powered inference (PPI) savings will very probably not appear in round 1. PPI narrows CIs only in proportion to how well the predictor correlates with the outcome. The ≤60% width criterion needs about rho ≥ 0.8 (sqrt(1 - rho^2) = 0.6). The round-1 predictors (E1, E2, E6, E7) are exactly the signals the proposal's own evidence calls near chance (HindSight rho = -0.29, MLRC innovativeness vs effectiveness -0.06, pilot judge 53% self-agreement). P1 (E1 is chance) and the PPI success criterion therefore contradict each other: if P1 holds, PPI buys almost nothing. The one cheap signal plausibly above 0.8 is E5, low-fidelity execution, and it is deferred to later rounds.

Phase-2 substance curves (about 12 ideas x 4 checkpoints) are the most novel part, a Gao-style curve on executed science. At that size, k* would be mostly noise. The underlying mechanism, overoptimization of a proxy reward, is well established (Gao, Schulman & Hilton 2022, arXiv 2210.10760). That study used a synthetic gold reward model. The trend is likely to transfer; the exact shape is not.
feas.eval_issues:
The ground truth is non-circular, which is good: executed effective-data multiplier, hidden held-out loss, a frozen evaluator, and judges only as the objects audited. The problems are in power and in how the predictions are set up.

1) Power asymmetry makes P1 close to unfalsifiable. P1 is confirmed whenever the 90% CI of V_E1(1/8) includes 0, and with about 60 ideas that is the default outcome whether or not E1 is useful. A null here would be read as "E1 is not hill-climbable" when it only means "not shown". The fix is to pre-register the minimum detectable V at each q and require an upper CI below a threshold before declaring an evaluator unlicensed.

2) P2 is inflated by construction. Opus 5.5's cutoff is June 2026, so on 2026-09-27 the post-cutoff arXiv window is only about 3 months. The E6 reference set is tiny, so a ≥30% false-zero rate is nearly guaranteed and says little about time-split metrics in general. The window length and corpus size should be reported and conditioned on.

3) PPI details:
- Raw scores (a rubric score, a Bradley-Terry strength, a cosine distance) are not predictions of the log-multiplier. They need a calibration map fitted on the labeled data with cross-fitting, or PPI++ power tuning, or the CIs are invalid or wasted.
- Non-uniform inclusion probabilities need the IPW/active-inference form of PPI (Zrnic & Candès, 'Active Statistical Inference', arXiv 2403.03208), not the original iid PPI of arXiv 2301.09633.
- The criterion "one evaluator's CI ≤60% as wide", chosen across 4-6 evaluators and 4 values of q, is a forking-paths target.

4) Budget allocation is inverted. The design spends 12 runs per idea (2 implementations x 2 tuning configs x 3 seeds) reducing measurement noise that is already small. OptiLex's proxy has a pooled seed sd of 0.015 on loss and detects 1.11x with 3 seeds (FEASIBILITY.md). The dominant variance, and the power bottleneck, is the number of ideas that land in each top-q cell.

5) There is no pre-specified rule for ideas that fail to implement or crash. Whether a failure is imputed as 0, dropped, or scored as negative can dominate V_E(q) at 1-3 positives per cell.

6) Self-preference: E1 and E2 are Opus judging Opus-generated cards, and the optimizer in step 5 is also Opus. The licenses therefore carry a same-family bias that should be named.

7) All licenses hold only at 7M-parameter proxy scale. The proposal already acknowledges this, citing DataDecide's roughly 20% pairwise mis-ranking across scale.

On the positives: contamination is well handled because the outcomes are freshly executed, and the patch-locked design resists Goodhart for presentation gaming.
feas.biggest_risk: A null result bought with $300-400 that the factory can't act on. About 60 ideas, 1-3 winners per top-q cell and near-chance round-1 predictors give CIs spanning 0 for almost every evaluator. That happens to "confirm" P1 while telling OptiLex nothing about which signal it may hill-climb. PPI does not rescue it, because the predictors are weak.
feas.cost_realistic:
Roughly yes, for compute: about $290-410 for round 1.
- 720 proxy runs of a 7M-parameter model on 1-4M tokens take a few GPU-minutes each on a rented GPU. That fits $60-180, although the paired-seed baseline arms appear not to be counted.
- Generation (about $26 at the measured $0.044 per idea) and judging (about $42) are credible.

What is under-counted:
- Human and agent time to verify 120 implementations and write the diff-lock harness.
- Implementation failures and reruns, which are likely a sizable share given efficiency ideas at proxy scale.

Phase-2 substance curves at $150-250 per evaluator are cheap but underpowered at 12 ideas. Quarterly re-anchoring at $400-600 is modest. Overall the dollar cost is small against the $2k-per-POC envelope. The real cost is opportunity cost: this is infrastructure and does not directly earn prizes, bounties, licensing or grants.
feas.fix:
Reallocate the execution budget from replicating each idea to covering more ideas, and bring E5 forward so that PPI has a strong predictor.

Concretely:
- Run 1 implementation x 3 paired seeds (3 runs per idea) on about 180-200 stratified ideas. Keep ≥20% of them uniform-random, and add a second implementation only for top-stratum ideas and apparent winners. This fits the same ~720 runs.
- Run E5 on the whole pool of about 600 ideas, as a 1-seed, 1/4-token low-fidelity execution. That is roughly 600 short runs, about $30-60.
- Use E5, calibrated with cross-fitting, as the PPI predictor inside the IPW (active-inference) estimator.
- Pre-register the minimum detectable V_E(q) and an equivalence rule for "unlicensed".

This roughly triples the ideas per top-q cell. It gives PPI the only cheap signal likely to reach rho ≥ 0.8. It also licenses or rejects the evaluator the factory most needs, cheap low-fidelity execution, which is the multi-fidelity gate every domain pack with an executable verifier will rely on.
feas.general_factory_value:
Moderate to high for the method, low for the specific numbers.

What transfers to every domain pack:
- Licensing each cheap evaluator for selection and optimization pressure against a small stratified executed sample, using IPW-PPI.
- The patch-locked or substance-locked rewrite test for presentation gameability.
- Tying each license to a generator version, re-checked every quarter.
In every pack, verifiers are expensive and critics are cheap, so this is the core control problem of a GENERAL engine. The presentation-gameability result for Opus rubric judges is largely a property of the judge rather than the domain, so it will partly transfer too.

What does not transfer: the actual curves, k* values and licenses. They are specific to LLM-efficiency ideas at 7M-parameter proxy scale and to today's generators. LLM-training optimisation is the right cheap calibration domain for building the method. Other domains, such as wet-lab or materials packs, have far scarcer executed labels, so the method would need to run there on even smaller samples. That makes the fix (more ideas, a low-fidelity predictor, IPW-PPI) matter even more.

There is no direct revenue path. The possible upside is a workshop or conference paper, since Goodhart curves for idea critics on executed ground truth are listed as unmeasured.

vetted.name: Scope-Bet Ledger: verbatim claim records with locked qualifiers and declared extrapolation bets

closest.title: Theorizer: synthesizing theories of LAW / SCOPE / EVIDENCE tuples from literature, backtested against later papers (arXiv 2601.16282)
closest.overlap: Stores each law with an explicit scope (domain constraints, known exceptions, special cases) and literature evidence, then backtests its predictions against papers published later. The full text was verified: scope is free-text LLM output, not character offsets into the source, and it is never checked against a machine-readable target context when ideas are generated. There is also no write-back of executed outcomes; the pipeline runs one way and is evaluated only against later literature. This covers the idea of stored scope, but not the contract, the code overrides, the bets or the write-back.

closest.title: TrialGPT: Matching patients to clinical trials with large language models (Jin et al., Nature Communications 2024)
closest.overlap: The closest cross-field structural analog to the premise table. For each eligibility criterion, the LLM labels the patient included / not included / not enough information, cites sentence-level evidence, and code then aggregates the labels. The target (the patient) is matched to the source's scope (the criteria) one qualifier at a time, with a three-way status close to HOLDS / VIOLATED / UNKNOWN. This comes from clinical matching, not ideation: nothing is priced as an extrapolation bet and nothing is written back. (DOI verified via Crossref; the per-criterion label details are from memory.)

closest.title: GRADE 'indirectness' / applicability assessment and PICO span extraction (EBM-NLP, RobotReviewer; LLM PICO extraction, JMIR preprint 2025)
closest.overlap: Evidence-based medicine already formalizes whether a source's population, intervention, comparator and outcome match the target question. That is the same move as comparing the context card with the source's scope slots, and PICO extraction is typically span-based. Here it is used to grade evidence in systematic reviews, not in a generator-critic-fixer ideation loop. Out-of-scope evidence is downgraded there, whereas the proposal turns it into a tested bet.

closest.title: Condition-aware fact extraction: Jiang et al., KDD 2019; joint fact-condition extraction (Information Processing & Management 2025); Conditional IE on a Fact-Condition Star Graph (WWW 2026)
closest.overlap: Extracts scientific claims together with their condition tuples, which overlaps the qualifier-slot index. These are extraction methods only: there is no contract at the point of use, no target-pack comparison, and they are not evaluated by how nuance propagates downstream. 2025-26 work continues the line, so condition slots on their own are not novel.

closest.title: Fidelity Before Structure: Verbatim Chunks Beat Lossy Artifact Extraction in Long-Conversation LLM Memory (Tao An, arXiv 2601.00821)
closest.overlap: The empirical basis for keeping verbatim spans with an additive index; verified. It uses conversational memory QA, not scientific claims, and does not use offset-pointer slots.

closest.title: Understanding Fine-grained Distortions in Reports of Scientific Findings (Wührl, Wright, Klinger, Augenstein, ACL Findings 2024); Peters & Chin-Yee, Generalization bias in LLM summarization of scientific research (R. Soc. Open Sci. 2025)
closest.overlap: Both define and measure qualifier-level distortions: certainty/hedging, generality/scope and causality (Wührl et al.), and overgeneralization (Peters & Chin-Yee). This is the same taxonomy as the proposal's flip types, but it is measured on single-step science communication or summaries. Neither traces loss stage by stage through extraction, knowledge base, generator, critic and fixer, and neither uses code-verified minimal flips with no-op controls.

closest.title: ClashEval (arXiv 2404.10198), FaithEval, and FactCC-style rule-based perturbations (negation / number swap; Kryscinski et al. 2020, from memory)
closest.overlap: These are counterfactual context perturbations built from minimal, code-generated edits (negation, number swaps, answer flips) and used to test faithfulness. The flip-generation method is established. What is new is applying it to qualifiers (scope, regime, hedge, effect size) and tracing them through a multi-stage ideation pipeline.

closest.title: HypER: Literature-grounded Hypothesis Generation and Distillation with Provenance (EMNLP 2025)
closest.overlap: Trains a model to tell valid from invalid literature reasoning chains under controlled distractions, then generates evidence-grounded hypotheses with provenance. This partly overlaps grounding at the point of use and perturbation robustness in hypothesis generation. There are no per-qualifier scope slots, no target context card, no bets and no execution.

closest.title: Kosmos: An AI Scientist for Autonomous Discovery (arXiv 2511.02824)
closest.overlap: A structured world model shared between the data-analysis and literature agents accumulates findings from executed analyses across about 200 rollouts. This is a form of executed-outcome write-back into a knowledge representation, which weakens the claim that no system does this (claim d). It does not attach executed scope evidence to specific literature claim records ('claim X held at 7M params / failed at n>10^4').

closest.title: Popper: Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications (Huang et al. 2025, from memory, not re-verified); ACE patch-only context editing
closest.overlap: Popper designs cheap falsification experiments before accepting a hypothesis, which is close in spirit to running bet checks before the full run. ACE already supplies the append/patch-only editing discipline used for the fixers. Neither ties its tests to declared violations of source scope.

closest.title: Who Broke the Pipeline? Traceability and Accountability in Multi-Agent LLM SE Pipelines (Research Square 2026)
closest.overlap: Measures silent error propagation across planner, executor and critic stages, with blame attributed to each role. The stage-wise attribution idea is similar, but it concerns task accuracy in software engineering, not nuance or qualifiers in scientific ideation.

art.to_make_novel: The individual parts all have prior art: condition-aware claim extraction, Theorizer's scope fields, PICO/GRADE indirectness and TrialGPT-style per-criterion HOLDS/VIOLATED/UNKNOWN labels, minimal-edit counterfactual perturbations (ClashEval, FactCC), distortion taxonomies (Wührl 2024, Peters & Chin-Yee 2025), patch-only editing (ACE), and executed-result memory (Kosmos world model). Two things appear unclaimed, and the novelty case should rest on them. (1) The stage-by-stage qualifier-flip propagation audit through an extraction, knowledge-base, generator, critic and fixer ideation pipeline, scored entirely by code with no-op controls. This is the strongest novel contribution and could be published on its own as a benchmark or measurement paper. (2) The scope contract at the point of use. Each idea labels every qualifier against a machine-readable target context card, code overrides wrong numeric labels, and violations become priced, pre-tested extrapolation bets instead of being downgraded as GRADE does. The bet-check AUC result would be new evidence. Changes to the write-up: soften claim (d), because Kosmos already feeds executed analyses back into a shared world model. The actual gap is narrower: executed scope evidence attached to individual literature claim records and reused by later ideas, which is the time-split write-back test. Cite TrialGPT/GRADE indirectness as the clinical precedent for per-qualifier applicability labels, and Wührl et al. 2024 for the flip taxonomy. Keep verbatim offsets as an engineering choice, not a novelty claim. Search caveat: the WebSearch budget ran out before this task started, and the arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited or down. Coverage therefore came from Crossref (which covers DOI-registered 2023-26 work, including preprint servers) plus direct arXiv abstract fetches. A 2026 preprint that exists only on arXiv could have been missed, so rerun a targeted arXiv search for 'qualifier', 'scope', 'overgeneralization' and 'hypothesis generation' before relying on the novelty claim.

feas.will_it_work:
Partly. The storage layer is sound and cheap. Two primary sources back it. Fidelity Before Structure (arXiv 2601.00821; single author; conversational memory, not science) found verbatim chunks at 43.9% vs extracted artifacts at 28.0% on LoCoMo, and 67.4% vs 45.4% on LongMemEval-S. Adding artifacts alongside chunks kept the accuracy, so an additive index over verbatim spans is the right design. Offset-pointer slots checked by code are simple engineering. Code comparison of numeric and unit slots against a pack context_card will reliably catch out-of-range numeric scale claims.

The contract layer has a problem. Its hard parts are the ones code cannot check: non-numeric qualifiers (population, conditions, assumptions) and qualifiers that sit in methods sections far from the claim sentence. For those the design falls back on Opus 5.5 declaring status and re-reading spans. That is ordinary reading comprehension, which a 2026 frontier model probably already does well once the spans are in context.

The evidence for how often scope loss happens is indirect:
- Peters & Chin-Yee measured single-pass summaries by 2024-25 models and found Claude models least affected, so their 26-73% overgeneralization rates do not transfer to Opus 5.5 with spans in context.
- ClashEval (arXiv 2404.10198: 1,200+ QA questions, 6 LLMs including GPT-4o, over 60% adoption of wrong context) shows models over-follow retrieved text. In a flip test, following the context is the correct behaviour. So ClashEval predicts the flips will be followed in every arm that sees spans; it does not show a gap this design closes.

The most relevant evidence is Kosmos: synthesis statements were 57.9% accurate vs 85.5% for data analysis, but that is expert-judged, 102 statements from 3 reports. Robin's 7.5x vs 1.75x error was an analysis error, not a scope-transfer error.

The genuinely valuable, domain-general piece is item 4: every extrapolation bet must carry the cheapest discriminating bet check, run before the full execution. This is staged evaluation with a declared hypothesis. It works whether or not the qualifier machinery does. Patch-only fixers (ACE: 18,282 tokens collapsed to 122, accuracy 66.7% to 57.1% on AppWorld) are also cheap and justified.

Net: storage hygiene, bet checks and patch-only fixers will work. The qualifier-slot contract is likely to add little on top of verbatim spans for Opus 5.5. The proposal's own falsification branch (arm A at 80% or more) is the probable outcome.
feas.eval_issues:
1) Circular for arm C. The scope flip is a numeric regime edit, and arm C's code then compares numeric slots against the context card and overwrites HOLDS. So C's scope-flip sensitivity is guaranteed by construction; it measures the script, not propagation through the model. Polarity, number and unit disagreements are also "settled by code". The 85% success bar and the at-least-15-point lead over A are close to guaranteed on numeric flips. Report C's model-only statuses before any code override, and weight non-numeric qualifier flips (population, conditions, hedge) separately; those are where the real risk is.

2) Arm A is a straw man. OptiLex's own IDEAS_FACTORY.md (line 61) record already includes a source span, but arm A shows the generator only the normal form. The fair baseline is arm B (verbatim spans with the same premise-table schema). The decision rule should be C vs B, and B will likely saturate.

3) The key comparison is not defined. Token matching between a short normal-form record and long spans plus re-reads is left unspecified: do you pad A? add more records?

4) "Dropped" counts as correct for polarity flips. A generator that simply stops using the flipped record scores as nuance-preserving. Each flipped record must be pinned as a required premise, or dropping must be scored separately.

5) Prior contamination. Flipping well-known results (e.g. a famous scaling finding) creates a conflict between the text and the model's prior knowledge (the ClashEval setting). Correct behaviour becomes ambiguous and gets confounded with how famous the claim is. Stratify flips by prior familiarity, or use obscure records.

6) Synthetic minimal edits are far easier to detect than real nuance loss, so even a pass says little about the real failure. The proposal admits this.

7) Power. The aggregate n=100 paired design is fine for a 15-point effect, since the standard error is about 5 points. But 25 records per domain are too few for per-pack claims.

8) The executed-outcome evaluations are the right target. But "premise-violation failure rate" needs failure attribution. The write-back test requires more than 100 executed ideas plus a time split; at SWARM throughput that is months away and will be underpowered for a failure-rate difference unless effects are large.

9) Goodhart: UNKNOWN gaming is capped, but BET inflation is not. Declaring everything a BET makes every scope flip "correct". The false-alarm control only covers no-op paraphrases, not over-declaration on the original records.
feas.biggest_risk: It solves a failure mode whose share of real executed failures is unmeasured and probably small for Opus 5.5 with verbatim spans in context. The flagship flip test cannot reveal that. It either saturates in the fair baseline (B, and likely A) or passes in C by construction through its code overrides. Meanwhile the build adds slot extraction, context cards for every pack, premise tables, re-reads and 15-25% runtime overhead. Idea quality and executed hit rate are the factory's real bottlenecks; scope-overreach is a guardrail against one kind of waste. Worse, a code-enforced HOLDS/BET contract plus critics can steer generation toward in-scope, conservative ideas, which is the collapse the factory is meant to escape.
feas.fix:
Reorder the plan: measure the problem on real executions before building the machinery. Ship only the cheap core now:
- verbatim spans (already planned)
- a free-text context_card per pack
- a premise table listing record IDs and the claimed transfer
- a mandatory bet check before each full run
- patch-only fixers

Then, over the first 50-100 executed ideas across the LM proxy and one non-ML pack (ALE-Bench AHC or VCC), have code and a human audit trace every failure. Classify each as scope violation, wrong mechanism, implementation bug, or null effect. Build qualifier slots and code overrides only if scope violations are at least roughly 20% of failures.

If a synthetic test is still wanted, run it as C vs B. Score C's model statuses before code overrides, use non-numeric qualifier flips, pin the flipped records as required premises, and stratify by how familiar the claim is to the model. That costs a few million tokens with stage-level prompts, not 50M tokens for the full generate-critique-fix pipeline. Also track the bet-check AUC from the start. That number (at least 0.7) is the design's most decision-relevant output and does not need any slot machinery.
feas.cost_realistic:
Build: roughly realistic. The IDEAS_FACTORY.md estimate is $300-700 of Haiku batch for 10-25k papers; about 30% more for offsets and number checks is plausible, but context cards and slot schemas per pack are unbudgeted human and engineering time.

First experiment: overbuilt. 1,200 full generator-critic-fixer runs at 35-45k tokens is about 50M tokens, roughly $250-450 at an Opus-class rate of about $5 per million input tokens; this is unverified for Opus 5.5, and output-heavy runs cost more. Or about a week of Max-plan quota, which competes with executor runs. Since the flip question is per-stage, stage-isolated prompts would answer it for about 10% of that.

Runtime overhead: the 15-25% per idea is an unmeasured own estimate. Re-reads of full paragraph, limitations and table spans for multi-record ideas could run higher.

Bet checks are cheap in the stated packs: a 1-seed LM proxy run, or a 5-instance AHC scorer run.
feas.general_factory_value:
Genuinely domain-general in form. Scope, regime, polarity and effect-size qualifiers apply to any literature, and a context_card per pack is a reasonable interface. Declared extrapolation bets with a cheapest discriminating check are useful in every pack and arguably the best idea here: they turn cross-domain transfer into cheap, pre-registered tests. The executed-outcome write-back into claim records is also domain-general and is one of the few things that compounds.

The limits:
- Slot extraction is weakest precisely in the high-impact non-ML domains (biology populations and conditions, chemistry assumptions), where qualifiers are non-numeric. The code-checked part mostly helps numeric, ML-like literatures.
- It is a defensive guardrail against wasted execution, not a source of higher-value ideas, prizes or licensing wins. Its expected value depends on how often scope violations cause executed failures, which is unknown.

vetted.name: Compute-First Import Exchange (CFIX): executable fingerprints as the cross-field join key

closest.title: Tao et al., crowdsourced project linking erdosproblems.com to the OEIS (blog, 31 Aug 2025; github.com/teorth/erdosproblems)
closest.overlap: This already runs CFIX's core math loop by hand. Contributors (including AI-written code) compute small-case sequences or decimal values of an Erdős problem, search the OEIS with them, and follow the hits to literature. Tao used AI to compute decimals of series and then searched the OEIS. The blog reports that the match with A371134 showed Erdős #259 had already been solved by Chen and Ruzsa. As of Sep 2026 the repo README reports 342 problems linked to 450 OEIS sequences. The stated purpose is literature discovery and unexpected connections, with AI output 'only used to locate more reliable human-generated resources'. Missing compared with CFIX: it is human-in-the-loop rather than an autonomous agent, it covers INT_SEQ and CONST only, it has no coincidence-null p-value, it has no fingerprints harvested from papers, and it has no controlled comparison against text retrieval.

closest.title: mathlas: an MCP toolset for math agents (Archerkattri, created Jun 2026; PyPI mathlas-mcp)
closest.overlap: This is the nearest agent-side implementation. An LLM agent calls identify_sequence (exact contiguous term match against a local OEIS copy of about 400k sequences), identify_constant and conjecture_relation (PSLQ, Ramanujan-Machine style), and search_existing_math (a 3.68M-document theorem index, dense + BM25). The results then go through applicability_checklist (a result's hypotheses split into atomic preconditions) and mapping_scaffold (needs-versus-guarantees structure mapping). verify_formal checks against the real Lean kernel, and add_finding writes verified results back into the index. Together these cover CFIX steps 2, 4 (exact matching only), 5 and 8 for mathematics. Its own agent benchmark is small: 18 tasks, Claude Fable 5, 18/18 with the tools vs 15/18 without. It is a retrieval test, not an import-yield test. Missing: superseeker-style transforms, coincidence p-values, fingerprints computed from paper spans or reference code, non-math fingerprint types, and a mandatory probe-first protocol.

closest.title: OEIS as a fingerprint file (Sloane, arXiv 2105.05111); Billey & Tenner, 'Fingerprint databases for theorems' (Notices AMS 2013, arXiv 1304.3866); FindStat; LMFDB; OEIS superseeker; Plouffe's Inverter / Inverse Symbolic Calculator
closest.overlap: These are the established human practice and the knowledge-base sources CFIX builds on. Billey & Tenner explicitly propose per-field fingerprint databases for finding unexpected connections between areas. Superseeker already implements the tolerant transform matching in CFIX step 4. FindStat matches a computed statistic, and maps between statistics, against a database. These are curated databases queried by people. Per-hit p-values and agents writing their own probes are absent. Tao's related databases, the Optimization Constants repository (Jan 2026, teorth/optimizationproblems) and the Exponent Pair Database (teorth/expdb), are ready-made CONST and EXPONENTS knowledge-base sources.

closest.title: Instance Space Analysis and Exploratory Landscape Analysis (Smith-Miles, Muñoz et al.); dataset meta-feature warm-starting in AutoML (e.g., Feurer et al. 2015, auto-sklearn; from memory, not re-verified this session)
closest.overlap: CFIX's LANDSCAPE and DATA_SIG channels already exist in this form. Computed instance or dataset features (fitness-distance correlation, autocorrelation, ELA features; dataset meta-features such as dimensionality and statistics) are matched against a library of previously characterized instances or datasets, and methods that worked on the nearest ones are transferred. This is a computed-feature join key for method import. It usually works within one problem class or ML task type and selects from a fixed algorithm portfolio. It is not an LLM ideation pipeline and does not pull methods from the literature.

closest.title: AlphaProof Nexus, 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search' (arXiv 2605.22763); OEIS Open benchmark (arXiv 2608.11941)
closest.overlap: These are agent systems attacking open Erdős problems (9 of 353 resolved) and OEIS conjectures (44/492 for AlphaProof Nexus; OEIS Open reports 147/492 for generic LMs at $50 per attempt). mathlas's README says AlphaProof Nexus uses OEIS as an oracle; I did not verify this. Both target proving, not retrieval by fingerprint. One finding bears on CFIX's T arm: OEIS Open reports that giving LMs 476k arXiv papers did not improve results on OEIS Open Lite. That concerns proving uncited-looking conjectures, not import retrieval, so it is weak evidence about CFIX.

closest.title: Kulikowski, 'Same Problem, Different Field' (JCDL 2026, arXiv 2609.07595); Zhou & Jia, 'Mechanism-centric cross-domain retrieval for scientific discovery: LLM agents for structural isomorphism beyond semantic similarity' (Knowledge-Based Systems 2026, doi 10.1016/j.knosys.2026.116667)
closest.overlap: These are the nearest cross-field retrievers in general science, and both key on text. Kulikowski uses LLM-distilled, domain-stripped skeletons. MCDF uses 26 domain agents that generate mechanism-equivalent keywords across 10 mechanism classes, plus a serendipity index that rewards semantic distance; it is evaluated on two case studies with LLM or human mechanism-alignment scores. Neither computes an executable invariant, which supports CFIX's claim that its key is different in kind.

art.to_make_novel:
The math channel is largely done, so CFIX should not claim that 'computed fingerprints as a literature join key' or 'an agent that does OEIS and constant lookup, then a premise check, then a Lean check' is new. Tao's Erdős-OEIS project does the first with AI-written code and has a documented literature find (#259). mathlas packages the second as MCP tools. Only the following combination is defensible as new.

(1) Fingerprints harvested from the literature itself: theorem formulas evaluated into terms, numeric tables parsed, and reference code run on canonical probe instances, each keyed to a verbatim span. This extends coverage beyond curated databases, and it is the part most likely to find imports that the OEIS does not index.
(2) A calibrated coincidence null: per-hit p-values against random records of the same type, with AUC against verified import success.
(3) One cross-type registry, with pre-registered tests showing that non-math packs (DATA_SIG, LANDSCAPE, PI_GROUPS, SPECTRUM) find imports that text retrieval misses. ELA/ISA and AutoML meta-learning already cover within-portfolio selection, so the claim has to be about pulling methods out of papers in other fields.
(4) IMPORT/PARTIAL/COINCIDENCE outcome typing used as a novelty gate, measured as verified import events per dollar.

Required changes to the first experiment:
- Add a fourth arm, M: the T arm plus the mathlas tools (identify_sequence, identify_constant, applicability_checklist). A win of C over T alone would only reproduce Tao's human workflow.
- Report separately how many hits came only through span-harvested or transform-based fingerprints and not through exact OEIS lookup.
- The OEIS 'late twin' backtest is a good contamination-free design; I found no prior use of it.

Search caveat: WebSearch was exhausted (200/200) and the arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex search endpoints returned 429 or 503. The searches ran through GitHub, Crossref, direct arXiv abstract pages and one blog fetch. Coverage of 2026 arXiv preprints is incomplete, especially for LLM + ELA work such as LLaMEA landscape features and for automated harvesting of sequences from papers.

feas.will_it_work:
It will work in mathematics, and the claim that it generalizes is unproven and probably weak.

**Mathematics.** Computing small cases and looking them up is already how mathematicians work. OEIS superseeker, FindStat and LMFDB do exactly this, and a code-enabled Opus 5.5 already does it unprompted when a problem has an integer-sequence form. So CFIX mostly formalizes an existing habit. Its real additions are the coincidence-null p-value and the IMPORT label in the ledger.

**Erdős problems.** Most are asymptotic or extremal statements, where small cases are either impossible to compute or say little about the answer. The known literature finds were largely made by text and LLM deep search, because the same problem was stated in similar words elsewhere. I expect under 30% of Tao-wiki 2(a) to be probe-able, and little gain over text search on the rest.

**Outside mathematics.** Most non-math fingerprints are either not discriminative or are old ideas under new names:
- PI_GROUPS: dimensionless groups such as Reynolds numbers are shared by huge families of unrelated problems.
- DATA_SIG: this is AutoML meta-feature algorithm selection, which historically gives modest gains over the single best solver.
- LANDSCAPE: this is ELA/ISA, which picks among known solvers, with limited transfer from benchmark suites to real instances.
- EXPONENTS and SPECTRUM: these are discriminative only in physics-like settings (universality classes, random-matrix statistics), where practitioners already match them.

**Verification of the proposal's evidence.** WebSearch was over budget this run, so I checked only two sources directly. arXiv 2601.22401 confirms 700 'open' Erdős problems, 13 addressed and 8 found in existing literature. The oeis/oeisdata repo has about 1,284 commits, which means bulk snapshots, not per-edit history; exact event dates must come from the oeis.org per-sequence history pages. The METR 6.7x 'imported' figure is unverified here. It is also mostly literature and paper imports within ML, not fingerprint-mediated imports, so it supports the value of imports in general, not CFIX's mechanism.
feas.eval_issues:
1. **The OEIS ground truth favours arm C by construction.** Most OEIS 'late twin' comments are created by a contributor who computed terms and searched OEIS, which is the CFIX mechanism itself. Arm C is re-enacting how the labels were made. Beating T on this set says nothing about fingerprints outside OEIS-style problems. Fix: stratify events by how they were discovered, or use identities found by other routes.

2. **The T baseline is unclear.** If T has a code sandbox plus the frozen OEIS snapshot as text, Opus 5.5 will compute terms and grep the stripped file itself, so C minus T measures scaffolding and prompting, not the idea. If T lacks code, it is a strawman. The honest baseline is 'same agent, same sandbox, same OEIS/LMFDB files, no fingerprint registry or matcher'.

3. **Answer leakage from the source paper.** The query comes from the cited source paper. That paper often contains the A-number or a 'see also' link, and it sits inside the frozen arXiv/OpenAlex corpus dated before the OEIS edit. The source paper and anything citing it must be excluded from the corpus, not just have the A-number and terms stripped from the query.

4. **Arm (a) is underpowered.** If 30% of 50-70 targets are probe-able, that is about 15-20 problems. A 10-point difference has a 95% interval of roughly ±20-25 points, so the stated threshold cannot be detected. Arm (b) with 80 paired events and a 20-point threshold (McNemar test) is marginally adequate.

5. **Dating is coarse.** oeisdata has about 1,284 bulk commits, so 'checked out the day before' has to be the nearest earlier snapshot. Edit dates need the oeis.org history pages.

6. **The generality claim is not tested until the expensive prospective stages (2)-(3).** Those stages have loose designs: two implementations per import, a vague 'industrial customer evaluator', and no power analysis.

On the positive side: metrics are scored by code, the success and falsification thresholds are pre-stated, the post-cutoff OEIS events are sound contamination control, and the calibration check (does the null p-value predict import success, measured by AUC) is well chosen.
feas.biggest_risk: The domain-agnostic claim fails and CFIX turns out to be a mathematics-only prior-art tool. Outside math and physics most problem cards have no crisp, discriminative invariant. The non-math types (DATA_SIG, LANDSCAPE, PI_GROUPS) collapse into existing AutoML meta-learning and ELA algorithm selection, with modest known gains. Mathematics, where it does work, pays mostly in reputation: Erdős prizes total about $60k across 152 problems. And every CFIX hit is by definition an IMPORT, which cannot be patented or claimed as novel. The design is also structured so the question gets answered late: the cheap first experiment tests only mathematics, and on a ground truth tilted toward C. So about $300 could buy a 'success' that says nothing about the general factory.
feas.fix:
Replace the OEIS-heavy first experiment with a cheap cross-domain backtest, and give it a fair baseline. The T arm gets the same sandbox and the same raw databases, so the only thing being tested is the fingerprint registry, the matcher and the null.

Build about 40 historical non-math transfer events whose outcome is known:
- physics and complex-systems universality-class identifications, via EXPONENTS and SPECTRUM;
- known method transfers between optimization problem families, via LANDSCAPE;
- dataset-to-method transfers with published winners, via DATA_SIG.

Alongside these, take about 40 OEIS events stratified by how they were discovered, with the source papers excluded from the corpus. Kill CFIX's generality claim early if C does not beat the sandbox-equipped T by at least 15 points on the non-math half.

Separately, deploy the math part now as a cheap novelty gate: an IMPORT check against OEIS, FindStat and LMFDB before any math-pack idea is claimed new. That value holds whatever the backtest shows.
feas.cost_realistic: The first experiment's costs are realistic: 150 targets x 3 arms at about $250-400, or inside the Max plan; data is free; probes run on local CPU. The fingerprint-harvesting figure ($100-300 of Haiku batch for 20k papers) covers parsing tables, but that estimate leaves out the hard part. Turning theorem formulas into correct computed terms is error-prone and needs validation, so expect low coverage or a few hundred dollars more for checking. Building the matchers and null models for 7 fingerprint types is mostly engineering time, not API dollars, and it is uncosted; plan for several engineer-weeks. The prospective math sweep at $1-2 per problem-arm is plausible. The under-$2k non-math POCs are plausible per pack, but with two independent implementations per import, spend multiplies quickly across packs.
feas.general_factory_value:
It has moderate value for a general factory, but mostly as infrastructure, not as a source of ideas.

1. **Novelty and prior-art gate.** This is its strongest general contribution. An IMPORT or COINCIDENCE label, backed by a computed match with a p-value, is much harder to game than an LLM novelty verdict. That matters because the repo's own pilot found LLM novelty ratings agreed with themselves only 53% of the time.
2. **Import channel.** It is a real import channel for math-like packs: combinatorics, number theory, and some physics and chemistry spectra.
3. **Non-math packs.** Here it largely reduces to meta-feature algorithm selection, useful but incremental.

It does not depend on the LLM-training domain. Its value is concentrated where money is scarce (reputational math), and it structurally cannot produce the novel, sellable or patentable ideas the factory's goal emphasizes.

vetted.name: Placebo-Labeled Transfer Atlas: executed, counterfactual labels for which cross-field sources help which problems

closest.title: Read, Grep, and Synthesize: Diagnosing Cross-Domain Seed Exposure for LLM Research Ideation (PaperGym; Choi & Song, arXiv 2605.11532, May 2026)
closest.overlap: Re-verified. This paper already contains the R-vs-D placebo contrast: targeted cross-domain retrieval compared with same-domain retrieval, no retrieval and a random diverse-seed control, across 7 ML domains. Cross-domain retrieval won more pairwise novelty comparisons than no retrieval and same-domain retrieval, but did not differ significantly from random diverse seeds. Rubric LLM judges scored novelty; no idea was executed, there was no weights-only analogy arm and no scramble arm, and no retrieval policy was learned from outcomes. The proposal's D arm is taken directly from this design. What is new in the proposal is execution, the W and S arms, and learning from the labels.

closest.title: Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning (Shen, Druckmann, Zou, arXiv 2605.11258, May 2026)
closest.overlap: This is the proposal's W arm. The model pulls out the problem's relational structure, generates its own cross-domain analogies and then searches for solutions, with no knowledge base. Claude Sonnet 4.5's novel-solution rate rose from 1.6% to 50.4%, as judged by an LLM, and 4 biomedical case studies were executed. It never compares self-generated analogies against retrieved real records or random records, so the proposal's R/D/W decomposition is not in it.

closest.title: Evaluating Retrieval Quality in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (eRAG; Salemi & Zamani, SIGIR 2024, arXiv 2404.13781)
closest.overlap: Closest match for labeling each retrieved item by downstream utility. Each retrieved document is given to the LLM on its own, and the resulting output is scored against the task's ground truth to produce that document's label. The setting is QA and fact-checking with answer-match metrics. There is no placebo or diversity control, no executed research idea, no cross-domain transfer atlas and no policy learning. It shows that per-item downstream-utility labeling is not new as a mechanism.

closest.title: EPR (Rubin, Herzig, Berant, NAACL 2022) and LLM-R (Wang et al., 2023/24): retrievers trained on downstream utility for in-context learning
closest.overlap: These train a retriever of demonstrations from labels derived from the LM's likelihood of the correct output given each candidate. Like the atlas, they learn from utility rather than relevance. The labels come from likelihood, not execution, the tasks are NLP benchmarks, and there are no placebo or weights-only arms. Cited from memory, not re-verified in this run.

closest.title: Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs (Zhou et al., arXiv 2508.16153, Aug 2025); related ReasoningBank / AWM-style experience memories
closest.overlap: A neural case-selection policy learns from environment rewards which stored cases to retrieve, and memory is rewritten from feedback. This is outcome-driven write-back of per-item retrieval utility, close to the proposal's step 7. Memento has no counterfactual placebo arms, and its memory holds past agent trajectories rather than cross-field literature. It does not pool what transfers where across domains through domain-stripped skeletons. A budget-matched evaluation (WebArena/WorkArena, cited in the proposal) found such memories matched or lost to a plain actor given the same tokens.

closest.title: MBA-RAG: a Bandit Approach for Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Tang et al., arXiv 2412.01572, Dec 2024); also Adaptive-RAG / Self-RAG
closest.overlap: A multi-armed bandit picks among retrieval strategies, including not retrieving, with a reward that trades accuracy against retrieval cost. This anticipates the proposal's portfolio rule of turning retrieval off where it does not pay per token. The domain is QA, the choice is between retrieval strategies rather than individual source records, there are no placebo controls and nothing is executed.

closest.title: Accelerating Innovation Through Analogy Mining (Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf, KDD 2017); Kang et al., Augmenting Scientific Creativity with an Analogical Search Engine (2022); Chan, Dow & Schunn 2015 on inspiration distance
closest.overlap: Human-subjects precedent for the question of whether a specific retrieved analogy beats another inspiration source. Hope et al. found that analogies retrieved by their purpose/mechanism model raised people's likelihood of generating creative ideas compared with analogies from traditional retrieval. From memory, the study also had a random-analogy condition, which the abstract could not confirm. Kang et al. and Chan/Schunn study analogical search and inspiration distance, with outcomes rated by humans or measured observationally. No LLM generator, no execution and no learned atlas.

closest.title: Learned inspiration retrievers: MOOSE-Star / ResearchBench, TCA-SIR (arXiv 2607.28498), MUSES (2609.00313), RATIO (2608.27394), HyBIRD (2606.28336)
closest.overlap: These learn P(inspiration | background) for hypothesis generation. Training and evaluation use the inspirations that authors cited or endorsed, and none uses counterfactual executed utility. They are the retriever the atlas would replace or re-weight. The panel's earlier verified map already names this gap: no benchmark labels inspirations by counterfactual downstream utility.

closest.title: Execution-trained ideators: Towards Execution-Grounded Automated AI Research (Si, Yang, ..., Hashimoto, arXiv 2601.14525); MLE-Ideator (Zhang et al., arXiv 2601.17596); HARPA-Scorer (2510.00620); Wen et al. (2506.00794)
closest.overlap: These use executed outcomes as the reward or label, through RL or evolution for the ideator, or through outcome-trained scorers of ideas. All of them attribute value at the level of the idea or the generator, never to the knowledge-base source that seeded the idea, and none has random-source or weights-only controls. The atlas's execution-labelled learning signal is established here; attributing it to the source record is not.

closest.title: Google ERA: An AI system to help scientists write expert-level empirical software (Aygün et al., Nature 2026)
closest.overlap: Research ideas from the literature are injected as text into an LLM tree search and scored by execution. The full text in the local cache was checked and has no random-idea placebo arm, no per-source utility labels and no learned source policy.

closest.title: OptiLex wf1 Single-Graft Distance Ladder (internal proposal in this panel)
closest.overlap: Thompson sampling over 4 field-distance bands of domain-stripped skeletons within the LM proxy, with a random-diverse-seed arm, all executed. The atlas extends it to a (target, record) granularity, adds W and S controls, pools across packs and writes labels back into the knowledge base. The underlying placebo logic and skeleton index are shared.

art.to_make_novel: Search caveat: live search was heavily limited. The session's WebSearch budget was already spent (200/200), and arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429. Only one arXiv API query ran, and it found nothing new beyond PaperGym, LacMaterial, RecEvolve and HippoSpark, none of which overlap on the core claim. The verdict therefore rests on 7 papers re-fetched here (PaperGym, AR, eRAG, Memento, MBA-RAG, the Hope 2017 abstract, RecEvolve), the ERA full text in the local cache, and the panel's earlier verified literature map (scratchpad lit.txt). That map states that no benchmark labels inspirations by counterfactual downstream utility and that nobody updates retrievers or knowledge representations from execution. The literature is not missing any single component. Per-item downstream-utility labels exist (eRAG, EPR/LLM-R). Outcome-learned retrieval memory exists (Memento). Bandit switching of retrieval against cost exists (MBA-RAG). The R-vs-random-diverse placebo exists, judged by LLMs (PaperGym). Weights-only analogies exist (AR). Execution-trained ideators exist (Si et al., MLE-Ideator). What was not found is the combination: executed, multi-implementation, token-matched paired labels that separate specific retrieval (R-D) from diversity (D-W) and from parametric analogy (W), with a scramble control, pooled across domain packs through domain-stripped skeleton features into a Bayesian atlas that drives Thompson retrieval and a per-pack rule for switching retrieval off. The novelty rests on four things. (1) The executed three-way decomposition, the core scientific contribution; the pilot with its pre-registered verdicts is novel as a result, whatever the outcome. (2) Held-out-pack prediction of specific utility (evaluation step 1), the test that cross-field transfer structure exists and is learnable. (3) Execution-derived utility written back per record and skeleton, with a test-retest check. (4) Accounting per token and per kWh. Five changes would sharpen it. Cite eRAG, EPR/LLM-R, Memento and MBA-RAG as mechanism-level prior art, so the claim is not 'first to label retrieval by utility'. Credit PaperGym for the D-arm design and state that the proposal's increment is execution plus the W and S arms. Merge with wf1's Single-Graft ladder as one shared-control experiment, since band-level Thompson sampling there is a special case of the atlas. Put the novelty claim on cross-pack pooling and held-out-pack prediction rather than on the Thompson policy, which follows standard bandit-RAG practice. Re-run a targeted search for the 2026 terms 'counterfactual inspiration utility', 'retrieval placebo' and 'executed ablation of literature grounding' once the search APIs recover, before claiming priority publicly.

feas.will_it_work:
Partly. The diagnostic core should work. The atlas built on top of it mostly will not at any budget OptiLex can afford.

What works: the three-arm placebo design (R = retrieved record, D = random diverse record, W = weights only) asks the right causal question. It is the question the evidence leaves open:
- PaperGym (Choi & Song, arXiv 2605.11532; 7 ML domains; rubric LLM judges) found that cross-domain retrieval beat no retrieval but showed "no significant difference from a random diverse-seed control". That is a judged result, not an executed one.
- Analogical Reasoning (Shen, Druckmann, Zou, arXiv 2605.11258; novelty judged by an LLM) raised the novel-solution rate from as low as 1.6% to over 50% with no knowledge base. It also reports 4 executed biomedical case studies, including a 13-fold gain on a perturbation metric.

So the weights-only baseline is strong and the D-arm null is real. Executing R against D against W is the correct next step, and each of the three pre-stated verdicts changes what gets built.

Why the atlas will not work:
(a) Per-record and per-(record, target) specific-utility labels (SU = y_R - y_D) are tiny differences of noisy, mostly-failed outcomes. The implementation-lottery audit (Ning et al., arXiv 2607.26587) found implementation variance 5-10x larger than same-artifact rerun variance. One implementation draw picked a different winner than the mean of the other two in 25.6% and 43.6% of decisions. DeepScientist had roughly 21 of 5,000 ideas show progress. Most labels will sit near zero with wide intervals, so Thompson sampling over records and record-level write-back will mostly be sampling noise.
(b) Pooling across packs through domain-stripped skeletons assumes transfer value is a property of the skeleton. Nothing yet supports that.
(c) The expected pilot outcome given the priors is 'diversity only', 'weights suffice' or 'inconclusive'. In any of those cases the atlas is never built. The pilot is where the value is.

Specific mechanism flaws:
- The W arm uses a different prompt (an Analogical-Reasoning prompt) from the R and D arms (structure-mapping). The D-minus-W contrast therefore mixes 'external text' with 'prompt style'.
- The LM pack has only ONE target, and each idea gets 1 implementation with 3 seeds. That breaks the proposal's own rule of at least 2 implementations. The 1.11x detectable effect from 3 seeds (FEASIBILITY.md) covers seed noise only, not implementation variance.
- ALE-Bench is AtCoder Heuristic Contest problems from before Opus 5.5's June 2026 knowledge cutoff, with published editorials and top solutions. The W arm can recall winning approaches. A 20-minute Claude Code session on a multi-hour optimisation problem mainly measures implementation quality (simulated annealing or beam-search tuning), not the seeded idea. Calling this 'conservative' understates it: it pushes the test toward an uninformative null.
feas.eval_issues:
Strengths: every result is executed; the verdicts are pre-registered; tokens are matched and logged; there is a scramble arm; there are 2 implementations per idea on ALE-Bench; held-out-pack prediction and time-split test-retest are both planned. The problems are power, clustering, arm construction and contamination.

1) The power claim is overstated. 48 R-D pairs give about 0.79 power for a paired effect of d = 0.4 only if the pairs are independent. They are nested in about 9 targets (1 LM target and 8 ALE problems). If SU varies between targets, the effective n moves toward 9, where power is about 0.22. A paired d of 0.4 is also optimistic given PaperGym's judged null for R vs D.

2) The KB-SPECIFIC verdict also requires Spearman(skeleton-match score, SU) >= 0.3. At n = 48 the 95% CI around 0.3 runs from about 0.00 to 0.55, and at 16 LM records from about -0.26 to 0.71. The rule will pass or fail largely by chance.

3) The arms are not isolated. W uses a different prompt template from R and D, so D - W is not a clean 'diversity' contrast. The fix is one template with a source slot: the retrieved record, a random in-band record, or a source the model generates itself.

4) The placebo leaks topicality. R is skeleton-matched to the target by construction, so R - D also measures 'on-topic text' against 'off-topic text'. The proposal names this risk and says residual topicality is reported, but reporting it does not remove it.

5) Contamination. The 40 ALE-Bench AtCoder Heuristic Contest problems predate Opus 5.5's June 2026 cutoff, and the extremal-constructions and OEIS-style content is likely in training data too. This inflates W and compresses R - D toward zero. Post-cutoff contests would avoid it.

6) The LM pack has 1 implementation per idea, so idea effects are confounded with implementation luck. The proxy also needs a locked evaluation harness (fixed token budget, no validation leakage, no tokenizer or eval edits), or ideas will game the multiplier.

7) 'Top idea per arm' needs a selection rule that is not an LLM judge, or the judge bias comes back in.

8) Held-out pack transfer uses a top-quartile vs bottom-quartile SU comparison. It is underpowered unless the new pack gets dozens of labelled records, which is expensive in VCC or metabolomics.

Not circular, and resistant to Goodhart where the verifiers use private or held-out cases. ALE-Bench should score on freshly generated seeds, not only the public cases.
feas.biggest_risk: Signal-to-noise. The true specific-retrieval effect (R vs D) is likely small; PaperGym found no significant R-vs-D difference even with LLM judges. Implementation variance is 5-10x rerun variance (arXiv 2607.26587), most executed ideas yield about nothing, and there are only about 9 targets. The pilot will most likely return a CI that includes 0, which can be read as either 'diversity only' or 'underpowered'. The expensive atlas and Thompson-sampling layer would then be built on labels that are mostly noise. Contaminated AHC problems and 20-minute sessions make this worse, because the ALE-Bench pack mostly measures implementation skill and recall of known solutions.
feas.fix:
Replace the atlas with a lean, target-heavy R/D/W diagnostic and treat it as a hard gate.
- Use one prompt template whose only difference between arms is the source slot: the retrieved record, a random in-band record, or a model-generated distant source (W).
- Add a manipulation check that the idea instantiates the source's skeleton roles.
- Spread the budget over many targets rather than many records: at least 30 targets across 3 cheap packs, with 1 R, 1 D and 1 W per target and at least 2 implementations each (the LM pack included).
- Use contamination-free targets: AtCoder Heuristic Contests after June 2026 with the official generators, fresh extremal-construction instances, and several distinct LM-proxy targets (e.g. data efficiency at different token budgets, or on different corpora).
- Score on held-out generated cases.
- Analyse target-level paired differences with a rank test and pre-register a smallest effect of interest (e.g. SU >= 0.2 SD per 1M tokens).
- Build per-record or per-skeleton write-back only if KB-SPECIFIC passes and a time-split replication follows.

This keeps the proposal's real value, a causal answer on whether the knowledge base pays, at roughly the same cost. It makes a null result interpretable and removes most of the atlas engineering.
feas.cost_realistic:
Realistic for the pilot, optimistic for everything after it.
- Haiku batch for 2,000 skeletons: $10-20 is plausible.
- LM proxy: 120 runs of 2-3 minutes each, about 6-8 rented GPU-hours, $15-30.
- ALE-Bench scoring on CPU is cheap.
- 200 agent sessions of about 20 minutes each (about 60-70 session-hours) fit in a Claude Max plan over one to two weeks of rate-limited running. The $250-400 API-equivalent figure is unverified.
- Under $500 in cash is credible.

Not counted:
- Roughly 1-3 engineer-weeks: the skeleton extractor, placebo matching on band, length and tier, a role-instantiation checker, a locked LM-proxy harness, ALE-Bench integration and the mixed-model analysis.
- Doubling LM implementations to meet the proposal's own rule of at least 2.
- Steady-state placebo labelling. At 3x per labelled target on 10-20% of targets that is affordable, but the atlas needs many labels per skeleton-pack cell to beat its prior. For expensive packs (VCC, metabolomics) that means thousands of dollars per pack, well beyond the stated figures.
feas.general_factory_value:
High for the diagnostic, low to moderate for the atlas.

The three-arm executed placebo protocol (R vs D vs W, token-matched, multi-implementation) is domain-agnostic. It answers the central architecture question of the general factory: does seeding Opus 5.5 with a human-research knowledge base pay for its tokens, compared with random diverse seeding or the model's own analogies? The answer decides retrieval spend in every pack, and the 'switch retrieval off' rule directly serves OptiLex's combined data, compute and energy efficiency goal. The protocol can be reused as a standing per-pack check on 10-20% of targets.

It is not tied to LLM-training work, since the LM proxy is only one calibration pack. But the proposed first packs (LM proxy, contaminated ALE-Bench) are weak stand-ins for the high-impact domains (VCC, metabolomics), and cross-pack transfer through skeletons is unproven. The record-level atlas and write-back are likely to be noise at factory scale.

vetted.name: Portable Mechanism Ledger (PML): cross-domain clade credit for domain-stripped mechanisms

closest.title: Memory Transfer Learning: How Memories are Transferred Across Domains in Coding Agents (arXiv 2604.14004, Apr 2026)
closest.overlap: This is the closest executed test of cross-domain transfer by abstraction level. The authors pool memories from 6 heterogeneous coding benchmarks at four abstraction levels, from concrete traces to abstract insights. Cross-domain memory improves average performance by 3.7%, and they find that abstraction dictates transferability: high-level insights transfer, while low-level traces cause negative transfer. What they transfer is mostly meta-knowledge (validation routines). There is no per-item credit, no variance split into portability, no gate that switches transfer off, and all domains are coding-agent benchmarks rather than structurally different packs. It is the natural baseline for PML: an uncredited pool of abstract insights.

closest.title: Read, Grep, and Synthesize: Diagnosing Cross-Domain Seed Exposure for LLM Research Ideation (PaperGym, arXiv 2605.11532, May 2026)
closest.overlap: This paper asks whether cross-domain mechanism retrieval helps ideation beyond simple exposure to diverse mechanisms. It covers seven ML domains, and its seeds are mechanisms extracted from papers. Cross-domain retrieval beat the no-retrieval and same-domain baselines but was not significantly different from a random diverse-seed control. It is judged by rubric rather than executed, so it does not measure realized outcomes. It is still the key prior result behind PML's random-skeleton placebo arm: PML's winner-skeleton arm must beat random skeletons, which PaperGym's targeted retrieval did not do on judged novelty.

closest.title: Hyperagents / DGM-H (arXiv 2603.19461, Mar 2026)
closest.overlap: Self-referential agents (DGM extension) evolve their own improvement procedure. The meta-level improvements they discover, such as persistent memory and performance tracking, transfer across domains and accumulate across runs. This is executed cross-domain transfer of discovered mechanisms, but only at the agent-scaffold level. It is not a ledger of task-level mechanisms, has no portability estimate, and uses no transfer bandit.

closest.title: optimize_anything (GEPA project, arXiv 2605.19633, May 2026)
closest.overlap: One LLM text-optimization system runs multi-task search with cross-problem transfer. The paper reports that multi-task search beats independent optimization at equal per-problem budget, with benefits growing with the number of related tasks (ablations across 3 domains). Transfer happens between related tasks through shared artifacts and side information. It is not transfer of domain-stripped mechanisms, has no credit model, and does not measure portability between unrelated domains.

closest.title: EMO-STA (Gozeten et al., arXiv 2605.22613, May 2026)
closest.overlap: This paper evolves a shared archive of executable programs across a task family, across 8 families (continuous optimization, geometric construction, modeling, algorithmic optimization). It reports robust transfer to unseen tasks within a family. I confirmed it has no mechanism abstraction and no lineage credit, and it does not transfer across families. The proposal's own description of it is accurate.

closest.title: Evolution Fine-Tuning / Finch Collection (arXiv 2606.29082, Jun 2026)
closest.overlap: It asks directly whether experience from one optimization domain (e.g. GPU kernels) helps another (e.g. math conjectures). It fine-tunes 2-9B models on 156K evolution trajectories spanning 371 tasks in 10 domains, and gets +10.22% on 22 held-out tasks. Cross-domain transfer is carried implicitly in model weights, not as an explicit, credited mechanism ledger, and portability is not decomposed per mechanism.

closest.title: What Do Evolutionary Coding Agents Evolve? (EvoTrace/EvoReplay, arXiv 2605.20086, May 2026)
closest.overlap: It annotates every edit in evolutionary coding traces (4 frameworks, 16 math and algorithm tasks) with one of 9 recurring edit types. It finds that most gains come from a few edit types and that about 30% of added lines are re-introductions of previously deleted code. This is close to PML's controlled operator vocabulary and its collapse and hyperparameter-only exclusions. It does not transfer across domains or credit mechanisms. It is useful as a vocabulary source and as a confound warning (re-tuning vs new structure).

closest.title: MFEA-II: Multifactorial Evolutionary Algorithm with online transfer parameter estimation (Bali, Ong, Gupta, Tan; IEEE TEVC 2020; cited from memory)
closest.overlap: This is classical evolutionary multitasking. It learns inter-task similarity online (a transfer-parameter matrix) and cuts cross-task transfer when it would be negative. Conceptually it is the same as PML step 6, where the estimated rho gates the transfer budget. It works on solution-level genetic transfer between numeric optimization tasks, with no LLM and no mechanism abstraction. PML should cite it as the precedent for learned transfer gating.

closest.title: HyFlex / CHeSC 2011 cross-domain hyper-heuristics (Ochoa, Burke et al.; cited from memory)
closest.overlap: The operators here are domain-independent classes (mutation, ruin-recreate, local search, crossover) behind a 'domain barrier'. Hyper-heuristics credit these operator classes online across six structurally different combinatorial domains, and cross-domain generalization of the selection policy is the benchmark's explicit goal. This is the long-standing analogue of crediting domain-stripped operator skeletons across domains. It is limited to combinatorial problems, with hand-written low-level heuristics and no LLM instantiation.

closest.title: Ideas Have Genomes / IG-Bench (arXiv 2607.08758, Jul 2026)
closest.overlap: It represents ideas as typed 'Idea Genome' objects, with a diff that records inheritance, mutation, external import (cross-lineage transfer) and novel insertion. That is structurally similar to PML's skeleton-plus-clade bookkeeping. It is a text benchmark with judged lineage fit, not executed outcomes, and has no portability measurement.

closest.title: Huxley-Godel Machine (arXiv 2510.21614) and Idea-Catalyst (arXiv 2603.12226)
closest.overlap: These are already listed in the proposal. HGM gives clade-metaproductivity credit within one domain. Idea-Catalyst does domain-agnostic reframing for cross-field retrieval, judged rather than executed. I found no newer paper that joins the two.

art.to_make_novel:
The pieces already exist separately:
- Executed cross-domain transfer of abstract insights: Memory Transfer Learning 2604.14004, Hyperagents 2603.19461, optimize_anything 2605.19633, EFT 2606.29082.
- Learned gating of transfer by estimated task similarity: MFEA-II.
- Crediting domain-independent operator classes across structurally different domains: HyFlex/CHeSC hyper-heuristics.
- Edit-type vocabularies: EvoTrace.
- Clade credit: HGM.
- Cross-domain mechanism seeding with a random-diverse-seed control: PaperGym 2605.11532, where targeted seeding did not beat random seeds on judged novelty.

I found no work that runs PML's core test. That test asks whether an executed mechanism's verified win in one structurally different domain (LM training, tabular ML, combinatorial heuristics) predicts the verified win of its domain-stripped skeleton in another domain. The design compares winner, loser and random skeletons, uses 2 independent implementations each, and estimates a portability variance split (rho) that turns transfer on or off. The novelty therefore rests on that pre-registered test and the rho gate, not on the ledger, the clade credit or the hindsight relabeling.

To make the novelty claim safe:
(1) Cite MFEA-II and HyFlex as precedents for learned transfer gating and cross-domain operator credit, and claim only the LLM-instantiated, executed-mechanism version.
(2) Add a Memory-Transfer-Learning-style arm: an uncredited pool of abstract insights from other packs. This shows that credit, not just abstraction, adds value.
(3) Treat PaperGym's null (targeted seeding did not beat random diverse seeds) as the headline risk. The pre-registered winner-vs-random contrast is the answer to it, so report it first.
(4) Use EvoTrace's edit taxonomy to exclude re-tuning and re-introduction gains before counting a skeleton as portable.
(5) Report per-pack-pair rho so that a near-pack effect (LM-tabular) is not presented as cross-domain portability. Do not generalize from these three packs to Lean or protein design until those packs are measured.

Coverage caveats:
- The WebSearch budget was exhausted, and arXiv and Semantic Scholar returned rate-limit errors (HTTP 429). I searched mainly through the Hugging Face papers index and OpenAlex.
- The Kulikowski paper (2609.07595) and the multi-objective hindsight paper (2609.26918) were not indexed there, so I could not check them.
- MFEA-II and HyFlex are cited from memory.

feas.will_it_work:
Partly. The bookkeeping will run: skeleton extraction, a ledger, and a mixed model are all easy to build. The scientific bet is the weak part. It assumes that an idea's executed success in one pack predicts the success of its coarse, domain-stripped skeleton in a structurally different pack. That is unlikely to be large, for four reasons.

(1) The vocabulary is small. 4 loci x 12 operators x 6 signals x 4 triggers is about 1.2k cells, and it throws away the domain-specific content that usually makes an idea work. Given OptiLex's own mode collapse (30 of 30 clean Opus ideas fell into 3 families; IDEAS_FACTORY.md), many stage-0 winners and losers will map to the same skeleton. The winner and loser labels then conflict at the skeleton level.

(2) Most of the target-pack variance will come from the instantiating LLM and from how tuned each incumbent is, not from the skeleton.

(3) Where portability does show up, it will probably be carried by stock, universally useful operators: average/ensemble, restart/perturb, precondition/rescale, schedule/anneal. Those pass the primary test but are known. The collapse-to-known filter removes them, and what is left is a tiny, underpowered subset.

(4) The stage-0 design assumes 36 true winners (12 per pack). In the LM pack, against a tuned incumbent at z>2 with reproduction required, a realistic in-pack win rate is more like 2-5 of 40. So the "top 12" will be mostly nulls, and the winner-vs-loser contrast will be attenuated.

The mechanism most likely to yield a real positive is the narrow one: search-procedure operators moving between the two combinatorial and tabular CPU packs (the proposal's "near" pairing). The ambitious cross-domain claims (LM to heuristics, or seeding protein binders before any in-pack data) are unlikely to be supported.

Hindsight goal switching is sensible bookkeeping. arXiv 2609.26918 (Bonin et al.) does report "19 of 36" degraded settings, but its mechanism is critic preference-coverage collapse in preference-conditioned MORL. That is only loosely analogous here, so keeping separate per-objective ledgers is sufficient.

Claims checked:
- EMO-STA abstract verified: "improves over matched-compute single-task evolution in most settings", but within a task family.
- The HGM CMP correlation numbers (0.51-0.87 vs 0.27-0.44) are not in the HGM abstract. They could not be verified in this pass, and they concern coding-agent self-modification, not cross-domain idea transfer.
- The web search budget ran out, so Mule et al. is unverified.
feas.eval_issues:
Circularity and contamination are handled well: the extractor is outcome-blind, there is a random-skeleton null, verifiers are code-owned, k=2 implementations are required, and the held-out fourth pack has a placebo arm and an IID baseline. The main problems are power and construct validity.

(1) Power is overstated. The proposal treats about 140 instantiations per arm as independent.
