But a win is defined as z>2 reproduced by the second implementation, so the real unit is the skeleton x pack cell: 36 skeletons x 2 packs = 72 cells per arm, clustered by skeleton. My simulation of the pre-registered contrast used a cluster-robust test at one-sided alpha 0.05, 36 skeletons per arm and 2 target packs. Power for +10pp was about 34-44% at 20-30% base rates, and about 47-63% at 5-15% base rates. The proposal claims 60-70%. Attenuation from mislabeled "winners" (winner's curse, too few true winners) lowers it further. The likely outcome is an inconclusive null, followed by a doubled stage 1.

(2) Binary wins waste information. Analysing continuous z at the skeleton level would give substantially more power.

(3) The pack-normalised z (gain divided by incumbent seed sd) is not comparable across packs. Near-deterministic heuristic scorers, or tabular accuracy with tiny seed sd, make z>2 trivially easy. The variance components, and therefore rho, then partly measure how noisy each verifier is, not how portable skeletons are.

(4) The primary test (winner skeletons beat loser skeletons) measures whether the credit carries predictive signal. It does not measure whether transfer is useful. Generic stock operators can pass it while adding no novel wins. The decision-relevant contrast, transfer vs native generation in wins per dollar, comes only in the later held-out-pack phase.

(5) The collapse-to-known check needs a knowledge base for the tabular and heuristic packs, and those do not exist yet.

(6) Minor: the numbers do not add up. 72 origin skeletons x 2 packs x 2 implementations = 288, plus 24 random x 3 x 2 = 144, gives 432 stage-1 instantiations, not "about 336". Adding stage 0 (120 + 72) gives about 624 executed implementations in total.
feas.cost_realistic:
GPU and CPU costs are plausible. The LM pack gets about 200-210 tier-1 run-sets (stage 0: 64; stage 1: 144). At 0.1-0.3 H100-hours and $1.7-2.7/h, that is about $35-170. This is still unmeasured on GPU; SWARM.md phase 0 has not run.

LLM cost is underestimated by about 3-5x. OptiLex's own funnel table budgets about $1.5 of LLM spend per implement-and-test ($30-45 for 20-30 experiments). With about 624 implementations plus paired extractions, that comes to about $950-1,300 at API prices, not $150-250. The first experiment therefore realistically costs about $1.0-1.5k. That is still within the under-$2k POC ceiling, but it uses most of it on a test with less than 50% power.

The proposal correctly flags that sustained automated runs should use an API key rather than the Max plan, so the "near zero on Max" scenario should not be counted on.
feas.biggest_risk: The experiment spends about $1-1.5k and ends inconclusive, or it ends positive for the wrong reason. Coarse operator-level skeletons will mostly port through generic, already-known tricks (averaging, restarts, rescaling, annealing). The genuinely novel residue that survives the collapse-to-known filter will be far too small to power. Meanwhile, pack-specific noise scales (the z normalisation) and LLM implementation variance swamp any skeleton main effect. The high-value cross-domain transfers PML is motivated by (for example the unit-distance class-field-tower import) cannot be expressed in this vocabulary at all.
feas.fix:
Make the skeleton the unit of analysis and run the portability test first where executions cost almost nothing. Use 3-4 CPU packs: tabular, two or three combinatorial heuristic families, and optionally an AlphaEvolve-style construction checker. Use 150 or more origin skeletons, with a continuous per-pack-standardised effect, standardised by practical effect size or a rank against a baseline pool, not by seed sd. The primary contrast should be "transferred skeleton vs native generation at matched LLM spend" plus the random-skeleton placebo, not winner vs loser. Report results only on non-stock instantiations.

Add the LM pack only as a confirmatory arm once CPU-pack rho is clearly above zero. Drop the numpyro clade credit and Thompson allocation until then; a spreadsheet ledger is enough.

This makes the test several-fold better powered for similar or lower cost. It also directly answers the question that matters to the factory: does cross-pack transfer add verified wins per dollar?
feas.general_factory_value: Moderate but narrow. The ledger and the portability measurement are domain-agnostic infrastructure, and a measured, near-zero rho would be a useful negative result that stops the factory spending on cross-domain analogy. The controlled vocabulary, however, describes optimisation and search procedures (loci: data, parameters, search moves, evaluation). Its transfers into the high-impact packs would therefore improve the search loop (for example, restarts or annealing in protein-binder or construction search), not supply the domain insights that win prizes, bounties or licences. It helps a general factory's optimizer layer, and it is no more tied to LLM-efficiency work than any other procedure-level tool. It is unlikely to be the source of high-impact new ideas by itself.

vetted.name: Near-Miss Contrast Critic (NMCC): cheap verifiers mint executed minimal pairs to train and refresh critics

closest.title: Crome: Robust Reward Modeling via Causal Rubrics (Srivastava et al., 2025)
closest.overlap: This is the closest structural match for the pair design. It trains a reward model on 'causal augmentations', which are pairs differing only along a quality-driving attribute, and on tie-labelled 'neutral augmentations' that vary only spurious attributes such as length and format. That corresponds to NMCC's categories (a)-(d), the style control (e) and the 'indistinguishable' class. The difference is the labels. Crome's come from an oracle LLM and the domain is chat responses, so there are no executed effects or research ideas. Verified via the arXiv abstract page.

closest.title: Wen et al., Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
closest.overlap: It fine-tunes a pairwise outcome predictor (GPT-4.1, 51.4% to 77%). It pairs ideas only within the same paper, to remove confounds from hyperparameters and preprocessing. That partly anticipates NMCC's shared-implementation argument, since same-paper pairs share a setup. But the labels are published results rather than the system's own executions, and the pairs are not substance-controlled minimal diffs. Checked in the cached full text.

closest.title: Mule et al., Teaching Language Models to Forecast Research Success Through Comparative Idea Evaluation
closest.overlap: Qwen3-8B is trained on 11,488 published idea pairs and scored swap-consistently. The authors test paraphrase robustness and cross-domain time-split transfer, where accuracy collapses to 46-49%. The critic form (C3/C4) and the transfer question are the same as NMCC's. The labels are literature-derived natural pairs, not executed minimal pairs.

closest.title: AI Can Learn Scientific Taste / Scientific Judge (Tong et al., 2026)
closest.overlap: It trains pairwise judges with swap-consistent accuracy and tests cross-field transfer by training on CS only and evaluating on unseen fields and bioRxiv. The transfer design is the same as NMCC's held-out-pack test, but the labels are citation-impact pairs of different papers, not execution.

closest.title: Rehearse: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch
closest.overlap: A focused memory of executed outcomes from similar past attempts is given to the pre-execution judge (selective accuracy 56.9% to 83.5% on nanochat-style loops). This is essentially NMCC critic C2's in-context mechanism, minus the deliberately minted near-miss pairs.

closest.title: Si et al., Towards Execution-Grounded Automated AI Research
closest.overlap: It executes many LLM ideas as code diffs on nanoGPT and GRPO, generates and executes 'exploit variants' of successful ideas, and uses execution reward for RL on the ideator. So executed idea variants as diffs already exist. They train the generator, not a pairwise critic, and the variants are not controlled mechanism-level ablations with contrast labels.

closest.title: Red Queen Godel Machine (co-evolving agents and evaluators)
closest.overlap: Evaluators are promoted only against ground-truth anchor sets. This is the same as NMCC step 6's anchored promotion rule.

closest.title: One Run Is Not an Idea: The Implementation Lottery in Automated Research
closest.overlap: It supplies the motivating measurement: implementation variance of 33-45%, against 4-6% for reruns. It does not propose minimal-diff paired labels for training critics.

closest.title: SciStyleBench: Style Wins, Substance Loses (Ji et al., 2026)
closest.overlap: Style-only perturbations of fixed-substance ideas as a judge diagnostic, which is NMCC's control (e). It has no substance-varied or executed pairs.

closest.title: BrainBench / BrainGPT (Luo et al., Nature Human Behaviour 2025)
closest.overlap: Minimal-pair discrimination between real abstracts and results-altered ones, with small trained models reaching expert level. The pairs are minimal, but the labels come from the literature rather than execution, and the task rewards consistency with the literature.

closest.title: AblationBench (Abramovich et al., 2025) and AbGen (Zhao et al., 2025)
closest.overlap: Corpora of paper ablations built for planning ablations and judging ablation designs. Published ablation tables are a free, pre-existing source of near-miss-like labelled pairs, which NMCC should use as a baseline. Neither benchmark trains outcome critics on them.

closest.title: Matched molecular pairs / DeepDelta (cheminformatics) and deep mutational scanning (protein engineering)
closest.overlap: Other-field precedent for the core idea. Predictors are trained on measured property differences between minimally differing, executed variants: one chemical transformation, or one mutation. This is decades-old in chemistry. Known failure modes are activity cliffs and poor transfer from local pairs to distant pairs. It is the conceptual ancestor of 'executed minimal pairs train a delta-critic' but has never been applied to research-idea critics. Cited from prior knowledge; not re-verified this session.

closest.title: PIE: Learning Performance-Improving Code Edits (Shypula et al., 2023); R2E-Gym hybrid verifiers; mutation testing as an RLVR reward
closest.overlap: Executed pairs of code edits with measured outcomes (speedups, test pass/fail) used to train models or verifiers. The execution-labelled, minimal-diff idea is established in code. The target is correctness or speed against a fixed spec, not research-effect sizes with confidence intervals. PIE is cited from prior knowledge.

art.to_make_novel:
Coverage caveat: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200), and the arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned HTTP 429. The search therefore relied on about 45 cached 2025-2026 papers in the scratchpad, two live arXiv fetches and prior knowledge. A 2026 paper on exactly this could have been missed, so one more live search is advisable before committing budget.

What I could find: no work trains a pre-execution research-idea critic on executed, patch-locked, substance-varied minimal pairs and then tests transfer to natural pairs in a held-out, costly pack. Each component already exists separately:
- Crome's causal pairs plus tie-labelled neutral pairs, which is NMCC's pair and label design without the execution.
- Wen's within-paper pairing to control setup confounds.
- Mule's and Scientific Judge's pairwise small-model critics and cross-domain transfer tests.
- Rehearse's executed-outcome memory, which is NMCC arm C2.
- Red Queen Godel Machine's anchored evaluator promotion.
- Si et al.'s executed idea-variant diffs.
- Matched molecular pairs and DeepDelta delta-learning in chemistry, and PIE-style executed code-edit pairs.

The contribution is therefore the label source and the transfer question, not the loop architecture, and the write-up should say so. To make the claim defensible:
1. Cite Crome and matched molecular pairs / DeepDelta as the direct conceptual ancestors. Frame NMCC as applying executed, CI-bearing labels to research-idea critics. Pre-register chemistry's known activity-cliff and locality failure as the hypothesis to rule out.
2. Add a cheap-labels arm, C5: a critic trained on ablation rows mined from published papers, e.g. from AblationBench/AbGen-style corpora or Wen's within-paper pairs. These are free near-miss-like labels. Without this arm, a reviewer will say executed minting is unnecessary. NMCC should show executed near-misses beat mined literature ablations at matched label count.
3. Add a Crome-style arm: near-miss cards labelled by an LLM oracle instead of by execution, at the same pair count. This isolates whether the gain comes from execution labels or merely from the contrastive pair structure.
4. Keep the headline result as the cross-pack test: CPU-verifier minimal pairs transferring to GPU-pack natural pairs, run at matched execution budget. Report reproduction of near-miss labels across implementations as a secondary measurement contribution.

If items 2 and 3 are not run, the work reads as an incremental combination of Crome, Wen/Mule and Rehearse.

feas.will_it_work:
It will work in part. Minting executed minimal pairs is sound and cheap on CPU packs. The pre-registered hypothesis, that near-miss critics beat natural-pair critics by 8 pp or more on held-out natural LM pairs, is unlikely to be met or shown.

1. Task mismatch. A near-miss label answers "is component X load-bearing inside this idea, in this implementation?" The test asks "which of two different ideas wins?" These are different skills. Transfer is weak even between tasks that are much closer:
   - Mule et al. (arXiv 2605.21491, Table 2): SFT Qwen3-8B gets 77.10% swap-consistent accuracy in-domain (PapersWithCode pairs) but 45.67% cross-domain. GPT-5 gets 45.96% cross-domain.
   - Wen et al. (arXiv 2506.00794): fine-tuned GPT-4.1 plus retrieval gets 77% on 1,585 published test pairs but 63.6% on unpublished, AI-generated ideas.
   - The proposal misstates Wen: 1,585 pairs is the test set, and training used about 6,000 pairs.

2. Label economics. Most bases at the 7M-parameter proxy will be null. OptiLex's proxy only resolves about 1.11x with 3 seeds (FEASIBILITY.md). Ablating, swapping or inverting a null idea's component also gives a null result. So most near-miss labels will be 'indistinguishable', and the informative contrasts come only from the minority of bases that actually worked.
   - Realistic yield is tens to low hundreds of decisive CPU pairs, not the 1-2k the risks section assumes. The design itself implies about 600 CPU pairs.
   - For comparison, Mule trained on 11,488 pairs and Wen on about 6,000. The C4 LoRA arm is therefore very likely data-starved. The in-context Opus arm (C2) is the realistic one.

3. The sign-agreement filter is weak. For null ideas, two implementations agree in sign about 50% of the time by chance. The filter keeps noise unless it also requires each implementation to be significant.

4. Low noise is not the same as validity. The implementation-lottery paper (arXiv 2607.26587; Ning et al.) supports the noise claim: implementation explains 33% and 45% of within-task variance, against 6% and 4% for reruns (13 OpenML tasks, DeepSeek v4 Pro implementers). That is exactly why a patch-locked label is precise but tied to one implementation. The ≥85% second-implementation reproduction check is the right guard, but it is not in the budget.

5. Where the idea has real value: executed near-miss pairs are a good source of retrieval evidence (Rehearse-style focused memory, arXiv 2607.27687: late-loop judge selective accuracy fell from 82.8% to 56.9%; focused memory restored it to 83.5%). They are also good for soundness and ablation triage.
feas.eval_issues:
The evaluation is non-circular in its labels, which is good: every label comes from execution, not a judge. It is underpowered, and one of its criteria is close to trivial.

(1) Power. The test set is about 150-250 'decisive' pairs, but they are drawn from only 30 LM ideas. Pairs are not independent, so the effective sample is about 30 items. Pairwise accuracy is then essentially a Kendall-tau statistic: its null SE is about 6-7 pp for n=30. The SE of a paired difference between two critics is roughly 5-7 pp. A pre-registered 8 pp margin therefore has power of about 30-50%, and the likely outcome is an inconclusive CI straddling zero.

(2) The style-control criterion is near-circular. Arm (e) has an identical patch, and the cards are canonicalized. Any critic that sees the diff, or reads canonicalized cards with the style stripped, gets 'no difference' trivially. The comparison to SciStyleBench's 0.504 (arXiv 2608.01666) is a metric mismatch: that figure is a substance-recognition rate over 600 ideas × 15 style variants, not a tie-rate on identical-substance pairs.

(3) Shortcut leakage. The original card is human- or generator-authored with a coherent rationale; variants are machine-minted. Unless the cards are rewritten blind, the critic can learn which card is the original. Repair variants exist only for failed bases, so the "original wins" prior persists on successful bases.

(4) Selection bias. Keeping only sign-stable bases and decisive test pairs makes the test easier for every critic. This is fine for comparing critics but inflates absolute accuracy, and the result must not be read as field accuracy.

(5) 'Held-out pack' is near-domain transfer: tabular ML plus combinatorial heuristics to LM training, both code-executable ML. A positive result says little about wet-lab or prize packs.

(6) The matched-executions design is asymmetric. n natural executions give about n²/2 correlated pairs, while near-misses give about 5 pairs per 6 executions. State which unit is matched, and bootstrap by idea for the training-side comparison too.

(7) The operational test (verified wins per executed run under critic ordering vs zero-shot Opus vs random) is the most decision-relevant endpoint. It is also resistant to Goodhart, since it scores fresh execution. But it is unpowered and unspecified: no number of ideas, no epochs, no MDE.
feas.biggest_risk: The most likely outcome is an expensive null. Skill at judging whether a component is load-bearing within one idea probably does not transfer to ranking different ideas; published outcome predictors already fall to near chance across domains (Mule SFT: 77.1% in-domain vs 45.67% cross-domain). And the held-out test, effectively 30 LM ideas, is too small to tell a real 8 pp gain from noise. The team would then build a patch-locked minting pipeline, a fidelity checker, three packs and a LoRA stack, and come away with no actionable answer on critic transfer.
feas.fix:
Stage it, and make it powered and pointwise:

1. Enlarge the held-out set. Raise it to 100 or more LM ideas; tier-1 proxy runs cost roughly $0.3-1 per 3-seed set. Change the primary endpoint to idea-level prediction ("beats the stacked baseline by at least the MDE", scored by AUROC or Spearman against executed effect) with a pre-computed power analysis. Pairwise accuracy over dependent pairs is not a good primary endpoint.

2. Drop the Qwen LoRA arm from the pilot. About 600 mostly-tie pairs will not train it. Test only C0 vs C1 vs C2, meaning Opus with retrieved natural vs near-miss executed evidence.

3. Run an in-pack check first. Before the cross-pack claim, spend about $30 to check whether near-miss evidence beats natural evidence on held-out ideas within the tabular pack. Only if that shows a gain of 5 pp or more should the LM transfer test and the operational queue-ordering test run.

4. Fix the style criterion. Replace the style-only criterion with blind-rewritten cards for both arms, so the original-vs-minted shortcut is removed.
feas.cost_realistic:
The compute figures are plausible; the LLM and engineering lines are underestimated.

- Compute: CPU packs under $20. The LM tier-1 runs are cheap (a 7M-parameter model on 1-4M tokens), so $45-120 GPU is plausible or even generous. LoRA at $10-20 is fine.
- Implementation tokens: roughly 210 base implementations (120 CPU + 60 LM, each twice) plus about 750 patch-locked variant implementations, plus fidelity checks. Agentic coding at about 50-200k tokens each comes to about 50-150M tokens. That is likely $300-900 at API prices, not $100-250, unless it runs on Max within rate limits.
- Critic scoring: C0-C2 in both orders over hundreds of pairs, with retrieved exemplars, is about 10-30M input tokens, so $50-150 is plausible.
- Unbudgeted: second-implementation replication of near-miss labels (needed for the 85% criterion) adds 20-50%.
- Realistic total: about $600-1,500 in cash, which is still under the $2k POC ceiling. The real cost is 2-4 weeks of engineering: the three pack harnesses, the diff-fidelity checker and the canonicalizer.
feas.general_factory_value:
Moderate. The critic, the outcome ledger and anchor-set promotion are the domain-agnostic heart of a general factory. A calibrated, execution-anchored triage critic would raise throughput in every pack, and the discipline of promoting critics only on executed anchors carries over to every domain.

But near-miss minting needs cheap, patchable, re-executable implementations. That exists in code/ML packs (tabular, heuristics, LM proxy, Kaggle-style), not in the expensive packs where a transferred critic would matter most (wet lab, hardware, prize submissions), where each variant costs as much as the base. The planned test (tabular to LM) is ML-to-ML transfer, so even a positive result would not show that the critic helps outside ML.

It does not directly produce sellable ideas, bounties or licensing revenue; it is infrastructure. The most transferable, low-cost piece is using executed near-miss pairs as retrieval evidence for the Opus critic in code-executable packs.

vetted.name: Fidelity-Weighted Ledger (FWL): randomized cross-rung audits that learn when cheap verifiers can be trusted, idea by idea

closest.title: Multi-fidelity Bayesian Optimization with Multiple Information Sources of Input-dependent Fidelity (iMFBO; Fan, Yoon, Dougherty, Urban, Alexander, Arroyave, Qian, UAI 2024)
closest.overlap: Directly models low-to-high fidelity trust as a function of the input x, using learnable, input-dependent noise models in a GP, so the optimizer learns where a cheap source can be trusted. This is FWL step 4, lambda_d(x) plus bias_d(x), inside one optimization problem. Related work also makes the cross-fidelity scaling input-dependent: Le Gratiet's recursive co-kriging with rho(x), Perdikaris et al. 2017's NARGP, and Kennedy and O'Hagan 2000 itself, which allows rho as a regression on x. The proposal's claim that MF-BO treats cross-fidelity correlation as 'usually stationary across inputs' is therefore overstated. What FWL adds is a pre-registered, judge-free novelty covariate and pooling across heterogeneous packs, not input-conditional fidelity itself.

closest.title: The Selective Labels Problem (Lakkaraju et al., KDD 2017); reject inference with below-cutoff random approvals in credit scoring
closest.overlap: Studies the core problem FWL step 3 addresses: outcomes are observed only for candidates a screening policy accepted, so a cheap screener's false-negative rate is unidentified. Credit-scoring practice approves a random or propensity-known slice of rejected applicants and reweights. This is the same device as FWL's randomized, propensity-logged promotion of R0 losers with IPW estimation of R0 error rates. The same idea appears as randomized 'shadow review' of auto-rejects in QA pipelines and as retesting random inactives to estimate HTS false-negative rates.

closest.title: Active Statistical Inference (Zrnic and Candes, 2024); Prediction-Powered Inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023); AutoEval Done Right (Boyeau et al., 2024); Prediction-Powered Active Testing (2607.08347, Jul 2026)
closest.overlap: A mature statistical framework for combining cheap proxy predictions with a budgeted sample of expensive gold labels. Labels are acquired with known, covariate-dependent probabilities (oversampling uncertain items), and estimates stay unbiased with valid CIs. PPI and AutoEval debias proxy-judge labels, and PPAT uses the proxy as a control variate. This covers FWL's estimator (stratified randomized promotion, IPW, bias correction of cheap labels) and is statistically stronger than the plain IPW the proposal specifies. FWL should adopt these estimators rather than claim the estimation method as new.

closest.title: Meta-analytic trial-level surrogate validation (Buyse, Molenberghs et al., Biostatistics 2000; Daniels and Hughes 1997); Surrogate Index (Athey, Chetty, Imbens, Kang, arXiv 1603.09326); Fleming and DeMets 1996 on surrogate endpoints
closest.overlap: Clinical surrogacy regresses the treatment effect on the true endpoint against the effect on the surrogate across many trials or interventions. It uses hierarchical models with measurement-error correction, i.e. R1_effect ~ lambda * R0_effect + bias with trial-level R^2. It is well established that surrogates validated for one drug class often fail for drugs with a new mechanism of action. That is FWL's hypothesis H1, novelty-conditional fidelity, in another field, and the hierarchical pooling across trials mirrors FWL's pooling across packs. This is the strongest precedent for FWL's statistical core and its central hypothesis.

closest.title: The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas (Si et al., arXiv 2506.20803)
closest.overlap: Measures cross-rung disagreement for research ideas. 43 experts executed randomly assigned ideas (100+ hours each), and LLM ideas whose proposals were rated more novel declined significantly more after execution than human ideas. This is closer evidence for 'the cheap rung over-rates or mis-rates novel ideas' than the confounded CACHE or Heuresis hints the proposal cites. However, its cheap rung is a human judgment of the proposal, not an executed R0, and novelty is not a pre-registered covariate on a fidelity slope.

closest.title: AlphaResearch (arXiv 2511.08522)
closest.overlap: The proposal already cites this. It is a one-off execution of 151 ideas that its reward model rejected, which found 43 false rejections. That is a single non-randomized audit at one rung (judge vs execution), with no conditioning covariate and no feedback into training.

closest.title: One Run Is Not an Idea: The Implementation Lottery in Automated Research (Ning, Zhong, Li, Zeng, Xiong, CMU, arXiv 2607.26587, Jul 2026)
closest.overlap: An 'Idea Reliability Audit' for automated research factories. It measures how often idea-level selection decisions flip across independent faithful implementations and reruns (25.6-43.6% selection instability), with blinded fidelity labels and pre-registered design. This overlaps FWL's reliability-vs-fidelity decomposition (step 4's independent R0 re-run) and its motivation that one cheap score is weak evidence. It does not audit across verifier rungs and does not condition on novelty.

closest.title: REHEARSE: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch (Tencent, arXiv 2607.27687, Jul 2026)
closest.overlap: Shows that pre-execution judgment reliability in autoresearch loops degrades as the incumbent improves. On AutoSOTA pairs, selective accuracy falls from 82.8% to 56.9% late in the trajectory. This matches FWL's drift component (re-audit when the incumbent changes). It concerns a judge-to-execution rung and trajectory position, not novelty-conditional fidelity between executed rungs.

closest.title: Where the Verifier Fails: A Category-Level Audit of Reward Signals in RLVR (arXiv 2609.01354, Sep 2026)
closest.overlap: Audits automatic verifiers' false-negative rates conditional on answer category, using certified equivalent variants: 307k verdicts across four verifiers, with errors concentrated in specific categories. This is a covariate-conditional audit of verifier error that informs reward signals for RL. It is analogous in spirit to FWL's idea-conditional fidelity, but for math-answer verifiers rather than research-idea verifier ladders, and with no novelty covariate.

closest.title: DataDecide (2504.11393), Wang et al. (2512.24503), Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers (2509.02046), and zero-cost or low-fidelity NAS proxy studies (e.g. White et al. 2022; Ning et al. 2021)
closest.overlap: The LM papers are already cited. They measure small-to-large proxy decision accuracy for one intervention family, without an idea-level novelty covariate. The NAS literature (from memory, not re-verified this run) documents that low-fidelity and zero-cost proxies are systematically biased toward certain architecture regions, such as parameter count. That is a known case of cheap-rung fidelity that varies across the candidate space.

art.to_make_novel:
Every mechanism in FWL has direct precedent:
- Idea-conditional fidelity: input-dependent multi-fidelity GPs such as iMFBO and NARGP.
- Randomized, propensity-logged promotion with IPW: selective labels, reject inference, and active or prediction-powered inference.
- A hierarchical effect-on-effect regression with measurement-error correction: meta-analytic surrogate validation.
- The hypothesis that surrogates fail for new mechanisms: known in clinical trials.

The defensible novel residue is empirical and applied:
- (1) The first pre-registered measurement of whether agreement between cheap and expensive EXECUTED verifiers (proxy training vs held-out, public vs shifted instances, few vs many tasks) declines with an idea's mechanism novelty, for AI-generated ideas, pooled across structurally different domains (H1).
- (2) Closing the loop: fidelity-weighted and debiased cheap labels as training signal for a self-improving factory's predictor, critic and harness-acceptance loops, tested prospectively against unweighted labels.

To stand as novel, the proposal should make four changes:
- Drop the claims that idea-conditional fidelity and randomized audits are new, and correct the statement that MF-BO assumes stationary cross-fidelity correlation.
- Cite the surrogate-endpoint and PPI literatures as the methods.
- Replace plain IPW with active or prediction-powered inference estimators, which give lower variance and valid CIs; this also strengthens H3.
- Position the Ideation-Execution Gap (2506.20803), AlphaResearch, One Run Is Not an Idea (2607.26587) and REHEARSE (2607.27687) as the adjacent AI-research measurements that FWL extends: from judge-vs-execution or rerun reliability to novelty-conditional, executed-rung-to-executed-rung fidelity fed back into learning.

The measurement-error step should explicitly separate implementation-lottery variance, per 2607.26587, from rung fidelity.

Search caveat: coverage of 2026 AI-scientist work was incomplete.
- WebSearch was exhausted at its 200-call session budget.
- The arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429.
- DuckDuckGo returned a CAPTCHA, which was not bypassed.
- Evidence came from a few DuckDuckGo queries before the block, arXiv site search and abstract pages, and cached full texts in the session scratchpad.

A preprint that measures novelty-conditional cross-rung fidelity inside an autoresearch loop may exist and was not found.

feas.will_it_work:
Partly. The core mechanism is sound and already established: a random, propensity-logged slice of cheap-verifier rejects gets promoted to the next rung, which gives unbiased false-negative and false-positive rates. This is standard shadow-review QA and the prediction-powered / active-inference family (Angelopoulos et al. 2023, cited from memory). It is cheap, domain-agnostic and worth building. The claim that is actually new is that cheap-to-expensive fidelity depends on novelty, and it has a plausible mechanism. The closest realized-outcome precedent is surrogate endpoints in medicine, which fail mainly for novel mechanisms (antiarrhythmics in CAST, torcetrapib and HDL; from memory). The proposal cites none of these, and it should.

Several problems stand between the idea and a result.

(1) The novelty-conditional part is unlikely to come out clearly in the first experiment.
- In LM data-efficiency most ideas are null. With the R0 noise floor at a 1.11x minimum detectable effect (3 seeds, FEASIBILITY.md), the spread of R0 effects is small next to their noise. The slope lambda is therefore poorly identified.
- An interaction (R0 effect x novelty) needs roughly 4x the sample of a main effect, and the LM pack has n=60.
- The equivalence kill (CI within ±10% per SD in all packs) is practically unreachable at these n, so the likely outcome is 'inconclusive'.

(2) What R0-to-R1 means differs between packs. In tabular (3 vs 10 OpenML tasks) and heuristics (public vs shifted instances), the rung gap mostly measures sampling noise and overfitting to the public set. That overfitting may track 'tuned-constant tweaks' more than novelty, so a pooled novelty slope may not exist. Discovering that is fine, but it undercuts the pooled hierarchical prior.

(3) Novelty is confounded with variance and breakage. Novel ideas are more heteroscedastic and more often buggy, which can mimic a novelty effect on lambda unless the model handles heteroscedasticity.

(4) If R0 is simply right that novel ideas are worse (the CACHE #3 pattern: novel chemotypes may bind less), FWL correctly measures that. It then yields no decision change, which is a legitimate but low-value outcome.

(5) The loops it would feed mostly do not exist yet: the outcome predictor, PML credit, NMCC critic labels and the Critic Overoptimization Curves. R2 (realized-value) data will be a handful of points for a long time, and the rung that matters for money cannot be estimated.

Prior-art correction: 'multi-fidelity treats correlation as stationary' is overstated. Kennedy-O'Hagan already allows rho(x) as a regression on inputs, and nonlinear autoregressive multi-fidelity GPs (Perdikaris et al. 2017, from memory) model input-dependent cross-fidelity relations. The genuine novelty is narrower: idea-level randomized audits across heterogeneous packs, fed back as label weights.

Evidence checks:
- AlphaResearch verified: 'filtered 151 ideas… 108 correct rejections… 43 erroneous rejections of viable ideas'. This is circle packing, first 400 iterations, with a 7B reward model. 'Viable' means it executed successfully, not that it beat the incumbent, so it overstates false negatives in the proposal's sense.
- DataDecide verified: about 80% of pairwise comparisons correct from 150M to 1B, across 25 data-recipe corpora.
- Heuresis, CACHE #3 and Aletheia figures could not be re-verified (search budget exhausted).
- Fantastic Optimizers is about tuning parity, not novelty.
None of this is direct evidence that fidelity varies with novelty. It is a hypothesis.
feas.eval_issues:
- **The ground truth itself is fine.** R1 execution on hidden or shifted instances is non-circular. The novelty covariates are judge-free and computed before execution, and the independent R0 re-run corrects for regression to the mean. That design is good.
- **Power.**
  - H1 is a pooled interaction test with a large effect threshold (25% per SD). The LM pack has n=60, and the 120-idea CPU packs are mostly null ideas, so H1 is badly underpowered.
  - The equivalence kill is effectively unreachable, so the likely outcome is inconclusive.
  - H2 replays about 300 ideas. With maybe 5-15% R1 winners, that is roughly 15-45 events, which cannot resolve a 25% winners-per-dollar improvement with a stable CI.
  - The '>=300 test items wherever selection is involved' rule conflicts with a total pool of 300 that is also used for fitting under cross-validation.
- **H3 is nearly tautological.** Inverse-propensity weighting (IPW) is unbiased by construction under known propensities, so subsampling the full audit only checks variance. It carries little information.
- **Contamination and Goodhart.**
  - The 10 held-out OpenML tasks are public and likely known to Opus-class generators.
  - A fixed hidden heuristic generator reused across epochs becomes the next target once promotion thresholds and label weights are tuned against it. It must be rotated.
  - Fidelity weights learned on R1 will be optimized against by the engine, a second-order Goodhart effect.
- **Confounds.**
  - Novelty correlates with implementation complexity, bug rate and effect variance. The diff-size and new-hyperparameter controls are partial; heteroscedastic noise can masquerade as a lambda interaction.
  - The R0 learning-rate sweep controls tuning only at R0; novel ideas may need re-tuning at R1 too.
  - Embedding distance to the knowledge base measures textual unfamiliarity as much as mechanistic novelty.
- **The prospective test is also underpowered.** It covers 2 rounds at matched R1 budget, and the metric is dominated by a few winners.
feas.cost_realistic:
The $250-480 estimate is somewhat optimistic; $400-900 is more realistic, which is still cheap.

- **LM R1:** SWARM.md puts tier 2 at 2-4 H100-hours at 5 seeds. At 3 seeds that is about 1.2-2.4 h per idea, so 60 ideas x about 1.2-2.4 h x $2.69/h comes to about $195-390, against the proposal's $110-250.
- **LM R0:** tier-1 cost is 'estimated, not yet measured on a GPU' (SWARM.md, phase 0 not yet done). The LR sweep for every idea (about 3-5 LRs) plus an independent re-run multiplies R0 by about 4-6x, so about $80-250 rather than $20-50.
- **CPU packs:** under $30 is plausible.
- **Implementations:** 300 at $90-150 assumes about $0.30-0.50 each. Debug-and-retry loops for heuristic and tabular code, plus Opus 5.5 output at $20/MTok, could double that.
- **Steady state:** audits at 10-20% of R1 spend are reasonable in compute packs. In a wet-lab pack (Adaptyv), randomly promoting losers costs real hundreds of dollars per design, and there the audit fraction must be small and justified by value of information.
feas.biggest_risk: The central novelty x fidelity result comes back inconclusive, and the factory builds label-weighting machinery on noise. The mostly-null idea population, n=60 in the one pack where the rung gap is a real scale transfer, and a pooled interaction test with an unreachable equivalence bound make 'we can't tell' the modal outcome. Meanwhile the downstream loops FWL would reweight largely do not exist yet, and the rung that matters commercially (R1 to R2, realized value) will have too few data points to estimate for a long time.
feas.fix:
Split it into two parts and power the part that is actually new.

1. **Infrastructure first.** Ship the cheap, certainly-useful half now as default ledger infrastructure in every pack:
   - 5-10% propensity-logged random promotion of R0 rejects
   - prediction-powered / IPW debiased false-negative and false-positive rates per pack, reported alongside every promotion decision
   - rotation of hidden R1 instance generators and held-out task sets each epoch

2. **Test the novelty hypothesis where n is cheap.** Put it in the CPU packs:
   - Use 800+ ideas each in heuristics and tabular, at a few dollars per 100 ideas of compute.
   - Enrich the sample for ideas with non-null R0 effects.
   - Replace the continuous-slope interaction with a decision-level primary endpoint: the R1 false-negative rate among R0 rejects in the top vs bottom novelty tercile, with a pre-registered minimum difference, e.g. 10 pp.
   - Keep the LM pack only as a small confirmatory replication.

Build the hierarchical fidelity-weighting of downstream loops only if that primary endpoint is positive in at least one pack.
feas.general_factory_value:
It is genuinely domain-agnostic, not only useful for LLM efficiency. Any pack with a verifier ladder can use randomized, propensity-logged cross-rung audits, and measuring cheap-verifier false negatives is exactly the failure a self-improving multi-domain engine needs to watch for.

Caveats:
- All three pilot packs are cheap computational domains. Pooled priors from these may transfer poorly to high-impact packs whose rung gaps have different failure modes (protein in-silico to wet lab, math numeric to Lean to curator).
- In those packs the audit itself is expensive and n is tiny.
- The unbiased shadow-audit layer has high general value per dollar. The novelty-conditional hierarchical weighting layer is speculative and should be earned by data.
- It is meta-infrastructure. It does not itself produce a sellable idea or a prize.

newProposals.name: Scope-Bet Ledger: verbatim claim records with locked qualifiers and declared extrapolation bets
newProposals.one_line: Store each claim as its verbatim source span, with qualifier slots (scope, regime, conditions, effect size, hedge, polarity) that may only point at exact substrings of that span. Every idea must then state, qualifier by qualifier, whether the target domain pack is inside the source's scope or is an explicit extrapolation bet. Bets are tested cheaply first, and nuance loss through the whole generator-critic-fixer pipeline is measured with counterfactual qualifier flips scored by code.
newProposals.mechanism: 1) Record = verbatim claim sentence + its paragraph + the paper's limitations/threats spans + any table cells it cites, kept on disk and navigated with grep/REPL tools (RLM style), never replaced by summaries. An ADDITIVE index sits on top: a claim normal form plus qualifier slots Q = {system/population, regime/scale range, conditions/assumptions, comparator/baseline, effect size + CI + units, hedge strength, polarity, evidence type (executed / observational / simulated / theoretical), n or seeds}. Each slot value is stored only as character offsets into the stored text. A code check rejects any slot that is not an exact substring, and numbers are parsed by code into (value, unit, CI). Haiku batch-fills the slots. A second pass checks every number against its span, as in the existing IDEAS_FACTORY record design. 2) Domain-pack interface: every pack publishes context_card() in the same slot vocabulary. Examples: LM proxy = 3-7M params, 1-4M unique tokens, multi-epoch; VCC = CRISPRi knockdown, unseen cell lines, zero-shot; ALE/AHC = instance-size ranges and time limit. 3) Generation contract: Opus 5.5 outputs the idea plus a premise table. Each row = record ID, role (support / mechanism source / contrast) and, for every filled qualifier, a status: HOLDS in the target, VIOLATED = BET, or UNKNOWN = PROBE. Code compares numeric and unit slots against the context card, so a model-declared HOLDS on an out-of-range scale is overwritten automatically. 4) Bets are neither penalised nor hidden. Extrapolation beyond stated scope is where cross-domain novelty lives, so each BET must come with the cheapest discriminating 'bet check' in the executor plan (for example a 1-seed run at the target regime, or a 5-instance scorer run), executed before the full run. 5) Point-of-use re-read: before the critic, a fresh call sees ONLY the verbatim spans (never the normal form) plus the premise table and marks disagreements. Disagreements on numbers, units and polarity are settled by code. 6) Fixers may patch ideas but may not delete or alter premise rows without a logged re-read of the spans (append/patch-only edits, ACE style), so critic-fixer loops cannot silently drop a qualifier. 7) Ledger write-back: executed outcomes and bet-check results are attached to each premise row. The executor's own logs become new verbatim records ('claim X held at 7M params / failed on AHC instances with n>10^4'), so the knowledge base learns each claim's true scope from executed tests. 8) Tokens spent on premise tables, re-reads and bet checks are logged per idea and charged against the arm in every comparison.
newProposals.closest_prior_work: Condition-aware scientific knowledge graphs: Jiang et al., 'The Role of Condition', KDD 2019 (fact tuples plus condition tuples; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3292500.3330942); nanopublications and ORKG claim bases. Theorizer's LAW/SCOPE/EVIDENCE tuples, backtested against later papers (arXiv 2601.16282). 'Fidelity Before Structure': verbatim chunks vs extracted artifacts (arXiv 2601.00821). Citation and evidence verification: PaperQA2 RCS and ContraCrow (arXiv 2409.13740), OpenScholar self-feedback (arXiv 2411.14199), RARR-style generate-then-attribute revision (Gao et al. 2023, from memory, not re-verified). Counterfactual-context robustness: ClashEval (arXiv 2404.10198) perturbs reference documents in more than 1,200 QA questions and found six top LLMs, including GPT-4o, adopting incorrect retrieved content more than 60% of the time. Overgeneralization measurement: Peters & Chin-Yee, R. Soc. Open Sci. 2025, on single-pass summaries (https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/12/4/241776/235656).
newProposals.why_novel: (a) Condition-aware knowledge graphs and LAW/SCOPE tuples store scope, but no ideation system turns scope into a CONTRACT at the point of use. Here each idea declares, per qualifier, whether the target pack's machine-readable context lies inside the source's scope. Code overrides wrong numeric declarations, and violations become priced, pre-tested extrapolation bets rather than silent overgeneralizations or reasons for rejection. (b) Qualifier slots are extractive pointers into verbatim text, not LLM paraphrases. This is the one design consistent with the finding that lossy distillation, not structure, causes the accuracy loss. (c) The evaluation is new. ClashEval and FaithEval-style tests flip ANSWERS in single-turn QA. Counterfactual QUALIFIER flips (scope, polarity, effect size, hedge) with no-op paraphrase controls, traced stage by stage through extraction, knowledge base, generator, critic and fixer, measure nuance propagation in a multi-stage ideation pipeline. The verified map lists this as an explicit gap: no study measures nuance loss through such a pipeline. (d) The ledger writes executed transfer evidence back into claim records. The map also lists this as missing: no system feeds executed outcomes back into the knowledge representation.
newProposals.evidence_basis: Fidelity Before Structure (single author, conversational memory, GPT-4o answerer, gpt-4o-mini extractor, LLM-judged QA): verbatim chunks 43.9% vs extracted artifacts 28.0% on LoCoMo, and 67.4% vs 45.4% on LongMemEval-S. Adding artifacts alongside chunks kept accuracy; substituting them lost it. Peters & Chin-Yee 2025 (10 LLMs, 4,900 summaries of scientific texts): DeepSeek, ChatGPT-4o and LLaMA 3.3 70B overgeneralized in 26-73% of cases even when prompted for accuracy, LLM summaries were about 5x more likely than human ones to generalize broadly, and Claude models were least affected. These are 2024-25 models. The mechanism, dropping scope-limiting details under compression, plausibly still applies to Opus 5.5, but its rate is unmeasured, which is why the first experiment measures it rather than assumes it. Kosmos (expert-judged, 102 statements from 3 reports): synthesis/interpretation statements were 57.9% accurate vs 85.5% for data analysis and 82.1% for literature, so errors concentrate where claims are combined. Robin (lab-validated, dry AMD): its own analysis reported 7.5-fold phagocytosis where human re-analysis found 1.75-fold. HypoKG (13,200 hypotheses, biomedicine): endpoint-only prompts got the highest rubric scores but were the least grounded, so judges reward dropped nuance. ACE (AppWorld): a monolithic rewrite collapsed an 18,282-token context to 122 tokens and fell from 66.7% to 57.1%, below the 63.7% no-memory baseline, which motivates patch-only fixers. Theorizer (AI/NLP, GPT-4.1, Sonnet 4.5 judging later papers): in novelty mode, literature-grounded laws had a supported/(supported+contradicted) ratio of 0.61 vs 0.34 for parametric laws, so grounding with explicit scope pays off exactly in the novelty regime.
newProposals.first_experiment: Qualifier-flip propagation test, cheap and code-scored. Corpus: 100 claim records with at least 2 filled qualifier slots, 25 from each of 4 pack literatures (LM-training efficiency, single-cell perturbation, heuristic/combinatorial optimization, metabolomics MS/MS identification). Four variants per record: original; SCOPE flip (code edits the numeric regime so the pack's context card falls outside it); POLARITY/EFFECT flip ('improved' to 'did not improve', or effect 2.1x to 1.02x with the CI spanning 1), a minimal edit that code verifies touches only the slot's offsets; NO-OP control (paraphrase of non-qualifier text, with qualifier substrings verified unchanged). Arms, token-matched, all emitting the same premise-table schema: A = the current IDEAS_FACTORY extracted record ({method, mechanism, claim, scale, multiplier}), where the generator sees the normal form; B = raw verbatim spans with no slots or checks; C = full Scope-Bet Ledger (slots, context card, code overrides, re-read, patch-only fixer). Pipeline per run: Opus 5.5 generator, then critic, then 1 fixer round. Scoring is entirely by code. On flips, a response is correct if the flipped record's status moves the prescribed way (HOLDS to BET for scope; support to contrast/dropped, or a BET, for polarity). On no-ops, any status change is a false alarm. Report survival after each stage. Pre-stated success: C reaches at least 85% flip-sensitivity after the fixer, with at most 10% false alarms, AND beats A by at least 15 points. Pre-stated falsification: if A already reaches at least 80%, Opus 5.5 preserves nuance through lossy records, so the qualifier machinery is dropped and only spans are kept, saving extraction tokens. If C is below 70%, the contract does not fix propagation and the design is revisited before any build. Size: 100 records x 4 variants x 3 arms = 1,200 pipeline runs.
newProposals.evaluation: No LLM-judge agreement is used anywhere. (1) Flip propagation, scored by code as above, rerun whenever the generator, critic or fixer prompts change: a regression test for nuance. (2) Executed outcomes in two verifier packs: the LM proxy, which detects 1.11x at 3 seeds, and one non-ML pack (ALE-Bench AHC scorer or the VCC cell-eval offline split). Arms B and C run at matched total tokens. Measures: (i) the premise-violation failure rate, defined as executed failures traced by code to a premise marked HOLDS whose qualifier the context card shows was violated, which should fall in C; (ii) the AUC of bet-check results for predicting the full-run outcome, which should be at least 0.7 for bets to be worth their cost; (iii) executed success rate per 1M tokens. (3) Write-back value, time-split: after the first 100 executed ideas, new ideas that reuse records carrying executed scope evidence should fail less than new ideas reusing records without it (executed outcomes only).
newProposals.cost_estimate: Build: about $300-700 of Haiku batch for a scoped 10-25k-paper corpus (the IDEAS_FACTORY estimate), plus about 30% for qualifier offsets and number checks. Runtime overhead: premise table, re-read and bet checks add roughly 15-25% tokens per idea (own estimate, to be measured and charged). First experiment: 1,200 runs at about 35-45k tokens each is about 50M tokens. That is roughly $250-450 API-equivalent at Opus-class list prices (unverified for Opus 5.5; check current pricing), or about a week inside the Claude Max plan. Flip generation and scoring are scripts; qualifier extraction for 100 records costs under $5.
newProposals.risks: Synthetic flips are cleaner than real nuance loss, where qualifiers hide in methods sections far from the claim. Mitigation: records also carry methods and limitations spans, and real cases are audited via executed failures. The model may game the contract by marking everything UNKNOWN, so the UNKNOWN rate is reported and capped. Critics may treat BETs as flaws and push the engine back toward conservative, in-scope ideas, re-creating collapse. Critics are instructed that bets are priced by bet checks, not penalised, and the BET rate per arm is monitored. Overhead tokens could erase the gains, as budget-matched studies found for memory modules (plain actors matched ReasoningBank and Agent Workflow Memory on WebArena), so every comparison is token-matched. Slot extraction is weakest for non-numeric qualifiers, such as population descriptions in biology.

newProposals.name: Compute-First Import Exchange (CFIX): executable fingerprints as the cross-field join key
newProposals.one_line: Before retrieving by words, have an agent write a probe that computes a canonical numeric invariant of the target problem: small-case sequences, constants, scaling exponents, spectra, dimensionless groups, dataset or landscape signatures. Look that invariant up in a knowledge base whose records carry the same fingerprints, computed from their verbatim tables, formulas and reference code, and import the matched cross-field result only after the pack's verifier accepts it.
newProposals.mechanism: 1) Fingerprint type registry, shared by all domain packs: INT_SEQ (small-case values of a counting or extremal function), CONST (high-precision limits and constants), EXPONENTS (scaling exponents or asymptotic forms fitted from simulated or small instances), SPECTRUM (eigenvalue-spacing class, spectral decay), PI_GROUPS (dimensionless groups and regime from dimensional analysis of the problem's variables), DATA_SIG (effective rank, replicate-noise ratio, tail index, share of variance explained by additive or mean baselines, train/test shift) and LANDSCAPE (fitness-distance correlation, autocorrelation length, constraint tightness, ELA-style features). 2) Pack plug-in: each pack exposes probe(problem) -> fingerprint and verify(artifact). For a new problem card, Opus 5.5 writes the probe in a sandbox. Probes are validated by code: brute force must agree with the clever computation on the smallest cases, and fitted exponents need CIs. 3) Knowledge-base side: (a) curated fingerprint databases imported as-is (OEIS snapshot from github.com/oeis/oeisdata, about 390k entries; FindStat; LMFDB; critical-exponent and universality-class tables; benchmark instance-feature tables); (b) fingerprints harvested from papers, where theorem formulas are evaluated by code into terms and numeric tables are parsed, each keyed to its verbatim span (compatible with the Scope-Bet Ledger records); (c) behavioural fingerprints of method papers with code, obtained by running the reference implementation on canonical probe instances. 4) Matching by code, not by an LLM: type-specific tolerant matchers (OEIS-superseeker-style transforms such as shift, scale, binomial and Euler; exponent equality within CI; KS test for spectrum class; standardized distance for signatures). Each hit gets a p-value against a null of random same-type records, so coincidental short-sequence matches are discounted. 5) Only after a numeric hit does Opus perform explicit structure-mapping from the source result to the target, citing the source's verbatim hypotheses and checking each one against the target (via the premise table). 6) Parametric-pointer channel: Opus may also say 'this looks like X in field Y' from its weights. A pointer counts only if its fingerprint and span resolve in the knowledge base. This merges AR-style parametric recall with a vocabulary-free check. 7) Outcome typing in the ledger: IMPORT (solved elsewhere; valuable, but no novelty claim is allowed, which turns CFIX into the strongest novelty gate), PARTIAL IMPORT, COINCIDENCE. 8) Verification by the pack: Lean or curator for math, the hidden or local scorer for optimization, the offline metric split for prediction packs.
newProposals.closest_prior_work: OEIS as 'a fingerprint file for mathematics' (Sloane, arXiv 2105.05111) and the proposal for per-field fingerprint databases of theorems (Billey & Tenner, Notices AMS 2013, arXiv 1304.3866), which already argues such databases help researchers find unexpected connections between areas. FindStat and LMFDB (from memory, not re-verified). IntSeqBERT (arXiv 2603.05556) learns OEIS embeddings toward finding similar sequences across fields. Exploratory Landscape Analysis and Instance Space Analysis (Muñoz, Smith-Miles et al.) use instance features to SELECT among known optimization algorithms. Kulikowski, 'Same Problem, Different Field' (JCDL 2026, arXiv 2609.07595) builds LLM-distilled, domain-stripped TEXT skeletons for cross-field retrieval. AI literature-search finds on Erdős problems: Tao's wiki section 2(a) and DeepMind's Gemini sweep of 700 problems (arXiv 2601.22401). SageMath-augmented math agents (arXiv 2607.06820) use a CAS but no fingerprint databases.
newProposals.why_novel: Fingerprint databases exist, but they are per-field tools that humans query after computing small cases by hand, and ELA features choose among algorithms within one field. CFIX makes executable invariants the domain-agnostic JOIN KEY of an autonomous ideas factory. Agents write the probes for arbitrary problem cards. Knowledge-base records get fingerprints computed from their own verbatim spans (tables, theorem formulas, reference code), which extends coverage beyond curated databases. Matches carry a coincidence-null p-value. The import is closed by the pack's verifier. Yield is measured as verified import events, not as retrieval precision or an LLM-judged 'analogy quality'. Kulikowski's skeletons are the nearest cross-field retriever, but they are still text produced by an LLM from abstracts. CFIX's key is computed by running code, so it cannot inherit the vocabulary or topical bias of text embeddings. I found no LLM ideation or AI-scientist system that uses computed invariants as its cross-domain retrieval key; searches this session turned up none, which is not proof of absence.
newProposals.evidence_basis: Importing known results is a major realized-value channel. METR's analysis of 77 NanoGPT speedrun records (31x total speedup; labels assigned by one author with Claude Code) says 'imported ideas drove 6.7x of the 31x total', vs 3.0x adapted and 1.6x invented. Tao's Erdős wiki has about 80 entries in section 2(a), Literature search (fetched 27 Sep 2026). In DeepMind's sweep of 700 'open' Erdős problems (Gemini), 8 of the 13 addressed problems already had literature solutions (5 found by search, 3 independent rediscoveries), and the authors warn of 'subconscious plagiarism'. Vocabulary is the retrieval bottleneck. In ResearchBench inspiration retrieval (GPT-4o, 12 disciplines), 23% of errors were missed other-discipline papers that use different terms, and 56% came from judging by title or abstract overlap. In Kulikowski's cross-field benchmark (18 method families, 109 papers), all four trained scientific embedders scored below abstract+TF-IDF because they encode topical proximity, the 'wrong signal'. On MUSES, the best retriever's Hit@100 fell from 0.534 to 0.171 on author-endorsed roots of new work. Frontier models picked the true inspiration from 15 candidates with hard negatives only about 45-55% of the time (MOOSE-Star). Computation beats text where invariants exist: in mathematics this is the established OEIS practice, and SageMath access added about 9.7 points on average for research-level math agents (RealMath).
newProposals.first_experiment: Import backtest with exact-match ground truth, scored by code. Targets: (a) Erdős problems from Tao-wiki section 2(a) whose source paper is named on the wiki or erdosproblems.com, expected 50-70 (Opus 5.5 may have seen these, which biases toward the baselines, so a win for C is conservative); (b) 80 contamination-free OEIS 'late twin' events mined from the oeis/oeisdata git log: edits dated on or after 2026-07-01 (after Opus 5.5's cutoff) that add a comment or reference identifying an existing sequence with a differently defined object. The query is the new object's definition from its cited source, with the A-number and terms removed. Frozen corpus per target: OEIS snapshot checked out the day before the event; OpenAlex metadata and arXiv full text up to the same date; erdosproblems.com and the wiki excluded. Arms at equal token budget: P = Opus 5.5 parametric recall only, reported as a contaminated upper bound on (a); T = Opus 5.5 with text tools (BM25, embedding search, citation traversal) over the frozen corpus; C = CFIX (probe, fingerprint lookup, structure-map) plus the same text tools. Metrics, all by code: Recall@10 of the ground-truth source (exact DOI, arXiv ID or A-number); probe-ability rate (share of targets with a validated fingerprint); cost per hit. Pre-stated success: on (b), C beats T by at least 20 points of Recall@10; on (a), C adds at least 10 points over T on the probe-able subset, and at least 30% of (a) is probe-able. Falsification: if C beats T by at most 5 points on both sets, fingerprints add nothing over text tools for Opus 5.5 and CFIX is dropped.
newProposals.evaluation: Prospective, realized outcomes, CFIX vs the T arm at equal budget. (1) Math packs: sweep 300 open Erdős problems and the about 40 unsolved FrontierMath Open Problems. Count curator-accepted literature finds and status changes on erdosproblems.com, Lean-verified results and Epoch-verified solutions per $1k; the notability tier is logged so that obscure wins are not overstated. (2) Optimization packs (ALE-Bench AHC problems; industrial routing or scheduling with a customer evaluator): hidden or held-out scorer gains of algorithms imported via LANDSCAPE matches vs text-retrieved imports vs no import, with at least 2 independent implementations each. (3) Prediction packs (VCC 2026 offline cell-eval split; Enveda CASMI): metric gains of methods chosen by DATA_SIG matching vs text retrieval, always against strong additive and mean baselines. (4) Calibration: the coincidence-null p-value should predict verified import success (AUC). The generality claim is falsified if non-math packs show no gain over T in (2)-(3).
newProposals.cost_estimate: Data is free: OEIS (CC BY-SA 4.0), OpenAlex (CC0), arXiv bulk text. Harvesting table and formula fingerprints for a 20k-paper corpus: about $100-300 of Haiku batch plus CPU. First experiment: about 150 targets x 3 arms, at about $0.10 (P), $0.50 (T) and $1 (C) per agent session API-equivalent, is about $250-400, or inside the Max plan. Probe execution is local CPU (negligible). Prospective math sweep: about $1-2 per problem-arm. Optimization or prediction packs: under $2k per POC, including repeated implementations.
newProposals.risks: Outside mathematics many problems have no crisp, discriminative invariant, so generality is the main risk; it is tested in evaluation steps (2) and (3) with a pre-stated falsification. Short sequences and loose exponent matches produce coincidences; the null p-value and structure-map check mitigate this but will not remove it. Probe code can be wrong, mitigated by brute-force cross-checks. Imports are not new. The factory must label them IMPORT, which rules out patents and novelty claims, although they still solve problems and win scorer points. OEIS's CC BY-SA share-alike terms apply to any derived database. Money in the math packs is reputational (Erdős prizes total about $60k across 152 problems), so CFIX's cash value depends on its non-math transfer.

newProposals.name: Placebo-Labeled Transfer Atlas: executed, counterfactual labels for which cross-field sources help which problems
newProposals.one_line: For each target problem, execute ideas seeded by the retrieved record against two token-matched controls: a random diverse record from the same field-distance band (the PaperGym null) and the model's own parametric analogy (the AR arm). Paired differences separate specific-retrieval value from diversity injection and from what the weights already know. Pool these labels across domain packs into a Bayesian 'what transfers where' atlas that drives retrieval and switches the knowledge base off where it does not pay.
newProposals.mechanism: 1) Unit = (target card T from any pack, source record R, mapping M). Features: R's domain-stripped mechanism skeleton (Kulikowski style, one cached Haiku call per paper), R's OpenAlex field and age, the field pair (R, T), a concept co-occurrence z-score of R's concepts with T's concepts (rarity, against a degree-preserving null), R's evidence tier, and T's pack plus its CFIX fingerprint type when available. 2) Paired, placebo-controlled generation per T, at matched generator tokens: R-arm = structure-mapping from the record chosen by the current policy; D-arm (diversity placebo) = a random record from the same distance band, matched in length and evidence tier; W-arm (weights) = Analogical-Reasoning-style prompt ('abstract the relational structure, find a distant domain yourself') with no knowledge-base text; S-arm (optional scramble) = R's text with the skeleton roles mis-assigned, testing whether the mapping or mere exposure matters. 3) The top idea per arm is executed in the pack's verifier with at least 2 independent implementations (implementation-lottery control) and equal tuning budgets. For the LM proxy: 3 paired seeds. 4) Labels: specific utility SU(R|T) = y_R - y_D; diversity utility DU = y_D - y_W; total knowledge-base value = y_R - y_W. Tokens per arm are logged, so every label is also a per-token value. 5) Atlas = hierarchical Bayesian regression (or a GP over skeleton embeddings) of SU on features, with pack random effects. Pooling across packs lets cheap packs (LM proxy, ALE-Bench, extremal constructions) inform expensive ones (VCC, metabolomics). 6) Retrieval policy = Thompson sampling from the atlas posterior. Rarely connected (low co-occurrence) pairs are explored because their posterior variance is high, so the anti-crowd strength is learned from executed labels instead of being fixed (as the Sourati-Evans beta of 0.2-0.3 is). 7) Write-back: each record and skeleton accumulates posterior SU per pack ('multigrid-type skeletons: +x on LM data efficiency, 0 on AHC routing'), a knowledge-base layer that no text index contains. 8) Portfolio rule: per pack, retrieval tokens are spent only where the posterior expected executed gain per token of the R-arm exceeds the W-arm. Otherwise the factory falls back to cheap random-diverse seeding (if DU > 0) or to weights only, and the knowledge base is kept for novelty gating and verification.
newProposals.closest_prior_work: PaperGym (arXiv 2605.11532): targeted cross-domain seeds showed no significant difference from a random diverse-seed control, judged by an LLM, ML only. Analogical Reasoning (Shen, Druckmann, Zou, arXiv 2605.11258): parametric analogies, no knowledge base. Retriever training from downstream utility in in-context learning: EPR (Rubin, Herzig, Berant, NAACL 2022) and LLM-R, which label demonstrations by LM likelihood, not execution (from memory, not re-verified). Scientific inspiration retrievers trained or evaluated on author-cited inspirations: TCA-SIR (arXiv 2607.28498), MUSES, RATIO (arXiv 2608.27394), MOOSE-Star. Outcome-trained idea scorers, at idea level rather than source level: HARPA-Scorer (arXiv 2510.00620), Wen et al. (arXiv 2506.00794). DeepScientist Findings Memory: never ablated. Within this panel, wf1's Single-Graft Distance Ladder Thompson-samples among 4 field-distance bands in one domain, with a random-diverse-seed arm.
newProposals.why_novel: It is the first design to label knowledge-base items by COUNTERFACTUAL EXECUTED utility with a placebo structure that separates the three explanations the literature leaves confounded: specific retrieval (R vs D), diversity injection (D vs W) and the model's own parametric analogies (W). PaperGym compared R to D with LLM judges only, and AR never compared against a knowledge base. Existing inspiration retrievers learn from author citations, and ICL retrievers from LM likelihood. Here the label is a paired, multi-implementation verifier outcome per token, which fills two gaps named in the verified map: no benchmark labels inspirations by counterfactual downstream utility, and nobody updates the retriever or knowledge representation from execution. It differs from wf1's Single-Graft ladder, which learns a preference over 4 distance bands in the LM domain with a single random-seed control. The atlas learns per-(target, record) utility with weights-only and scramble controls, pools across domain packs through domain-stripped skeleton features, writes the result back into the knowledge base, and includes an explicit rule for switching retrieval off, which serves OptiLex's combined data, compute and energy efficiency goal.
newProposals.evidence_basis: Whether targeted retrieval beats diversity is unresolved. PaperGym (rubric LLM judges, 7 ML domains): cross-domain retrieval beat no retrieval but showed no significant difference from random diverse seeds. AR (novelty judged by Claude Sonnet 4.5 against Semantic Scholar retrieval): parametric analogical prompting alone raised Sonnet 4.5's novel-solution rate from 1.6% to 50.4% and GPT-5.2's from 9.0% to 58.8%, with 4 executed biomedical case studies, so the weights may already hold the polymath knowledge. Budget-matched evaluation (WebArena/WorkArena; Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5.4-mini, Qwen 3.6-27B): a plain actor with the same total tokens matched or beat Agent Workflow Memory, ASI and ReasoningBank. Knowledge-base gains must therefore be charged for their tokens. Where signal lives: Wen et al. found a GPT-4.1 fine-tuned on outcomes reached 77% on 1,585 post-cutoff idea pairs, while off-the-shelf o3 with the same retrieval was no better than random, so outcome labels, not retrieval context, carry predictive signal. Theorizer (AI/NLP, LLM-judged support against later papers) found grounding raised the novelty-mode evidence ratio from 0.34 to 0.61, so specific retrieval can matter. DeepScientist (about 5,000 ideas, about 1,100 validated, 21 with progress, 20,000 GPU-hours; memory never ablated) shows that funnels this sparse need causal attribution. The implementation-lottery audit (arXiv 2607.26587) motivates at least 2 implementations per idea. The LM proxy detects 1.11x with 3 seeds (OptiLex FEASIBILITY.md), which makes paired labels affordable.
newProposals.first_experiment: Does the identity of the retrieved record matter under execution? Pack 1, the OptiLex LM proxy (7M params, 1-4M unique tokens; target = data-efficiency multiplier over the tuned multi-epoch baseline): 16 R records (skeleton-matched to the target from a 2,000-paper cached skeleton index spanning 4 distant fields), 16 D placebos (random, same bands, length-matched) and 8 W generations. Each gives 1 idea, 1 Claude Code implementation and 3 paired seeds: 120 runs of about 2-3 min on a rented GPU. Pack 2, ALE-Bench (40 past AtCoder Heuristic Contest problems with local scorers): 8 problems x (4 R + 4 D + 2 W) x 2 implementations = 160 implementations, each a 20-minute Claude Code session scored on the public test cases and normalized to the pack's baseline solution. Pre-registered analysis: a paired mixed model y ~ arm + (1|target) + (1|implementation), pooling 48 R-D pairs, which gives 80% power for a standardized paired effect of about 0.4. Pre-stated verdicts. KB-SPECIFIC: mean SU > 0 with a 95% CI excluding 0 AND Spearman(skeleton-match score, SU) >= 0.3 among R records; then build the atlas. DIVERSITY-ONLY: the SU CI includes 0 while D - W > 0 with a CI excluding 0; then replace targeted retrieval with cheap random-diverse seeding and save the retrieval tokens. WEIGHTS-SUFFICE: R, D and W are indistinguishable; then keep the knowledge base only as novelty gate and verifier. Each verdict changes what OptiLex builds.
newProposals.evaluation: Executed and realized outcomes only. (1) Held-out pack transfer: fit the atlas on the LM proxy, ALE-Bench and an extremal-constructions pack (deterministic bound evaluator), then predict SU for a new pack (VCC 2026 offline cell-eval split, or Enveda CASMI validation) before running it. Success = the top-quartile predicted records realize higher SU than the bottom quartile, one-sided p < 0.05. (2) Prospective budget test: at a fixed token and GPU budget per pack, compare atlas-driven retrieval, always-retrieve (skeleton match), random-diverse seeding and weights only on verifier outcomes per 1M tokens and per kWh (NVML), plus realized channel outcomes where they exist (leaderboard placement, accepted solutions). (3) Write-back check, time-split: records flagged by the atlas as high-SU in earlier batches keep positive SU in later batches in the same pack (test-retest correlation of at least 0.3); otherwise record-level write-back is noise and only skeleton-level pooling is kept.
newProposals.cost_estimate: Skeleton index of 2,000 papers: about $10-20 of Haiku batch. First experiment: about 6-8 rented GPU-hours for the LM proxy (about $15-30); ALE-Bench scoring on CPU (under $20); about 200 agent sessions (40 LM implementations plus 160 ALE implementations) inside the Max plan, or about $250-400 API-equivalent at Opus-class list prices (unverified for Opus 5.5). Total under $500. At steady state the placebo arms roughly triple generation and execution cost per labelled target. Labelling is therefore run on a 10-20% sample of targets, with the rest spent by the atlas policy.
newProposals.risks: Implementation-lottery and seed noise may swamp SU at pilot scale. The pilot is powered only for moderate effects, and a null result is 'no large specific utility', not proof of none. Opus may ignore the seeded record. This is checked by code: the idea must instantiate the skeleton's roles, and the scramble arm tests mere exposure. Placebo matching can leak, because R records are more on-topic by construction; length, tier and band are matched and residual topicality is reported. ALE-Bench and OEIS-era content may be in Opus 5.5's training data, which inflates W and biases against the knowledge base (conservative). Cross-pack pooling may fail if transfer is pack-specific; evaluation step (1) tests that directly. Thompson exploration toward rare pairs spends budget on low-yield regions early. Close overlap with wf1's Single-Graft ladder must be managed by running them as separate arms with shared placebo controls rather than duplicating infrastructure.

newProposals.name: Portable Mechanism Ledger (PML): cross-domain clade credit for domain-stripped mechanisms
newProposals.one_line: Credit each executed idea's domain-stripped mechanism skeleton with the verified results of its re-instantiations in other domain packs and on other objectives. Measure how portable mechanisms really are, and let the engine Thompson-sample skeletons into new packs only when that portability is measurably above zero.
newProposals.mechanism:
1) Skeleton extraction. After an idea is executed in pack d, a separate Opus call that has not seen the outcome maps the idea card onto a fixed controlled vocabulary with domain nouns and method names removed (Kulikowski-style). Packs include the LM-training proxy, tabular ML, combinatorial heuristics, and later Lean constructions and in-silico protein design. The vocabulary axes are:
- locus: data/instances | parameters/state | search moves | evaluation
- operator: reweight | filter | reorder/curriculum | augment/symmetrize | restart/perturb | schedule/anneal | decompose | relax-then-round | average/ensemble | cache/reuse | precondition/rescale | prune
- signal: difficulty/loss | uncertainty | sensitivity | coverage/diversity | staleness | external prior
- trigger: static | warmup | cyclic | adaptive-on-signal
- assumption class
Reliability gate: two independent extractions must agree on at least 4 of 5 axes. Skeletons that fail are dropped.

2) Re-instantiation. A different call sees only the skeleton, the target pack's incumbent code and a one-paragraph pack brief. It writes k=2 independent patches, which controls for the implementation lottery. A collapse check against the target pack's knowledge base flags instantiations that equal a stock technique there. These are kept but reported separately.

3) Normalised outcomes. Each pack's code-owned verifier scores z = (gain over incumbent) / (incumbent seed sd). A win means z > 2, reproduced by the second implementation. The full measurement vector is logged:
- LM: data multiplier, FLOPs, NVML energy
- heuristics: score per instance class, runtime
- tabular: accuracy, fit time

4) Hierarchical credit. A Bayesian mixed model (numpyro or brms) is fitted: y = mu_d + alpha_s + beta_{s,d} + e.
- alpha_s is the skeleton's main effect.
- beta_{s,d} is the skeleton-by-pack interaction.
- Portability is rho = tau_alpha^2 / (tau_alpha^2 + tau_beta^2).
Clade credit: a skeleton's credit also includes its descendants, meaning skeletons produced by mutating or recombining it. This follows HGM's clade-metaproductivity (CMP), taken as the posterior mean gain over all descendant instantiations in all packs.

5) Hindsight goal switching. An instantiation that fails its target objective but is a noise-gated win on another logged objective (energy instead of data efficiency, or another instance class) credits the skeleton only in that objective's own ledger. It also opens a task for that objective.

6) Allocation. Each round splits budget between native knowledge-base-seeded generation and transfer.
- Transfer draws (skeleton, target pack) by Thompson sampling from the posterior of alpha_s + beta_{s,d}.
- Priors for a new pack are shrunk by rho.
- If the 90% upper bound on rho falls below 0.1, the transfer budget automatically goes to zero.

7) The resulting asset is a ledger of executed mechanisms with measured cross-pack portability. It becomes the highest-trust knowledge-base layer, and it seeds a new, expensive pack (e.g. protein binders) before any in-pack data exist.
newProposals.closest_prior_work:
- EMO-STA (Gozeten et al., arXiv 2605.22613, May 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22613): evolves a shared archive of executable programs across a task family, then adapts it per task. It beats matched-compute single-task evolution 'in most settings'.
- Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21614): clade-metaproductivity credit inside one tree of coding agents.
- The Station (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06309): one anecdotal import of 'density-awareness' from clustering into scRNA-seq integration, with no ablation.
- POET and Innovation Engines goal switching (Wang et al. 2019; Nguyen et al. 2016; cited from memory).
- ERA (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06503): pairwise recombination of methods within one field.
- Idea-Catalyst (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.12226): recasts problems in domain-agnostic form to retrieve inspiration from other fields. It reports +21% novelty; the abstract does not say how this was judged.
- Kulikowski domain-stripped fingerprints (arXiv 2609.07595): retrieval only.
- AgentHER (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21357) and SOAR (https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.14172): hindsight relabeling of failed agent trajectories and programs.
- In-panel: the Single-Graft Distance Ladder (literature skeletons grafted into LM training, with a bandit over distance bands) and the Equal-Tuning Headroom Archive (clade credit inside one domain's lineages).
newProposals.why_novel:
Prior transfer either moves executable programs within a task family (EMO-STA) or retrieves analogies by text (Idea-Catalyst, Kulikowski). Credit either stays inside one domain's lineage (HGM, the in-panel Equal-Tuning Headroom Archive) or attaches to distance bands (the in-panel Single-Graft Distance Ladder).

PML differs in three ways:
