- Its unit of credit is an executed, domain-stripped mechanism, credited through verified outcomes in structurally different domains: training a network, searching a combinatorial space, fitting tabular models. Programs cannot move between these domains; mechanisms can.
- It measures portability directly (the variance split alpha vs beta), and that number switches cross-domain transfer on or off, instead of assuming analogies help.
- It extends clade credit across domains and objectives through hindsight relabeling. The verified map lists both goal switching in research ideation and clade credit on idea lineages as untested.

No published system tests whether an idea's executed success in one domain predicts the success of its abstracted mechanism in another.
newProposals.evidence_basis:
- Lineage credit beats selection on an item's own score where it has been tested. HGM's clade estimator correlated 0.51-0.87 with empirical descendant productivity, against 0.27-0.44 for own-score selection (DGM, SICA). Context: self-modifying coding agents on SWE-Verified-60 and Polyglot, single runs.
- Recombining known methods pays off in executed terms. In ERA, 24 of 55 pairwise recombinations beat both parents on the OpenProblems scRNA-seq batch-integration task (held-out datasets, Gemini 2.5 Flash tree search). 29 of 55 recombinations beat the leaderboard, against 1 of 12 AI co-scientist ideas; that comparison is not controlled for difficulty or sample size.
- Cross-field transfer produced the highest-value AI results so far, but these are anecdotes, not rates. The unit-distance disproof (Erdos #90, a $500 problem) imported class-field towers into discrete geometry; it is human-verified and its compute is undisclosed. The Station's scRNA-seq result (0.5877 vs 0.5867) came from a clustering idea, with no ablation.
- Program-level sharing across tasks already helps within task families (EMO-STA, matched compute).
- Counter-evidence that makes the test necessary:
  - Learned outcome predictors do not transfer across ML areas. Mule et al. report 77.1% in-domain vs 45.7-49.1% cross-domain swap-consistent accuracy on 705 non-NLP PapersWithCode pairs; chance is about 25%.
  - Multi-objective hindsight relabeling degraded 19 of 36 multi-objective RL settings (arXiv 2609.26918), so relabeled credit needs its own gate.
- OptiLex pilot: all 30 clean Opus prompts fell into 3 mechanism families. Structured, externally sourced variety is needed, and executed foreign skeletons are one such source.
newProposals.first_experiment:
Packs (all have code-owned verifiers):
- (A) OptiLex LM tier-1 proxy, 3 paired seeds. It was calibrated to a 1.11x minimum detectable effect at 3 seeds on the 6.9M-parameter M1 grid.
- (B) Tabular ML on 6 OpenML tasks, CPU, 5 seeds.
- (C) Two combinatorial heuristic problems with instance generators and a local scorer (ALE-Bench-style), CPU, 50 instances.

Stage 0:
- Generate 40 knowledge-base-seeded Opus ideas per pack, implement each once, and execute.
- Re-implement the top 12 and bottom 12 (clear nulls) per pack to confirm their labels.
- This gives 72 origin skeletons (36 winners, 36 losers). Add 24 random skeletons sampled uniformly from the vocabulary as a null.

Stage 1:
- Instantiate every origin skeleton in both non-origin packs, and every random skeleton in all three packs, 2 independent instantiations each. That is about 336 executed instantiations.

Pre-registered test: mixed-effects logistic regression with skeleton and pack random effects.
- Primary: the target-pack win rate of origin-winner skeletons exceeds that of origin-loser skeletons by at least 10 pp (one-sided p < 0.05), and winner skeletons also beat random skeletons.
- Secondary: the 90% lower credible bound of portability rho is above 0.1.
- Kill: if the primary test fails, cross-domain credit is dropped and PML stays a within-pack ledger.
- Results are reported again after excluding collapse-to-known instantiations and hyperparameter-only skeletons, and per pack pair (near: LM-tabular; far: LM-heuristics).
- Power: about 140 instantiations per arm gives roughly 60-70% power for 10 pp at a 20-30% base rate before clustering. This pilot is sized for a large effect; if the result is inconclusive, stage 1 is doubled.
newProposals.evaluation:
Execution only.

Pilot scoring:
- A target-pack win is a noise-gated verifier result: the proxy's held-out-loss data multiplier with paired seeds, the score on hidden heuristic instances, or accuracy on held-out OpenML tasks.
- Every win must be reproduced by a second, independent implementation.

If the pilot passes, a prospective, pre-registered comparison follows in a fourth, held-out pack. The pack has deterministic evaluators: AlphaEvolve-style construction problems, or the SAIR Andrews-Curtis local checker. Three arms run at matched LLM and compute budget:
- (i) native knowledge-base-seeded generation
- (ii) native generation plus PML transfer
- (iii) native generation plus random-skeleton transfer (placebo)
An IID-sampling baseline is included, following Gideoni et al., and at least 300 test items are used to avoid selecting on noise.

The metric is verified wins per dollar. The novelty of each win is audited by a literature and knowledge-base collision check, not by an LLM novelty score. Realized outcomes are added where they exist, e.g. SAIR or Kaggle leaderboard results.
newProposals.cost_estimate:
First experiment: about $250-450.
- GPU: about $50-150 for roughly 250-300 tier-1 proxy run-sets. SWARM.md estimates tier 1 at 0.1-0.3 H100-hours per idea at about $1.7-2.7/h; this is not yet measured on GPU.
- CPU packs: under $20.
- LLM implementation, extraction and instantiation calls: about $150-250 at API prices, near zero marginal cost on a Max plan if automated use is permitted.

Ongoing: about 2 extra LLM calls per executed idea (roughly $0.1), plus whatever transfer executions the bandit chooses.
newProposals.risks:
- Vacuous skeletons: very abstract skeletons such as 'reweight by difficulty' port trivially. Mitigation: collapse-to-known flags, and portability is reported only for instantiations that are not stock techniques.
- The controlled vocabulary may miss the real insight. Deep transfers like the unit-distance disproof rest on heavy machinery, not operator-level skeletons.
- LLM extraction may be unreliable (gated by the two-extraction agreement check).
- Implementation-ease confound: simple skeletons are easier to implement. Diff size and failure rate are logged as covariates.
- Winner's curse in the stage-0 labels (mitigated by re-implementation).
- Portability may exist only between near packs (reported per pair).
- Hindsight relabeling can hurt (arXiv 2609.26918), so relabeled credit is kept in objective-specific ledgers.
- Terms of service: Anthropic's consumer terms prohibit bot or script access except via API key or explicit permission, and Claude Code docs direct production automation to API keys. Sustained automated runs should use an API key.

newProposals.name: Near-Miss Contrast Critic (NMCC): cheap verifiers mint executed minimal pairs to train and refresh critics
newProposals.one_line: Turn each executed idea into several mechanism-level near-miss variants, implemented as minimal diffs on the same code, and execute them. The low-noise contrast labels that result are used to train, calibrate and continually refresh the factory's pre-execution critic across domain packs, and the pilot tests whether a critic trained on cheap CPU verifiers transfers to a costly pack.
newProposals.mechanism:
1) Base pool. Every executed idea with a stable outcome (at least 2 independent implementations agree in sign) becomes a base.

2) Near-miss minting. A separate call writes canonicalized variant cards in fixed categories:
- (a) ablate the load-bearing component
- (b) swap its signal source for the most plausible alternative
- (c) invert the direction or sign of the key operation
- (d) add a plausible but mechanistically irrelevant component
- (e) a style-only rewrite with an identical patch, as a control
- (f) for failed bases, a 'repair' variant that removes the component a critic blamed, so labels are not always 'original wins'

3) Patch-locked implementation. Each variant is a minimal diff against the base implementation. A fidelity checker rejects any diff that touches more than the stated component or exceeds a size cap. Because both arms share code, the label carries rerun noise instead of implementation-lottery noise.

4) Labels. Execution uses paired seeds. The label is the paired effect difference with its confidence interval. Pairs with |z| < 2 get an explicit 'indistinguishable' class, which teaches the critic to answer 'no difference'.

5) Two critic forms, because Opus 5.5 cannot be fine-tuned:
- (i) a small open model (Qwen3-8B LoRA or a ModernBERT cross-encoder) trained on canonicalized pair cards to output P(A>B) and P(tie), scored swap-consistently;
- (ii) Opus with the most similar executed near-miss pairs retrieved as in-context evidence (Rehearse-style focused memory).

6) Anchored self-improvement. Each epoch:
- New natural executed outcomes are compared with the critic's predictions.
- Ideas where the critic was confidently wrong get priority for new near-miss minting (active learning on errors).
- A new critic version is promoted only if it beats the incumbent on a frozen anchor set of executed natural pairs.
- Anchor sets rotate out of training.

7) Deployment. The critic triages (execute now, flag, or deprioritize) and never hard-gates. Its calibration is tracked per pack. In expensive packs (wet lab, prizes), a critic trained on CPU-cheap packs is used only where its held-out-pack accuracy has been demonstrated.
newProposals.closest_prior_work:
- Wen et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00794) and Mule et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21491): predictors fine-tuned on pairs of different published ideas, labelled by reported benchmark results.
- BrainBench/BrainGPT (Nature Human Behaviour 2025): tells real abstracts from results-altered ones. Labels come from the literature, not execution.
- SciStyleBench (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01666): style-only perturbations of fixed-substance ideas. A trained style extractor raises substance recognition from 0.504 to 0.759, but there are no substance-varied or executed pairs.
- Execution-labelled verifiers and mutation-based rewards in code, e.g. R2E-Gym hybrid verifiers (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07164) and mutation testing as an RLVR reward: correctness against a fixed spec, not research-effect sizes.
- Red Queen Godel Machine (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26294): evaluators promoted on ground-truth anchor sets.
- Rehearse (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27687): a focused outcome memory for the judge.
- Implementation lottery (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26587).
- AblationBench and AbGen: planning ablations, not predicting their outcomes.
- In-panel: Critic Overoptimization Curves (evaluator overoptimization) and CHSP (hashed critic predictions).
newProposals.why_novel:
Every research-idea critic to date learns from one of two sources:
- natural pairs of different ideas, whether published or executed once;
- non-executed perturbations: style-only rewrites, or abstracts with altered results.
None trains on executed, substance-varied minimal pairs.

The distinction matters for label quality. Near-miss arms share one implementation, so their labels escape implementation variance. Implementation choice accounts for 33-45% of outcome variance in single-implementation labels, against 4-6% for reruns.

The pairs also target the critic's documented blind spots: load-bearing vs decorative components, direction errors, and style.

The self-improvement loop chooses what to execute next from the critic's own confident errors. It promotes a new critic only against executed anchors, never against other judges.

The pre-registered question is whether critics trained on cheap CPU-verifier minimal pairs transfer to natural pairs in a GPU-costly pack. That is the general-engine question, and no study has asked it.
newProposals.evidence_basis:
- Implementation variance swamps rerun noise. Implementation choice explains 33% and 45% of within-task variance, vs 6% and 4% for reruns. Leave-one-implementation-out winner reversals were 25.6% and 43.6%. Context: 13 OpenML tabular tasks, 312 assignments, DeepSeek v4 implementers, 39 decisions per setup, wide CIs.
- Outcome-label fine-tuning is what moves critics. Wen et al.: 51.4% zero-shot to 77% fine-tuned on 1,585 post-cutoff published pairs (GPT-4.1 plus retrieval). Fine-tuning on self-generated chain-of-thought gave no gain. Mule et al.: Qwen3-8B supervised fine-tuning reached 77.1% in-domain vs GPT-5-high at 61.1% (swap-consistent). The cross-domain collapse to 46-49% is exactly the transfer risk this experiment measures.
- Current judges miss substance:
  - SciStyleBench: direct judges' substance recognition was 0.504, and style alone changed 7.5% of top-10 membership (open judges up to DeepSeek-V3.2 size).
  - SoundnessBench: Claude Opus 4.6 accepted 71.8% of proposals that ICLR reviewers rated low-soundness. The labels are reviewer opinions, not execution.
- Executed outcome memory helps judges. Rehearse: without memory, the judge's selective accuracy fell from 82.8% to 56.9% after 3 or more accumulated successes; focused memory restored it to 83.5%. The nanochat loop improved 10.7% vs 7.1% (5 seeds, 4,000 runs).
- Small specialists trained on labelled contrasts can be strong. A 124M model trained from scratch reached expert level on BrainBench's altered-results task, with calibrated perplexity confidence. Caveat: that task rewards consistency with the literature.
- Prompted frontier models are weak effect forecasters. In Query2Effect, prompted GPT-5.2 (MAE 0.2374) lost to a constant (0.1946) on development-economics RCT effects, while a fine-tuned encoder pipeline reached 0.1722.
newProposals.first_experiment:
Packs:
- Training packs (CPU): tabular ML on 6 OpenML tasks, and combinatorial heuristics.
- Held-out test pack: the OptiLex LM tier-1 proxy (3 paired seeds).

Bases: 60 ideas per CPU pack and 30 LM ideas, reusing a shared stage-0 pool, each implemented twice. Only bases whose two implementations agree in sign are kept.

Near-misses: 5 per base (a-d, with f replacing d for failed bases, plus the style control e). That gives about 600 CPU variants (5 seeds each) and about 150 LM variants (3 paired seeds).

Test set: all LM natural pairs with a decisive difference, expected to be about 150-250 pairs, bootstrapped by idea.

Critics compared:
- C0: zero-shot Opus, both orders
- C1: Opus with retrieved natural-pair exemplars
- C2: Opus with retrieved near-miss exemplars
- C3: Qwen3-8B LoRA trained on natural CPU-pack pairs
- C4: Qwen3-8B LoRA trained on near-miss CPU-pack pairs
C1 vs C2 and C3 vs C4 are matched on the number of executions spent creating their training labels.

Pre-registered success, on held-out LM decisive natural pairs:
- The best near-miss critic (C2 or C4) beats its natural-pair counterpart by at least 8 pp swap-consistent accuracy, and beats C0 by at least 10 pp.
- Style-only controls are judged 'no difference' at least 75% of the time (the direct-judge baseline is 0.504).
- Near-miss labels reproduce on a second implementation in at least 85% of pairs (natural pairs are expected at about 60-75%).

Kill: if near-miss critics do not beat natural-pair critics on held-out natural pairs, near-misses teach only diff detection. They are then kept for soundness triage only.
newProposals.evaluation:
Offline test:
- Every accuracy figure is computed against executed outcomes on a held-out pack and on held-out natural pairs.
- Scoring is swap-consistent, with CIs bootstrapped by idea. No LLM judge supplies labels.

Operational test, matched budget, 2 packs: verified wins per executed run when the queue is ordered by:
- the near-miss critic
- zero-shot Opus
- random order (DeepScientist-style ablation)

Goodhart monitoring: once generators are selected against the critic, accuracy is re-measured on fresh executed ideas every epoch. Near-miss labels also feed the Critic Overoptimization Curves proposal's evaluator panel.

Transfer to realized outcomes: where a pack has delayed real results, the critic's rank order is compared against them. Examples are the SAIR checker result or a Kaggle private leaderboard.
newProposals.cost_estimate:
First experiment: about $250-500.
- LM variant runs: about $45-120 GPU (150 tier-1 run-sets).
- CPU packs: under $20.
- Near-miss cards, minimal-diff implementations and fidelity checks: about $100-250 at API prices (less on Max if permitted).
- Qwen3-8B LoRA training: 2-4 A100-hours, about $10-20.
- Critic scoring calls: about $50-120.
All figures are estimates. The stage-0 pool is shared with the PML and Fidelity-Weighted Ledger experiments.
newProposals.risks:
- Shortcut learning: critics may learn 'originals beat ablations' or 'longer card wins'. Mitigation: repair variants, the indistinguishable class and canonicalization.
- Too few labels: about 1-2k pairs may be too few for the open model (Mule used 11,488). The in-context Opus arm hedges this.
- Minimal-pair skill may not transfer to natural pairs of different ideas. This is the measured outcome, not an assumption.
- Patch-locked diffs can break code subtly. Execution failures are tracked by category.
- Critics may overfit pack-specific cues. Pairs are split by base idea.
- Near-miss minting spends execution budget. It must pay for itself through better queue ordering, which the operational test checks.
- Data governance: consumer-plan data retention and training settings for unpublished ideas.

newProposals.name: Fidelity-Weighted Ledger (FWL): randomized cross-rung audits that learn when cheap verifiers can be trusted, idea by idea
newProposals.one_line: In every domain pack, promote a random, propensity-logged slice of cheap-verifier losers and middling ideas to the next verifier rung, and learn how agreement between the cheap and expensive rungs varies with an idea's novelty. Use those fidelity estimates as label weights and promotion thresholds wherever the factory learns from cheap verifiers, so the self-improving engine does not absorb the proxy's bias toward incumbent-like ideas.
newProposals.mechanism:
1) Ladders. Each pack declares rungs: R0 (cheapest executable), R1 (higher fidelity) and R2 (realized value).
- LM: tier-1 proxy, then tier-2 BabyLM strict-small with hidden held-out loss, then tier 3 or an external leaderboard or merged speedrun PR.
- Heuristics: public small instances, then a hidden, shifted instance generator, then a live contest or private leaderboard.
- Tabular: 3 OpenML tasks, then 10 held-out tasks.
- Math constructions: numeric evaluator, then Lean proof, then curator acceptance.
- Protein: in-silico complex confidence, then Adaptyv wet-lab binding.

2) Judge-free novelty covariates, pre-registered and computed before execution:
- (i) mechanism-family distance from the incumbent: Hamming distance over PML skeleton axes, gated by extraction agreement
- (ii) embedding distance to the pack's knowledge base (SPECTER2-class)
- controls: diff size, number of new hyperparameters, and R0 measurement SE

3) Randomized promotion. Beyond the normal policy (promote R0 winners), each non-winner is promoted with known probability pi(x), e.g. 10-20%, stratified to oversample high-novelty ideas. Propensities are logged. Inverse-propensity weighting then gives unbiased R0 false-negative and false-positive rates.

4) Fidelity model. Per pack, R1_effect ~ lambda_d(x) * R0_effect + bias_d(x).
- A measurement-error correction uses an independent R0 re-run, which separates R0 reliability from R0-to-R1 fidelity and guards against the winner's curse.
- lambda and bias are functions of the novelty covariates.
- The model is hierarchical across packs, so a new pack starts from the pooled novelty slope.

5) Uses:
- (a) Promotion becomes value-of-information-based and novelty-conditional: promote when E[R1 value | R0, x] / cost clears a threshold, including ideas that R0 under-rates.
- (b) Every loop that consumes R0 labels weights each label by its estimated fidelity and subtracts its expected bias. This covers the outcome predictor, PML skeleton credit, NMCC critic labels, AIDE2-style harness acceptance and the Critic Overoptimization Curves.
- (c) When R2 outcomes arrive (prize, merge, lab result), the same model extends one rung up and learns fidelity to realized value.

6) Drift. Fidelity is re-estimated each epoch. A new incumbent, i.e. a newly co-adapted baseline, triggers a re-audit.
newProposals.closest_prior_work:
- Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization: Kennedy & O'Hagan 2000 co-kriging, and Kandasamy et al. MF-GP-UCB 2016 and BOCA 2017 (cited from memory). They model cross-fidelity correlation within one problem, usually as stationary across inputs.
- Hyperband and ASHA successive halving.
- DataDecide (https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11393): rankings at 150M pick the 1B pairwise winner about 80% of the time, for data recipes.
- Wang et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24503): proxy fidelity depends on the proxy's training protocol; reduced learning rates preserve data-recipe ordering across 23 recipes.
- Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02046): under equal tuning, speedups shrink from 1.4x at 0.1B to 1.1x at 1.2B.
- LEVI (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09764): rank-preserving proxy evaluation.
- AlphaResearch (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08522): a one-off execution of 151 ideas its reward model rejected found 43 false rejections.
- AIDE2 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26457, 22 Sep 2026): a public inner-loop signal separated from private held-out acceptance for harness self-improvement.
- Randomized 'shadow review' of auto-rejected candidates, a standard QA practice in screening pipelines.
- In-panel: Critic Overoptimization Curves (evaluator selection curves at one rung) and the Equal-Tuning Headroom Archive (tuning gap at one rung).
newProposals.why_novel:
Multi-fidelity optimization treats cross-fidelity correlation as a property of one problem. Proxy-validity studies (DataDecide, Wang et al., Fantastic Optimizers) measure it for a single family of interventions. AlphaResearch measured false rejections once, at one rung.

FWL changes this in four ways:
- Fidelity becomes an idea-conditional quantity, with novelty as a pre-registered covariate.
- It is estimated without selection bias, through randomized, propensity-logged promotions.
- It is pooled across structurally different packs.
- It is fed back as label weights into every learning loop of a general engine.

This closes a gap specific to self-improving factories. A loop that learns from cheap verifiers inherits any bias those verifiers have toward incumbent-like ideas unless it measures that bias. No study has measured whether cheap-to-expensive verifier agreement depends on an idea's novelty; the verified map lists only the analogous gap for forecasters.
newProposals.evidence_basis:
- Proxy fidelity is imperfect even for known intervention families:
  - DataDecide: about 80% pairwise decision accuracy from 150M to 1B (data recipes).
  - Fantastic Optimizers: matrix-optimizer speedups shrink from 1.4x to 1.1x between 0.1B and 1.2B once baselines are equally tuned.
  - Wang et al.: proxy fidelity changes with the proxy's training protocol.
- There are hints that rung disagreement grows with novelty, but all are confounded:
  - Heuresis: across 3,222 scored runs, novel ideas never approached the top known-recipe scores on executed val_bpb; the authors call this an optimization gap. The novelty labels there were LLM-judged.
  - CACHE #3: over 85% of picks were chemically novel, yet 27 of 28 confirmed hits used the canonical scaffold. This is correlational: novel chemotypes may simply bind less often.
- One-rung filters hide false negatives. AlphaResearch's reward model rejected 28.5% (43/151) of ideas that were viable when executed (circle packing, 7B reward model trained on ICLR reviews).
- Verifier-passed does not mean valuable. Aletheia's natural-language verifier flagged 212 of 700 Erdos problems; human grading found 13 of 200 (6.5%) meaningfully correct.
- Separating inner and outer signals helps self-improvement. In AIDE2, reward hacking on held-out kernel tasks fell from 55% to 32% across its self-improvement trajectory (acceptance on private held-out grades). Evolved AIME scaffolds lost more than 10% from validation to test by selecting on noise (Gideoni et al.).
- OptiLex already has a calibrated tier ladder: a 1.11x minimum detectable effect at 3 seeds, and tier 1 to tier 3 gates in SWARM.md.
newProposals.first_experiment:
Packs and rungs:
- LM: R0 is the tier-1 proxy with 3 paired seeds plus an independent R0 re-run for reliability. R1 is a reduced tier 2 (BabyLM strict-small 10M words, 3 seeds, hidden held-out loss).
- Tabular: R0 is 3 OpenML tasks; R1 is 10 held-out tasks.
- Heuristics: R0 is 20 public instances; R1 is 50 instances from a shifted hidden generator.

Ideas: 60 LM, 120 tabular and 120 heuristic, drawn from a mix of generators chosen to spread novelty: clean, ask-for-novelty, noisy-persona and distant knowledge-base seeds. In the OptiLex pilot these spanned 3 to 15 families.

Full audit: every idea runs at both R0 and R1, so the randomized-promotion estimator can be checked by subsampling against full truth. A small learning-rate sweep at R0 for every idea separates 'untuned' from 'non-transferring'.

Pre-registered hypotheses:
- H1: in a pooled mixed model with pack random slopes, the interaction of R0 effect and novelty on R1 effect changes the fidelity slope lambda by at least 25% per SD of novelty. Its 90% CI must exclude 0, with the same sign in at least 2 of 3 packs.
- Equivalence kill for H1: if the CI lies within ±10% per SD in all packs, cheap verifiers are novelty-neutral and uniform weights suffice.
- H2: replaying the ledger with cross-validation by idea, a novelty-conditional promotion rule recovers at least 25% more R1 winners per R1-dollar than the uniform R0-threshold rule.
- H3: inverse-propensity estimates from a simulated 15% randomized promotion recover the full-audit false-negative rate within ±5 pp.
newProposals.evaluation:
Ground truth is R1 execution: higher-fidelity training, hidden or shifted instances, and held-out tasks. It is never a judge.

Prospective test: over the next 2 rounds, the fidelity-weighted promotion policy is compared with the uniform policy at matched R1 budget. The metric is R1-verified wins per dollar, plus the downstream accuracy of the outcome predictor when trained on fidelity-weighted vs unweighted R0 labels, scored on fresh R1 outcomes.

When realized R2 outcomes arrive, fidelity to them is measured the same way. Examples are a BabyLM leaderboard entry, a contest result, or a Lean-checked construction accepted by the curator. All thresholds are pre-registered, and at least 300 test items are used wherever selection is involved.
newProposals.cost_estimate:
First experiment: about $250-480.
- LM R1 dominates: 60 ideas at about 1-1.5 H100-hours each, about $110-250. This is a reduced tier 2 at 3 seeds, scaled from SWARM.md's estimate of 2-4 H100-hours at 5 seeds.
- LM R0: about $20-50.
- CPU packs: under $30.
- About 300 implementations: about $90-150 at API prices.

In steady state, randomized promotions cost about 10-20% of R1 spend. They should be kept only if H1 or H2 shows that the correction changes decisions.
newProposals.risks:
- The novelty covariates may be noisy (LLM skeleton extraction, embedding distance). Mitigation: agreement gating and two covariates.
- R0 to R1 fidelity may not predict R1 to R2 (value) fidelity, so the realized-value rung must be audited when data arrive.
- Limited power in the LM pack at n=60. Mitigation: pooling across packs with pack random slopes.
- Novel ideas may just be under-tuned, which overlaps with the Equal-Tuning proposal. The R0 learning-rate sweep controls for this.
- Regression to the mean may mimic novelty effects. The independent R0 re-run corrects for it.
- The fidelity model can overfit. Mitigation: cross-validation by idea and by pack.
- If fidelity turns out novelty-neutral, the audit budget is overhead and should shrink to periodic drift checks.

targets.name: SAIR Lean Kernel Challenge Stage 1: number-theory and recurrence problems (fib, partition, mertens, primecount)
targets.what: For each of four fixed Lean specs (n-th Fibonacci number, partition function p(n), Mertens function, prime counting pi(n)), submit one human-readable Submission.lean (at most 1 MiB) containing impl : Nat -> Output and a universal proof impl_correct : forall n, impl n = spec n. Every problem has its own leaderboard. Rank is the sum over test cases of the median kernel-replay instruction count across 3 replays, lowest first. Rules R1-R5: no partial/unsafe code, no sorry/admit/native_decide or unapproved axioms, no precomputed lookup tables, and correctness only buys entry. Submissions went live 2026-09-15 on competition.sair.foundation.
targets.reward_or_value: No cash prize is published on the rules, repo, Tao's announcement (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/16/sair-competition-lean-kernel-challenge/) or the SAIR API record. SAIR's privacy policy mentions collecting tax info 'solely for prize distribution', so prizes are possible but unannounced; treat cash as unknown or zero. Realized value is a public ranking on a Lean FRO co-run board (organisers de Moura, Morrison, Breitner, Tao) plus reusable verified-computation techniques. Competition state from SAIR's public leaderboard API, daily board with data cut-off 2026-09-27 00:00 UTC: 272 registered participants. Ranked teams: fib 27, partition 24, mertens 18, primecount 18. Team 'memcon.ai' is #1 on all four, e.g. partition 1,429,499 instructions vs #2 1,438,118 (b-mehta), so the margins at the top are about 0.6%.
targets.deadline: 2026-11-20 23:59 AoE (API submissionDeadline 2026-11-21T11:59:59Z). The latest formal entry per team and problem counts, not the best one. Stage 2 is announced for December 2026.
targets.verifier: Lean 4 kernel on a pinned toolchain, run locally with lake build (checks code and universal proof). There is an optional local evaluator (evaluation/run.py) that measures wall time. Official scoring is instruction counts over 3 replays on SAIR infrastructure. Limits: 600 s correctness comparator, target replay 30/60/120 s per repetition, and a 4 GiB memory cap (provisional). Fully machine-checked with no human judging.
targets.eligibility: SAIR Competition Rules (https://competition.sair.foundation/sair-competition-rules): individuals at the age of majority in their jurisdiction; SAIR staff and judges are excluded. One account per person and one team per person or organisation. A real legal name is required. Sponsors must be disclosed; rule 3.1 lists 'paid API access' as sponsorship, so disclose the Claude Max use. Country or sanctions restrictions not found.
targets.ai_policy: There is no challenge-specific AI clause in the LKC rules or Tao's post. SAIR Rules 4.1: participants 'are permitted to utilize any publicly available or private external models, APIs, and datasets to generate their submissions'. The participant must comply with third-party ToS and warrant the output can be open-sourced (4.2). SAIR gets a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to all submissions (5.2), and the repo is Apache-2.0.
targets.poc_cost: Near zero. Lean and elan run on a laptop CPU with no GPU. Claude Max plus at most about $100 of optional cloud CPU for replay benchmarking. Playground allows 2 runs per day.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the purest verifier the factory can get: a Lean proof plus a deterministic instruction-count score. The generator can propose many algorithm and representation ideas (sieve variants, Meissel-Lehmer/Lucy-Hedgehog prime counting, Euler pentagonal recurrence, binary-representation tricks for kernel reduction), and the critic-fixer loop is driven by lake build errors. It is a fast calibration domain for a Lean pack, with a ledger of instruction counts per idea. Caveat: the top is tightly contested (under 1% gaps), so the edge must come from new representations, not tuning.

targets.name: SAIR Lean Kernel Challenge Stage 1: heavy-compute problems (permanent, polydisc, sha256, ca-rule110)
targets.what: Same format as above, for four problems with much larger kernel workloads. Permanent: the permanent of a generated 0/1 matrix, with an 8 GiB memory cap. Polydisc: the exact discriminant of a generated monic degree-24 polynomial. Sha256: repeated hashing of a 32-byte digest. Ca-rule110: evolution of a seeded 256-cell cyclic Rule 110 row. Each is a separate leaderboard ranked by summed median kernel instruction counts, with a mandatory universal Lean correctness proof.
targets.reward_or_value: Cash is not published (see the fib/partition target). Leaderboard state at the 2026-09-27 cut-off: ca-rule110 has 22 ranked teams, permanent 19, polydisc 18, sha256 18. The gaps are much wider than on the number-theory problems. Permanent: #1 memcon.ai 143,756,271 vs #2 b-mehta 193,510,038 (about 35% gap). Polydisc: #1 1,232,868,831 vs #2 1,676,430,860 (about 36% gap). This suggests representation and algorithm choices (e.g. Ryser/Glynn formula for permanent, subresultant or modular-CRT discriminant) still matter a lot. Kernel-efficient verified implementations of these routines have lasting value for Mathlib and Lean users.
targets.verifier: Pinned Lean 4 kernel with a universal proof (impl n = spec n for all n). Official instruction-count replays on SAIR; local lake build plus an optional unsandboxed evaluator.
targets.eligibility: Same SAIR Competition Rules: age of majority, one account and one team, real legal name, sponsor disclosure including paid API access.
targets.ai_policy: SAIR Rules 4.1 permit external models and APIs, subject to ToS compliance and an open-source-release warranty (4.2). There is no LKC-specific restriction on AI assistance. All submissions are licensed to SAIR irrevocably (5.2).
targets.poc_cost: Claude Max plus roughly $0-300 of CPU. Proofs of correctness for the Ryser formula or the discriminant via resultants are the hard part, and they cost Lean-engineering time rather than compute.
targets.why_factory_fits: The wide gaps at the top mean that one genuinely better algorithm or representation idea can move a team several ranks. That is what an ideas factory is for: analogical search over the algorithms literature, then proof-carrying implementation, then an automatic score. The main risk is proof effort. The fixer rounds need a Lean-competent executor, and at least one strong human Lean hand is advisable for the harder universal proofs.

targets.name: SAIR x Caltech Andrews-Curtis Conjecture Challenge: Discovery Track (AC and Stable AC leaderboards)
targets.what: For a fixed pool of 10,115 balanced two-generator presentations of the trivial group (including many from the AK(n) series, per Tao), submit explicit move sequences. AC paths use move IDs 0-13 and must end exactly at <x,y | x,y>. Stable AC paths use moves 0-256, may use up to 8 generators, and must end at the empty presentation. Submission is a submission.txt of 'challenge_id: [moves]' lines. On each challenge, the k teams tied for the shortest verified path each earn 2^(1-k) points, and the first solver of each presentation is noted separately. Status from SAIR's public snapshot at 2026-09-27 10:35 UTC: 7,443 of 10,115 AC presentations solved and 2,672 unsolved. For Stable AC the same split holds, 7,443 solved and 2,672 unsolved. 3,702 AC challenges (3,757 Stable AC) currently have a single record-holder.
targets.reward_or_value: No cash prize is published (Tao's post, repo rules and SAIR API all silent). Value comes as points on two public leaderboards and first-solver credit. All valid paths are released after the competition. A trivialization of an open AK(n) case (e.g. AK(3)) would be research-grade: Tao links the conjecture to exotic smooth 4-spheres and the smooth 4D Poincare conjecture. The Discovery Track has 135 registered participants (ACC total, SAIR API).
targets.verifier: The official Python replay verifier (PYTHONPATH=competition/tools python3 -m verifier --manifest competition/tools/verifier/data/manifest.json) is identical locally and on SAIR. Limits: at most 100,000 moves, relator length at most 10,000 letters after each move, total work at most 5,000,000, 500 lines per file, 10 MB, and 40 submissions per team per UTC day.
targets.eligibility: SAIR Competition Rules: age of majority, one account and one team, real legal name, sponsor disclosure (paid API access counts). Individuals or teams.
targets.ai_policy: Tao: 'AI tools are welcome, and participants can enter individually or as teams.' SAIR Rules 4.1 also permit any external models or APIs subject to ToS. Submissions are licensed to SAIR and all valid solutions are released publicly; the repo is Apache-2.0.
targets.poc_cost: Claude Max plus about $100-500 of CPU for beam, greedy or RL-guided search (the verifier is pure Python, so a C or Rust reimplementation of the move engine is worthwhile). No GPU needed unless an RL policy is trained.
targets.why_factory_fits: The action space is small, the checker is exact and local, and there are two scoring modes. Shortening one of the 7,443 known solutions is a dense reward, while cracking one of the 2,672 unsolved presentations is a sparse, high-value one. The factory's generators can propose diverse heuristics (potential functions, supermove or macro libraries mined from solved paths, Stable-AC detours through extra generators, analogies to the Caltech 'path-finding' and 'two-hump' work), and the executor scores each by solved count and length reduction. Evidence caveat: the organisers' own RL and combinatorial search (Shehper et al., arXiv 2408.15332, on the Miller-Schupp series) is the baseline to beat. An LLM-heuristic edge over purpose-built search is unproven, so the ledger should track 'new solves per CPU-hour' against a plain BFS/greedy baseline.

targets.name: SAIR x Caltech Andrews-Curtis Challenge: the 2,672 currently unsolved pool presentations (first-solver credit)
targets.what: A sub-target within the Discovery Track: presentations in the official pool with no verified trivialization from any team as of the 2026-09-27 10:35 UTC snapshot. There are 2,672 each for AC and Stable AC, per SAIR's public endpoint https://api.sair.foundation/api/acc/discoveries/snapshot?problem=ac. Per Tao, first solvers of each presentation are recorded separately from the shortest-path points, and the pool runs from easy cases to open research problems, including AK(n)-series members. Stable AC gives extra room: up to 8 generators at any step.
targets.reward_or_value: Uncontested points: a sole solver takes the full 1 point per presentation until someone shortens the path. There is also first-solver attribution in the published results and possible research value if a long-standing hard case falls. No cash has been announced. Some of these may be potential counterexamples, and then no path exists: the snapshot does not separate 'hard' from 'possibly non-trivializable'.
targets.verifier: Same official replay verifier and manifest as the Discovery Track. A path counts only when the verifier returns ok: true.
targets.eligibility: Same SAIR Competition Rules as the Discovery Track.
targets.ai_policy: 'AI tools are welcome' (Tao, ACC announcement). SAIR Rules 4.1-4.2 and 5.2 cover external model use and open licensing.
targets.poc_cost: Claude Max plus about $200-1,000 of CPU for deep or long search, since unsolved cases likely need large intermediate relator lengths within the 10,000-letter and 5,000,000-work caps.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is a clean novelty gate: 'unsolved in the public snapshot' is an objective, machine-readable open-problem list that refreshes daily. The factory can pull the list, generate targeted strategies per structural family (e.g. AK(n) members vs Miller-Schupp-type), run the search, verify locally, and log every solve in the outcome ledger. Rediscovery risk is low because any verified path to an unsolved item is new to the board by construction.

targets.name: SAIR x Caltech Andrews-Curtis Challenge: Proof Track (proofs, disproofs, partial results, optional Lean)
targets.what: Submit ideas, partial results, or full proofs or disproofs of the AC conjecture or the Stable AC conjecture at any finite rank. Counterexamples need not come from the pool. Each submission is a required description with citations, optionally a public GitHub Lean 4 formalization (full commit hash) against the official AC.lean definitions, and optionally an arXiv link. Submissions are auto-published in the SAIR Contributor Network for community peer review.
targets.reward_or_value: No cash or points are published. The value is public, timestamped, credited contributions in the Contributor Network, where others can build on them with credit. A full resolution would be a major result in combinatorial group theory and 4-manifold topology. Realistic factory outputs are formalized partial results, e.g. Lean-verified invariants that separate candidate counterexamples, or formal proofs that whole families such as parametrized AK(n)-type or Miller-Schupp subfamilies are AC-trivial. Per the rules, 'being recorded does not certify mathematical correctness'.
targets.verifier: Human community peer review of the description. An optional Lean 4 formalization using the official AC.lean definitions can be machine-checked, which is the factory's only hard verifier here. Unverified prose claims carry little weight.
targets.eligibility: SAIR Competition Rules. Checking the public-sharing agreement box is required to submit.
targets.ai_policy: 'AI tools are welcome' (Tao). The Proof Track requires citing others' work used, including papers, repos, submissions and comments, which the dedupe/novelty gate must enforce. SAIR Rules 4.1 allow external models.
targets.poc_cost: Near zero in compute: Claude Max plus Lean on a laptop. The cost is Lean formalization time.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is lower-probability and higher-ceiling. Use it only with Lean-checked outputs, e.g. auto-generalizing families of Discovery-Track solutions into parametric proofs, formalized in Lean against AC.lean. That way the factory's LLM-judge-free verifier principle holds. The rediscovery risk is high (60 years of literature), so the novelty gate needs a deep literature search before submission. Treat this as reputational output, not a cash channel.

targets.name: Erdős prize problems that a finite example can settle (the site labels them VERIFIABLE, FALSIFIABLE or DECIDABLE)
targets.what: Open prize problems that one explicit object would settle, found by constructive search and checked by a program. #647 ($44, VERIFIABLE): find n>24 with max_{m<n}(m+tau(m)) <= n+2. #97 ($100, FALSIFIABLE): find a convex polygon in which every vertex has 4 other vertices equidistant from it. #128 ($250, FALSIFIABLE): find a triangle-free graph in which every induced subgraph on >= n/2 vertices has more than n^2/50 edges. #107 ($500 for a proof, but only $100 for a disproof; the Happy Ending problem): find a point set that breaks f(n)=2^{n-2}+1. #64 ($1000, FALSIFIABLE): find a finite graph with minimum degree >= 3 that has no cycle of length 2^k. #7 ($25, VERIFIABLE): find an odd distinct covering system. #19 ($500, DECIDABLE): Erdős–Faber–Lovász, which is proved for all large n, so only a finite check remains. Source: prize tier pages, fetched 2026-09-27.
targets.reward_or_value: Erdős cash prizes of $25 to $1,000 as listed above. The FAQ says the site does not pay. The Combinatorics Foundation (administered by Steve Butler) pays 'only... after the publication of a solution in a reputable journal', with documentation that Erdős offered that amount. The main value is a public status change on the site, credit, and a paper. Correction to the input digest: across the whole site, 114 problems carry prizes, 55 are solved and 59 are open, with $34,120 of open prize value. The digest's figures of 100 open and 152 total are wrong.
targets.deadline: None (rolling). Statuses were last changed 5 Sep 2026.
targets.verifier: A deterministic program checks the witness (exact or integer arithmetic, SAT/ILP certificates). The claim can then be restated in Lean: formal-conjectures has human-written open statements for #7, #19, #64, #97, #107, #128 and #647. After that come community review on the problem's proof-claims thread and curator (Thomas Bloom) acceptance.
targets.eligibility: Anyone. Posting on the forum needs a free erdosproblems.com account. Prize claims go to the Combinatorics Foundation after journal publication.
targets.ai_policy: Forum rules say AI assistance 'is allowed, but should be disclosed'. Every claim must be 'independently verified by a human before posting'. You may post only after (a) understanding and verifying the maths yourself or (b) obtaining a 'sorry and bug-free Lean formalisation'. The rules also warn that 'the harder the problem, the higher the bar'. Caveat: Bloom's blog post of 12 Sep 2026 ('Tell me what should change') puts the site's handling of AI output under review, with a decision due after about two weeks of consultation, i.e. around early October 2026. Commenters proposed an intermediate status for Lean-verified AI proofs that nobody has read. Re-check the rules before submitting.
targets.poc_cost: Claude Max ($100-200/mo) plus $0-500 of CPU for local search (SAT/ILP/evolutionary search with a numeric verifier). Lean and Mathlib run locally for free.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the cleanest executor loop: generator, program checker, then a Lean restatement, with no judge in the loop. An AI model settled #90 (unit distances) the same way in May 2026 (arXiv 2605.20695). Caveats: these are well-studied problems. Erdős himself called an answer to #647 'extremely doubtful'. #64 is proved for large minimum degree (Liu–Montgomery). #107 is famous. Expect a hit rate well below the 0.57% novel-full-solution rate that DeepMind reported over 700 mostly obscure problems (arXiv 2601.22401), and give these problems a high notability weight in the ledger.

targets.name: Open Erdős problems with human-written Lean statements in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (proof/disproof sweep)
targets.what: Prove or disprove open Erdős problems whose formal statement a third party has already written in Lean. As of repo HEAD on 27 Sep 2026 there are 780 Erdős problem files, 414 of which contain at least one `category research open` statement. The database lists 635 open of 1,221 problems (last status change 5 Sep 2026). Using a pre-written statement avoids the AI misformalising its own target.
targets.reward_or_value: Status changes to 'PROVED (LEAN)' or 'DISPROVED (LEAN)' on erdosproblems.com, a `formal_proof` link in formal-conjectures, arXiv write-ups and reputation. There is no cash unless the problem carries an Erdős prize. Realized-outcome base rates, which cover all labs and are not a benchmark: Tao's wiki (frozen 30 Jun 2026) lists 18 distinct problems fully solved by AI alone in Jan–Jun 2026 (GPT-5.x Pro, Aristotle, the DeepMind prover agent, Claude Mythos and others) and 10 incorrect AI-alone claims. DeepMind's Gemini run over 700 'Open' problems gave 2 full novel solutions (arXiv 2601.22401). Recent example: #477, marked solved in Sep 2026, partly by GPT for even d >= 6.
targets.deadline: None (rolling)
targets.verifier: The Lean 4 kernel. PROOFS.md requires `#print axioms` (no sorryAx and no custom axioms) and a check that the linked statement implies the repository statement. Community review on the forum and curator acceptance follow.
targets.eligibility: Anyone. PRs to formal-conjectures need the Google CLA signed.
targets.ai_policy: formal-conjectures follows Mathlib's AI conventions. Contributors 'must explain this in the PR description' (which tools and how), and add an LLM-generated label for substantial AI code. They must also 'understand all the content written by an AI' and be able to justify it without AI. PROOFS.md says 'Do not add an informal proof of an open research problem' and prefers long proofs to be kept externally and linked. The erdosproblems.com forum rules apply as in the first target, and the site's policy is under review (Bloom, 12 Sep 2026).
targets.poc_cost: Claude Max only. Lean/Mathlib builds locally. Optionally add Harmonic's Aristotle, the formaliser cited in the #728 solve.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the candidate's core channel: many attempts per target, a free kernel verifier, and an outcome ledger. The statement is pre-formalised by humans, which addresses the wiki's warning that it is 'best if the statement... is formalized by a human or a third party'. Risks: labs are sweeping these problems, wins cluster on obscure ones, and the DeepMind authors say many problems were open 'through obscurity rather than difficulty'. The notability field is mandatory.

targets.name: Lean formalisation of solved-but-unformalised Erdős results (upgrade to PROVED (LEAN))

Among prize problems these are: #633 ($25); #27, #54, #72, #88, #182, #211, #720 ($100); #55, #166, #591, #607, #703 ($250); #67, #92 ($500); #625 ($1000, solved Sep 2026); #4 ($10,000). There are many more non-prize solved problems (filter 'solved' plus 'unformalised' on the site). In formal-conjectures, #4, #67, #92, #591 and #633 have solved statements but no formal_proof, and #27, #54, #55, #88, #182, #211, #607 and #625 have no file at all. #72, #166, #703 and #720 already carry formal_proof links, so check them first.
targets.reward_or_value: Status upgrade on erdosproblems.com, a `formal_proof` attribute in formal-conjectures and contributor credit. There is no cash, because prizes are for solutions, not formalisations. Precedent: Tao's wiki counts 185 formalisation entries, 173 of them successful, by 30 Jun 2026. This is reputational and infrastructural value, useful as evidence in grant applications.
targets.deadline: None (rolling)
targets.verifier: The Lean 4 kernel plus `#print axioms` and a check that the statement matches the repository statement (formal-conjectures PROOFS.md). This verifier is nearly perfect, and no novelty judgment is needed.
targets.eligibility: Anyone. Formal-conjectures PRs need the Google CLA.
targets.ai_policy: Mathlib/formal-conjectures conventions: disclose tools in the PR, label LLM-generated code, and understand and justify every formalisation decision without AI. The erdosproblems.com forum accepts a 'sorry and bug-free Lean formalisation' as grounds for posting.
targets.poc_cost: Claude Max only. Size varies a lot: #4 (large prime gaps, Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao) and #67 (Tao's discrepancy theorem) are multi-month formalisation projects, not proofs of concept. Pick short elementary proofs first.
targets.why_factory_fits: This has the highest verifier certainty of any target, and there is zero rediscovery risk because the result is known by construction. It gives the factory a reliable calibration and throughput stream for its executor and critic-fixer rounds, and it builds the Lean library used by the first two targets. Impact per item is modest, so do not count these as 'new ideas'.

targets.name: Literature-status corrections: find existing solutions to problems marked open (the 'import' channel)
targets.what: Search the literature for published results that already resolve, or substantially advance, problems the database lists as open. Submit them as comments under the problem or by email to the curator. The FAQ explicitly says the database is not up to date and warns 'Do not assume that an 'unsolved' problem is in fact unsolved'.
targets.reward_or_value: The problem's status changes and the contributor is credited under 'Additional thanks to'. There is no cash. Precedent: Tao's wiki counts 68 AI literature-search finds by 30 Jun 2026. In DeepMind's 700-problem run, 8 of the 13 problems 'addressed' already had solutions in the literature (5 found by literature search, 3 rediscovered independently; arXiv 2601.22401).
targets.deadline: None (rolling)
targets.verifier: The curator (Thomas Bloom) and community check the cited paper against the problem statement. This is expert acceptance, not a formal check, although the cited result can sometimes be restated in Lean.
targets.eligibility: Anyone (a free account for comments; email is also accepted).
targets.ai_policy: Same forum rules. AI-assisted search is allowed if disclosed, and a human must verify the claim before posting. Tao's wiki recommends AI deep-research tools plus forward and backward citation search (Google Scholar, MathSciNet, zbMATH). It warns against solving a misstated version and against announcing too early.
targets.poc_cost: Claude Max only (web search, arXiv and zbMATH are free).
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the factory's retrieve-before-invent operator. The same literature-search module is the novelty and dedupe gate for the first two targets, so every run produces both credited finds and a cleaner target list. It also guards against the main failure mode seen in 2026: presenting rediscoveries as new results.

targets.name: Small-cash open Erdős prize problems ($10-$78) with computational handles
targets.what: Open problems in the lowest prize tiers (pages /prizes/10, /25, /50, /78). #470 ($10): do odd weird numbers exist? None exist below 10^21 (Fang), and any such number needs at least 6 prime factors. #1052 ($10): are there only finitely many unitary perfect numbers? Five are known; the page was edited 2 Sep 2026. #634 ($25): which n allow a triangle to be cut into n congruent triangles? Whether 19 works is a finite sub-question. #32 ($50): can an additive complement to the primes have O(log N) density? #661 ($50): bipartite distinct distances o(n/sqrt(log n)). #710 and #711 ($78 each, converted from rupees): Erdős–Pomerance divisor-selection problems. Van Doorn (2026) settled the second part of #711, and the first part is still open.
targets.reward_or_value: $10-$78 each through the Combinatorics Foundation after journal publication. That is trivial cash, so the value is a credited solution and a paper. Partial results, such as settling n=19 in #634 or extending the odd-weird-number search bound, can be accepted on the page as progress without resolving the problem.

targets.verifier: Lean where statements exist (formal-conjectures covers several; #710's page shows 'Formalised statement? No'). Otherwise program-checked computation for the sub-questions, then community and curator review.
targets.eligibility: Anyone. Prize money requires journal publication and documentation.
targets.ai_policy: Same erdosproblems.com forum rules: disclose AI use, human verification or a clean Lean proof before posting, and a higher bar for harder problems. The site policy is under review (Bloom, 12 Sep 2026).
targets.poc_cost: Claude Max plus $0-300 of CPU for exhaustive or search computations (for example, extending the odd weird number bound or tiling searches for n=19).
targets.why_factory_fits: These give a narrower ideation target with a known state of the art on each page, which is good seed material for the analogy and knowledge-base generators. Caution: #470 and #1052 are classic hard questions (Guy's B2/B3), and cash is negligible. Rank these below the first three targets, and log partial progress separately from full solves.

targets.name: Optimization Constants in Mathematics repository (Davis, Ivanisvili, Tao), bound tables for 88 constants
targets.what: A crowdsourced table of 88 optimization constants (C1 to C88 plus variants) whose bounds keep improving. Many bounds come from explicit constructions scored by a scalar objective, for example the Sidon autocorrelation constant C1a, the sum-difference constants C3a to C3c, cap-set constant C4, sphere-packing density in R^4 (C36), moving sofa (C41) and the Erdős maximum-term constant (C51). The table is very active: the README's 'Recent progress' section lists more than 30 bound changes in Feb to Sep 2026, including four C9 improvements between 23 Jul and 31 Aug 2026 and C4b raised to 0.75806770413 on 21 Sep 2026 (Lean-formalized). You contribute by opening a Markdown-only pull request that updates the constant page and the README cell, citing your certificate or paper.
targets.reward_or_value: No cash. Value is a public, dated record on a table maintained by Tao, Davis and Ivanisvili, credibility for arXiv papers and grant applications, and an externally checked hit or miss for the factory's outcome ledger. Competition is real: AI-heavy entrants already appear, e.g. Numaro (C3a, 23 Jul 2026), Mosaic Intelligence (C3b) and OpenAI (C88a ≤186, 30 Aug 2026, Lean 4 formalization conditional on three declared axioms).
targets.deadline: Rolling (no deadline). Pull requests are merged in the chronological order of the claims.
targets.verifier: Your own deterministic scalar evaluator produces the certified bound. The maintainers then review for 'minimal standards of plausibility and replicability'. A bound gets an asterisk ('unverified') if it is too large to check by hand and exists only as a self-archived artifact. The asterisk is dropped once the result is refereed, formalized (e.g. a Lean proof registered on Palomar) or independently replayed. Record the directly recomputable value, not an extrapolated limit.
targets.eligibility: Anyone with a GitHub account, via pull request. Code and certificates must be hosted elsewhere (your own repo, Zenodo, arXiv ancillary files), preferably with a DOI or a pinned commit hash.
targets.ai_policy: CONTRIBUTING.md: 'Use of AI to help prepare submissions is permitted, so long as this is noted in the submission text'. A human must review and verify all references and other information the AI provided. Minor uses such as spellcheck need no disclosure.
targets.poc_cost: Low. A Claude Max subscription plus roughly $100-1,000 of CPU/GPU for a ShinkaEvolve/OpenEvolve-style loop per constant. Evaluators are cheap numerical programs (LP/FFT-based autocorrelation, entropy certificates). Adding a Lean formalization to avoid the asterisk costs more human or agent time but little compute.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the most direct match to the candidate: one scalar evaluator per constant, a public 'best known' column that doubles as the literature/dedupe gate, and fast public crediting (days). It also calibrates the factory, because most runs will only match the known bound, as AlphaEvolve's did. Pick constants where recent improvements came from computation (C3a/C3c, C1a, C4b, C9) and budget for crowding: several constants moved multiple times within weeks in Jul to Sep 2026.

targets.name: Epoch AI FrontierMath: Open Problems, the unsolved construction problems
targets.what: A benchmark of 49 research problems, each with a bespoke verifier; 40 are unsolved as of the 16 Sep 2026 changelog. Unsolved extremal and construction problems include: The Ramsey Number R(6,6) (exhibit a 2-coloring of K_n, n ≥ 102, with no monochromatic K6; current bounds 102 ≤ R(6,6) ≤ 160); 4x4 matrix-multiplication tensor rank ≤ 47 (exact coefficients in Q[t]/(f); the best known is 48); No-Three-in-Line (a family with more than 1.8n points for arbitrarily large n); Chowla's cosine problem; Littlewood polynomials with normalized Mahler measure above 0.97 at every degree up to 500,000; Large Steiner Systems; Leech Trees; sensitivity vs degree; Earth–Moon; Hirsch conjecture in dimension 4; Heesch number 7. Most are Python programs of the form solution(n) -> witness, checked on a laptop within minutes.
targets.reward_or_value: No prize money is disclosed. Value is notability: each problem carries an editorial grade (Moderately interesting, Solid result, Major advance, Breakthrough), and a solution meets the bar of being 'worthy of publication in at least a standard specialty journal'. Epoch credits solutions publicly; for example, it marked the Hadamard matrix of order 668 (solved by three humans with Claude) as solved on 12 Aug 2026. Nine problems are solved so far (4 AI, 5 human + AI).
targets.deadline: Rolling, until each problem is solved. Epoch also removes problems whose verifiers it judges inadequate, e.g. the Ramsey-hypergraph and stretched Littlewood-Richardson problems.
targets.verifier: Epoch's private bespoke verifier: 'Email math@epoch.ai and we will do our best to run the relevant verifier in a timely manner.' Mathematicians then confirm accepted solutions before the headline result is updated. Verifier code is sold rather than published (so far only OpenAI has bought access). Several problems can still be checked independently in-house, e.g. an exact polynomial-identity check for a rank-47 decomposition, or a K6-free check of a coloring on at least 102 vertices.
targets.eligibility: Any party can email a solution in the format specified on the problem page.
targets.ai_policy: AI solutions are explicitly welcome. Since 16 Sep 2026 there is a 'human + AI' label, used when AI 'was instrumental' but not autonomous. The label 'Solved (AI)' requires that the core ideas be 'unambiguously contributed by AI', judged largely from author attribution.
targets.poc_cost: Per problem: Claude Max plus $200-2,000 of compute. The R(6,6) and matrix-rank problems are heavier searches (SAT or local search, or flip-graph search over tensor decompositions). Mahler-measure, Chowla and no-three-in-line are cheap: FFT or geometry evaluators on a laptop.
targets.why_factory_fits: These are posted, expert-graded, machine-verifiable construction targets with a public solved/unsolved ledger, exactly the verifier-first shape the candidate needs. Caveat: they were selected because professionals tried and failed ('at least two professional mathematicians have tried'), and frontier labs (OpenAI with verifier access, Anthropic researchers) are active here. The expected hit rate per problem is therefore low, and each solved problem is a strong, citable realized outcome.

targets.name: SAIR Andrews–Curtis Conjecture (ACC) Challenge, Discovery Track (plus Proof Track)
targets.what: Find the shortest sequences of AC moves (move IDs 0-13), or Stable AC moves (IDs 0-256, at most 8 generators), that trivialize each of 10,115 published balanced presentations of the trivial group. The pool includes the Akbulut–Kirby family AK(n) (notably AK(3), a long-standing potential counterexample), presentations up to length 13 studied by Miasnikov/Myasnikov and Havas/Ramsay, and a four-generator example from Bridson. The organizers say the examples range from easy to open research problems. A separate Proof Track takes ideas, partial results or full proofs or disproofs of AC and Stable AC.
targets.reward_or_value: No cash prize is stated in the official rules or in the announcement. Scoring: on each challenge, the k teams tied for the shortest verified path each earn 2^(1-k) points, with separate AC and Stable AC leaderboards. Proof Track submissions are published in the SAIR Contributor Network with credit. A trivialization of AK(3), or a verified counterexample, would be a research result relevant to exotic 4-spheres.
targets.deadline: 30 Nov 2026, end of day AoE (both tracks). Opened 11 Sep 2026.
targets.verifier: Deterministic open-source Python verifier (competition/tools/verifier) that replays the move sequence. Limits: 100,000 moves, 10,000-letter relator length, 5,000,000 total work, 500 solution lines per file, 40 uploads per team per UTC day. A Lean 4 formal statement (AC.lean) is provided for proofs.
targets.eligibility: You need a SAIR account with a completed profile, and must accept the SAIR competition terms. Enter individually or as a team, one team per individual or organization, with sponsors declared in advance. Participants pay their own compute.
targets.ai_policy: The Tao blog announcement (11 Sep 2026) says 'AI tools are welcome, and participants can enter individually or as teams.' The repository rules set no AI restriction; the anti-cheating rules cover sockpuppet teams only.
targets.poc_cost: Low. Claude Max for writing search heuristics plus about $100-800 of CPU for BFS, greedy or evolutionary path search across 10k presentations. Local verification is free.
targets.why_factory_fits: A dense, graded target set with a free local verifier and a live leaderboard: the executor-plus-evolver half of the factory gets thousands of scalar-scored (path length) instances and an external ranking before 30 Nov 2026. The Caltech Math-AI group (RL and search) organizes it and reports that important cases resisted their methods, so shortening known paths is realistic, while cracking AK(3) is a long shot.

targets.name: Fast matrix multiplication algorithms catalogue (Sedoglavic, Univ. Lille): rank records for fixed formats
targets.what: A catalogue of 5,426 fast matrix multiplication schemes <X×Y×Z:N> for almost all formats from 2x2 up to 32x32, with a JSON summary on GitHub. It credits recent AI and search contributors: Novikov et al. (AlphaEvolve 2025), Kauers & Wood 2025 (flip graphs), Moosbauer & Poole 2025, and Perminov 2026. Current square records it lists: <3×3×3:23> (Laderman 1976), <4×4×4:48> (AlphaEvolve 2025), <5×5×5:93> and <6×6×6:153> (Moosbauer & Poole 2025). Many rectangular formats improved during 2025-26, so many cells can still be beaten.
targets.reward_or_value: No cash. A new record for any format goes into the de facto reference table and usually into an arXiv note. It also improves asymptotic exponents computed from the table and is directly usable in libraries. Beating 4x4 rank 48 in the complex setting would also solve Epoch's FM:OP matrix-multiplication problem, which asks for rank ≤ 47.
targets.deadline: Rolling.
targets.verifier: Exact algebraic check that a decomposition reproduces the matrix-multiplication tensor (Brent equations), in exact arithmetic over Z, Q or an algebraic extension. The check is deterministic, takes milliseconds to seconds, and is run by the factory itself. The maintainer adds records by contact: 'any feedback is welcome'.
targets.eligibility: Open. Contact the maintainer (Alexandre Sedoglavic) or cite a public arXiv or GitHub scheme, as Perminov 2026 did.
targets.ai_policy: No stated policy. The catalogue openly credits AI-found schemes (Fawzi et al. 2022 RL; AlphaEvolve 2025).
targets.poc_cost: $200-2,000 of compute. Flip-graph random walks or SAT/ALS search on CPU, with Claude writing and evolving search heuristics.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the flagship AlphaEvolve precedent domain (4x4 in 48, the first improvement in 56 years), with a perfect scalar verifier and an authoritative record table that works as the dedupe gate. The candidate entry already names matrix-multiplication schemes. It is crowded (AlphaEvolve is now generally available on Google Cloud; Kauers, Moosbauer, Perminov are active), so target less-searched rectangular formats or ranks over Z/Z2 rather than 4x4 alone.

targets.name: Erdős Problems with prizes that are 'FALSIFIABLE' or 'VERIFIABLE' by a finite construction
targets.what: Prize-carrying Erdős problems that a finite example settles, so a construction search plus a checker applies. Current open examples: #64 ($1000): is there a finite graph with minimum degree ≥ 3 and no cycle of length 2^k? #107 (Happy Ending, f(n)=2^(n-2)+1): Erdős offered only $100 for a disproof, meaning a point set with no convex n-gon larger than conjectured. #128 ($250): a triangle-free graph meeting the n^2/50 dense-induced-subgraph condition. #114 ($250): a monic polynomial whose lemniscate |p|=1 is longer than for z^n−1; Tao [Ta25] settled all sufficiently large n, so only small n remain. #97 ($100): a convex polygon in which every vertex has 4 other vertices equidistant from it. #647 ($44) and #7 ($25, a distinct covering system with all moduli odd) are 'VERIFIABLE' by a finite example.
targets.reward_or_value: Small cash: $25-$1,000 for these problems. The site lists $34,120 of unsolved prize value in total, most of it for proofs rather than constructions. The site FAQ says prizes are paid by the Combinatorics Foundation (Steve Butler) 'only… after the publication of a solution in a reputable journal'. The main value is reputational: Erdős results draw expert attention (e.g. #1's disproof by GPT-6 Astra, exposition by Bloom, Sep 2026).
targets.deadline: Rolling, until each problem is solved.
targets.verifier: The factory's own exact checker (graph cycle-length enumeration, convex-position test, covering-system check), then human expert review on the erdosproblems.com forum and, ideally, a Lean formalization. For the prize itself: journal publication.
targets.eligibility: Anyone. The prize requires journal publication plus documentation that Erdős offered the amount.
targets.ai_policy: Forum rules: 'AI assistance in generating ideas or helping to formulate the text of a comment is allowed, but should be disclosed.' All claims must be verified by a human before posting. The forum 'does not exist to serve as a benchmark for AI progress'.
targets.poc_cost: Claude Max plus about $50-500 of compute per problem (local search or SAT on small graphs and point sets).
targets.why_factory_fits: These are cheap, famous, binary-verifiable targets that use the same generator-evaluator-evolve loop. Expected hit rate is low: several are believed true (e.g. #64 is proved for large minimum degree by Liu–Montgomery, and #107 is widely believed), so no counterexample may exist. Treat them as a small, high-notability slice of the portfolio, and run a literature-dedupe gate first, because rediscovery is the dominant failure mode in AI Erdős work.

targets.name: AI for Math Fund Seed Grants (Renaissance Philanthropy with XTX Markets)
targets.what: Rolling seed grants for early-stage AI-for-maths work. Eligible categories include 'early-stage research or prototypes exploring new approaches to automated theorem proving, AI-assisted proof development, or mathematical reasoning', datasets and benchmarks, tools or infrastructure experiments, and field-building. An open-source, Claude-driven extremal-construction evolver with a public ledger of verified bound improvements fits the prototype and tooling categories.
targets.reward_or_value: Up to $100,000 per seed grant. The main round, which offers $100k-$1M over 12-24 months, is closed: its abstract deadline was 30 Mar 2026.
targets.deadline: Rolling ('Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis'). No new main-round deadline is announced as of 2026-09-27.
targets.verifier: Human review by the fund. Here the verifiers from the other targets do the persuading: dated, externally checked records (optimization-constants table entries, FM:OP solves, ACC leaderboard rank, catalogue records) make the application credible.
targets.eligibility: Open to 'individuals and teams worldwide' (main-fund language). For seed-grant specifics, see the linked application form.
targets.ai_policy: Not applicable to authorship; the fund exists specifically to fund AI for mathematics.
targets.poc_cost: Only the time to write the application, but it should follow the first verified results from the targets above to be competitive.
targets.why_factory_fits: The candidate's value path lists 'Credibility for Renaissance AI for Math seed grants' as its only cash channel. This is the one open, rolling source of money that turns the zero-cash construction wins into funding and pays for later factory compute. Sequence it after one or two external verifications.

checks.name: Optimization Constants in Mathematics repository (Davis, Ivanisvili, Tao), bound tables for 88 constants
checks.correction: Verified against the live repo (last commit 26 Sep 2026) and CONTRIBUTING.md. The claims check out: 88 numbered constants (115 table rows including variants); maintainers Davis, Ivanisvili and Tao; Markdown-only PRs with code and certificates hosted elsewhere (DOI or pinned commit preferred); PRs merged in chronological order of claims; the asterisk policy, with the marker removed on refereeing, Lean/Palomar formalization or independent replay; 'record the certified value, not the limit'; and the AI-disclosure quote with its spellcheck exemption. Recent-progress items also match: four C9 improvements on 23 Jul, 30 Jul, 31 Jul and 31 Aug 2026; C4b = 0.75806770413 by JD Jones on 21 Sep 2026, Lean formalization registered on Palomar; Numaro C3a on 23 Jul 2026; Mosaic Intelligence C3b; OpenAI C88a <= 186 on 30 Aug 2026 with three declared axioms. The Mosaic C3b entry is also asterisked and undated. (2) 'Cap-set constant' is C4a. C4b is the Furstenberg–Sárközy constant. (3) The moving-sofa upper bound 2.2195 is still asterisked.

checks.name: Epoch AI FrontierMath: Open Problems, the unsolved construction problems
checks.correction: Core facts verified. These come from the page, the FAQ and the CC-BY data zip (49 problem rows): 9 solved (4 AI, 5 human + AI) and 40 unsolved. R(6,6), 4x4 matrix-multiplication rank <=47 (exact coefficients in Q[t]/(f), best known 48), no-three-in-line (>1.8n points, solution(min_n)), Littlewood/Mahler >0.97 (n up to 500,000, 5-minute limit), Chowla, Steiner, Leech trees, sensitivity-vs-degree, Earth–Moon, Hirsch d=4 and Heesch 7 are all listed and unsolved. The FAQ quote 'Email math@epoch.ai and we will do our best to run the relevant verifier in a timely manner' is exact. Verifier access is sold, and OpenAI was the only purchaser as of Jul 2026. The 16 Sep 2026 changelog introduced the 'human + AI' label ('AI was instrumental... but did not solve it autonomously') and removed stretched Littlewood-Richardson. The Ramsey-hypergraph problem was removed on 31 Jul. Corrections: (1) Apéry-style irrationality (Breakthrough tier) was solved as human + AI on 17 Sep 2026, after the 16 Sep changelog. Counts still read 9 solved and 40 unsolved, but the page header says 'expanded to 50 problems' while only 49 are listed. (2) Hadamard 668 was marked solved on 12 Aug 2026 as 'solved by AI'. The data now labels it human + AI, consistent with 'three humans with Claude'. (3) The 'at least two professional mathematicians' quote is not verbatim. The FAQ's lowest tier requires that the problem was posed 10+ years ago and 'worked on by at least two independent teams of mathematicians'. The main page says the problems 'resisted serious attempts by professional mathematicians'. (4) The 'standard specialty journal' wording could not be confirmed. The page says a solution should be 'a publishable result in its own right'. No prize money is stated anywhere, which is correct.

checks.name: SAIR Andrews–Curtis Conjecture (ACC) Challenge, Discovery Track (plus Proof Track)
checks.correction: Verified from the official repo rules (overview.md, discovery.md, problems/README.md, verifier data) and Tao's 11 Sep 2026 blog post. The following all match: 10,115 presentations in both AC and Stable AC (20,230 scored challenges) plus 424 unscored training examples; AC move IDs 0-13 and Stable AC IDs 0-256 with at most 8 generators; 2^(1-k) tie scoring with separate leaderboards; limits of 100,000 moves, 10,000 letters, 5,000,000 work, 500 lines per file and 40 uploads per team per UTC day; Discovery opened 11 Sep 2026 16:00 UTC and closes 30 Nov 2026 AoE; the Proof Track; Lean AC.lean; the SAIR account/profile/terms requirement; one team per individual or organization, with sponsors registered in advance; participants bear their own compute; no cash prize anywhere; the blog quote 'AI tools are welcome'; and 'many important cases have resisted all our efforts'. Correction: every pool presentation is a balanced TWO-generator presentation <x, y | ...>. Bridson's four-generator example appears only as background in Tao's blog and is not in the Discovery pool; it is relevant only to the Proof Track. AK(3) itself appears to be in the pool: a length-13 entry of the form (y^-1x^-1y^-1xyx, y^-4x^3) is present. Miasnikov–Myasnikov and Havas–Ramsay are cited as background ('all other candidates with length <= 13 are AC-trivial or AC-equivalent to AK(3)'). The repo says the pool derives from the SAIR dataset and the 'MS-1190 open set'.

checks.name: Erdős Problems with prizes that are 'FALSIFIABLE' or 'VERIFIABLE' by a finite construction
checks.correction: Verified from the individual problem pages, the prizes page, the FAQ and the forum rules. Tags and amounts match: #64 FALSIFIABLE $1000; #97 FALSIFIABLE $100; #107 FALSIFIABLE, listed at $500 for a proof ('only offers $100 for a disproof', and Graham offers $1000 for a proof); #114 FALSIFIABLE $250, Tao [Ta25] covers all sufficiently large n; #128 FALSIFIABLE $250; #647 VERIFIABLE $44; #7 VERIFIABLE $25.
