Entrants may use 'any modeling strategy' and train on any data. virtualcellchallenge.org did not render, so the rules page itself was not read.

checks.name: Anthropic AI for Science Program (API credits, rolling monthly review)
checks.correction: The help-center page confirms: up to $20,000 in API credits over 6 months, submissions evaluated on the first Monday of each month, researchers at academic and nonprofit institutions, and a biosecurity screen. It covers the standard model suite only, with no experimental or non-public models, and there are no individual responses to rejected applications. The closed rare-disease track was confirmed: announced 20 Jul 2026, up to $50k, closed 2 Aug 2026. It had two tracks, one of which was for early-stage biotechs. The Claude Science track ($30k, closed 15 Jul 2026) was not independently verified.

targets.name: Anthropic x Adaptyv Protein Design Competition - Track 3, Challenges 3-5
targets.what: Five weekly de novo binder-design challenges, each on a different disease target, released 28 Sep - 31 Oct 2026; targets and requirements are published only when each problem opens. Remaining windows: Challenge 3 12-18 Oct, Challenge 4 19-25 Oct, Challenge 5 26-31 Oct 2026. Track 3 (open track) needs no application and permits any tools; Tracks 1 and 2 closed on 24 Sep 2026.
targets.reward_or_value: No cash: the terms state 'The Competition does not award a cash prize to Participants.' Value is Anthropic + Adaptyv sponsoring $1M+ of wet-lab validation across 5,000+ synthesized proteins at no cost to entrants, plus 'special non-cash prizes' (still TBA), a public validated dataset on Proteinbase and inclusion in the community results paper. The compute awards (up to $50k Claude credits academic / $25k industry for ~30 Track 1 teams; Claude Max 20x for Track 2) are no longer reachable - that application window was 16-24 Sep 2026.
targets.deadline: Per-challenge weekly windows; Challenge 3 closes 18 Oct, Challenge 4 25 Oct, Challenge 5 31 Oct 2026. All submissions close 31 Oct 2026. Experimental validation by 30 Nov 2026; results published on Proteinbase 15 Dec 2026.
targets.verifier: Adaptyv's automated lab in Lausanne: protein expression plus label-free binding (BLI/SPR) giving yes/no binding, kinetic curves and KD/kon/koff. Which designs get tested is decided by a 'pre-defined and jointly agreed upon Claude-based workflow', not a single in-silico metric. Allocation is the risk: Track 1 has ~15 designs per challenge reserved, while Tracks 2 and 3 share one 384-well plate per problem with no guaranteed allocation. Prior-round realized hit rates (Proteinbase): EGFR-1 2.5% of 201 tested (best 491 nM), EGFR-2 14% of 400 (1.21 nM), Nipah 9.3% of 1,200 (0.37 nM), RBX1 2.8% of 322 (23.7 nM).
targets.eligibility: Individuals 18+ or teams of any academic or commercial affiliation. Excluded: legal residents of, or entities domiciled in, Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, Russia, Sudan, Syria, Crimea, and the so-called Donetsk/Luhansk People's Republics. Track 3 is explicitly 'open to all others' - no application, no institutional affiliation needed.
targets.ai_policy: AI-generated designs are the point of the competition; no restriction on AI-assisted or fully AI-generated sequences. Claude is optional in Track 3 - 'Use of Claude is not required to participate in the Competition generally but is a condition of receiving Support.' Human review of designs before submission is required. Participants keep ownership of their designs but grant the sponsors a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free, perpetual and irrevocable licence to publish sequences, methods and measurements, released under ODC-BY, so there is no IP or trade-secret value in a winning design.
targets.poc_cost: About $0 lab cost. Compute only: structure-prediction and design GPU time, roughly $200-1,000, on top of an existing Claude Max subscription. Note the live constraint from the candidate record: the Opus 5.5 bio classifier falls back to Opus 5 on molecular-design prompts, and LSVP does not cover individual plans.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the cheapest path the factory has from generated idea to a realized, third-party-measured outcome, and it matches the engine's shape exactly: run several independent design pipelines per target, gate on dedupe/novelty and in-silico confidence, submit only a small diverse set, and write every measurement into the outcome ledger as ground truth for the domain pack. Weekly target reveals give three independent shots (Ch3-5) inside five weeks. Discount it honestly: Track 3 can end with zero designs tested, so treat lab data as upside and the pipeline calibration as the guaranteed return.

targets.name: Anthropic AI for Science Program (research credits)
targets.what: Rolling application for free Claude API credits for high-impact scientific projects, expanded on 27 Aug 2026 alongside 10,000 free and discounted Claude Team seats for scientists. Biological sciences has been the largest recipient category to date.
targets.reward_or_value: Credits toward Anthropic offerings, not cash; reported at up to $50,000 per project for teams whose use outgrows their seat allocation. The official rules say only that Anthropic 'determines the specific credit amount in its sole discretion'.
targets.deadline: Rolling - submissions are evaluated on the first Monday of each month, so the next decision points fall in October, November and December 2026.
targets.verifier: Anthropic's internal review: 'objective evaluation' plus a biosecurity assessment 'to ensure they do not raise concerns around accelerating harmful applications', with the highest-scoring eligible applications receiving credits. This is expert review, not a realized outcome - weigh it below wet-lab evidence.
targets.eligibility: Individuals 18+ (or local age of majority); institutional consent required if affiliated with a university or employer. Same excluded-country list as the competition (Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, Russia, Sudan, Syria, Crimea and disputed territories), plus US sanctions/export-control exclusions. Secondary coverage of the Aug 2026 expansion describes the seat allocation as requiring PI-or-equivalent status at an academic or nonprofit institution - worth confirming on the application form before assuming an unaffiliated entry qualifies.
targets.ai_policy: The program exists to fund AI-driven research, so AI-generated work is in scope by construction. Molecular and protein design applications go through the biosecurity screen, which is the same mechanism behind the Opus 5.5 bio-classifier fallback the candidate record flags. Anthropic may publish anonymized, aggregated findings and takes publicity rights over winners' names and likenesses.
targets.poc_cost: Application effort only; the award directly offsets the engine's inference and generation bill.
targets.why_factory_fits: It funds the factory's dominant recurring cost - Opus generation across many parallel design pipelines - and the protein pack is precisely the kind of project the program has funded most. Rolling monthly review means it can be applied for now and re-applied for, unlike the Adaptyv compute tracks that already closed.

targets.name: Cancer Grand Challenges - gastroesophageal cancer targeted call
targets.what: Two targeted challenges on gastroesophageal cancers: reversing the early tissue changes that lead to these cancers, and explaining the biological mechanisms behind geographical variation in incidence. Applications are open now.
targets.reward_or_value: Up to $34m per team over a flexible period (the launch announcement framed the wider round at up to $25m per team).
targets.deadline: Full application 24 November 2026; a Letter of Interest must be submitted at least two weeks earlier. Shortlisted teams are interviewed on 20 January 2027 in New York City.
targets.verifier: Peer review by the Cancer Grand Challenges Scientific Committee, then a shortlisting interview. Expert rating, not experimental validation - the weakest verifier class of the six listed here.
targets.eligibility: One Team Lead plus up to seven Co-Investigators. Teams must be international, with no more than 50% of Co-Investigators and no more than 50% of overall funding in a single country. No UK or US leadership requirement. Biomedical, software/technology, engineering and social-science disciplines all welcome.
targets.ai_policy: No stated rules on AI-generated or AI-assisted proposals.
targets.poc_cost: Proposal writing only, but the funded work is orders of magnitude above the $2k-per-POC envelope, and the team-composition rule makes a solo or small-team lead application non-viable.
targets.why_factory_fits: Poor near-term fit and listed for completeness: it is the only large, currently open, post-15-Oct call in an adjacent disease-biology space where a de novo binder capability is a credible component. The realistic play is not leading an application but offering the validated binder-design pipeline as the AI/design workstream inside someone else's team - which only becomes credible after Adaptyv wet-lab data exists in December 2026.

targets.name: Longevity Impetus Grants
targets.what: Rolling, fast-turnaround grants for high-risk longevity and aging-biology science, funded by the Rosenkranz Foundation and Hevolution Foundation and run by Norn Group. The live round emphasises AI-enabling datasets: high-quality data relevant to human disease, organism-level perturbation studies and intervention trials.
targets.reward_or_value: Up to $500,000 per grant. The round targets ~$15M for roughly 50 grants, with the first $5M in commitments matched 1:1.
targets.deadline: Rolling - no fixed deadline, with decisions historically within three weeks of application.
targets.verifier: Expert reviewer panel (rating, not realized outcome). The downstream verifier for anything funded would still have to be built - e.g. Adaptyv binding assays.
targets.eligibility: Scientists at any career stage, including independent investigators and people new to aging research. The page does not state an institutional requirement, so an unaffiliated applicant should confirm before investing effort.
targets.ai_policy: Not addressed on the programme page - no stated restriction on AI-generated proposals or AI-designed molecules.
targets.poc_cost: Proposal only; an award would itself fund validation well beyond the $2k POC envelope.
targets.why_factory_fits: Rolling plus a three-week decision is the fastest cash channel found for this domain, and a binder against an aging-relevant target, validated for ~$1-2k at Adaptyv, is exactly the kind of cheap concrete deliverable a proposal can promise. Caveat to check first: the live round's stated emphasis is datasets rather than molecule design, so confirm the current call's scope before writing.

targets.name: ACS Precision Chemistry - 'Precision Polypeptides' special issue
targets.what: Open call for Articles, Letters, Perspectives and Reviews for a special issue of Precision Chemistry (ACS, open access) on polypeptides, with listed topics including polypeptide library construction and screening and 'binding and function modulation to target biomolecules'.
targets.reward_or_value: No money. Value is a peer-reviewed, open-access publication and the citation impact that follows - the realized-outcome currency for the reputation path in this candidate's value model.
targets.deadline: 30 November 2026.
targets.verifier: Journal peer review. Stronger than an LLM-judge or in-silico score, weaker than wet-lab measurement; it is a check on the write-up, not on the binder.
targets.eligibility: Open submission to any authors; standard ACS authorship and originality requirements.
targets.ai_policy: The call itself states nothing about AI-generated content; ACS-wide policy requires disclosure of generative-AI use and bars AI tools from being listed as authors, so plan on a disclosure statement.
targets.poc_cost: Effectively $0 beyond writing, but it is a downstream channel: it needs data in hand, which means pairing it with the Adaptyv competition results (published 15 Dec 2026, after this deadline) or with self-funded Adaptyv assays run in October and November.
targets.why_factory_fits: It converts the factory's methods contribution - multiple independent design pipelines plus dedupe/novelty gating and a Claude-driven shortlist - into a citable artifact on a fixed date. Timing is the catch: competition results land 15 Dec, after 30 Nov, so a submission by this deadline has to rest on self-funded assay data, and a methods paper without measurements is a much weaker bet.

targets.name: Adaptyv Bio protein binding service (rolling self-funded verifier)
targets.what: Open, rolling ordering of the same wet-lab pipeline the competition uses: protein expression plus label-free BLI/SPR binding characterization on any submitted sequence, with an API aimed at automated and agentic workflows. Not a prize - a posted, priced, always-available verifier.
targets.reward_or_value: No reward. Its value is that it removes the factory's single largest dependency: it turns a designed sequence into third-party measured binding data (yes/no, kinetic curves, KD/kon/koff, expression yield) on demand rather than only inside a competition window.
targets.deadline: Rolling - ordering is open continuously; 3-4 weeks from submission to data release, with Adaptyv claiming as little as 3 days in its fastest configuration.
targets.verifier: Adaptyv's automated lab - the identical instrument stack and readouts that verify the Anthropic x Adaptyv competition, so results are directly comparable to the published Proteinbase rounds.
targets.eligibility: Open to any customer via the platform; no competition, institution or track membership required.
targets.ai_policy: None - it is a commercial assay service with no restriction on how sequences were generated, and no requirement to publish. Unlike the competition, data stays private, so IP and licensing value is preserved.
targets.poc_cost: Binding from $99/protein for screening; $169/sequence quoted for full affinity characterization in duplicate. Expression alone is cheaper. A 10-15 design validation round therefore lands at roughly $1-2.5k - at or just inside the sub-$2k POC ceiling, and well inside it if screening mode is used.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the fallback that makes the whole protein pack robust: if Track 3 receives no testing allocation, the factory can still buy a real verifier for a few hundred dollars and keep the outcome ledger fed with realized measurements. It also preserves IP that the competition would publish under ODC-BY, which is the only route in this domain where a validated binder retains licensing value.

checks.name: Anthropic x Adaptyv Protein Design Competition - Track 3, Challenges 3-5
checks.correction: Page and terms page are live and the competition is real. Verbatim confirmations: 'The Competition does not award a cash prize to Participants.'; 'Use of Claude is not required to participate in the Competition generally but is a condition of receiving Support.'; Track 3 is 'open to any Participant that is not in Track 1 or Track 2'; licence is 'a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free, perpetual, and irrevocable license' with publication 'under ODC-BY'; excluded-country list matches exactly (Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, Russia, Sudan, Syria, Crimea, so-called Donetsk/Luhansk People's Republics); 18+/age of majority; $1M+ wet-lab validation and 5,000+ proteins; Track 1 ~15 designs/challenge reserved vs no guaranteed allocation for Tracks 2/3; timeline 28 Sep start, 31 Oct final submission, 30 Nov validation, 15 Dec results; Track 1/2 application window 16-24 Sep 2026 is closed as described. THREE CORRECTIONS. (1) TIMING - the record is scoped wrongly and in your favour. As of today, 27 Sep 2026, the competition has not started; it begins TOMORROW, 28 Sep. Challenges 1 and 2 have not happened, so all FIVE challenges are still ahead, not three. The framing 'Remaining windows: Challenge 3 12-18 Oct...' is wrong - that is five independent shots, not three. (2) The per-challenge dates are NOT published. Terms say only that problems are released 'approximately weekly' and that 'deadlines for submitting designs for each problem will be communicated'. The specific Mon-Sun windows (Ch3 12-18 Oct, Ch4 19-25 Oct, Ch5 26-31 Oct) are the record's inference, not published fact, so they cannot be planned against. (3) 'Human review of designs before submission is required' is NOT in the terms - no human-review or human-oversight clause exists, and the only design warranty is that 'your submission is your original work, or you otherwise hold all rights necessary to submit it'. What actually exists is a post-submission gate outside your control: 'Every design submitted for wet-lab synthesis will be screened for biosecurity risk before DNA synthesis', plus a sole-discretion right for sponsors to 'reject or disqualify any submission that raises a biosecurity concern' with no obligation to explain. Minor: Track 3 needs no APPLICATION but registration is still required. Not verifiable on these pages: the prior-round hit rates (EGFR-1 2.5%/201, EGFR-2 14%/400, Nipah 9.3%/1,200, RBX1 2.8%/322) - treat as unverified.

checks.name: Anthropic AI for Science Program (research credits)
checks.correction: Rules page live, program open and rolling. Verbatim confirmations: credits not cash, 'as determined by Anthropic in its sole discretion'; 18+ or age of majority; institutional consent required if affiliated; identical excluded-country list; biosecurity assessment 'to ensure they do not raise concerns around accelerating harmful applications'; publicity rights over 'names, biographical information, photographs, voices and/or likenesses ... worldwide in perpetuity without compensation'. The 27 Aug 2026 announcement confirms 'up to $50,000 in credits per project', 10,000 seats, standard seats free and premium seats at '$15 per month' with 5x usage limits. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The 'first Monday of each month' review cadence is unsupported - neither the official rules nor the announcement states any review day or schedule, so 'next decision points fall in October, November and December 2026' is not a published commitment. There is no stated decision timeline at all; plan for an unbounded wait. (2) The eligibility caveat resolves in your favour. The PI-or-equivalent-at-an-academic-or-nonprofit requirement attaches only to the 10,000 Claude Team SEATS. For the credits, the announcement states 'Any researcher is eligible to apply' - no PI status and no institutional affiliation needed. Institutional consent is still required if you happen to be affiliated.

checks.name: Cancer Grand Challenges - gastroesophageal cancer targeted call
checks.correction: No corrections - every stated detail checks out. Both gastroesophageal challenges are open (reversing early tissue changes; biological mechanisms behind geographical variation in incidence); 'up to $34m in funding over a flexible time period'; full application '24 November 2026'; LOI at least two weeks earlier; interviews '20 January 2027' in New York City; one Team Lead plus up to seven Co-Investigators; 'Teams must be international in nature, with no more than 50% of the Co-Investigators and overall funding being based in a single country'; biomedical, software, engineering and social sciences all welcomed; no AI policy stated anywhere on the page. One addition the record omits: winners are announced March 2027, which pushes any funded work well past the factory's near-term horizon and reinforces the record's own verdict that the viable play is joining another team's application rather than leading one.

checks.name: Longevity Impetus Grants
checks.correction: Round is live and matches on the money and timing: up to $500,000 per grant; ~$15M targeted for roughly 50 grants; first $5M matched 1:1 by anchor donor Robert Rosenkranz; run with Hevolution and Rosenkranz foundations as stated; rolling with no fixed deadline; decision turnaround stated on-page as 'no more than 3 weeks from application to decision'; no AI policy restricting AI-generated proposals. TWO CORRECTIONS, both material to whether you write. (1) Eligibility is in fact stated, and favourably - eligible applicants are scientists at ANY career stage, explicitly including independent investigators and those new to aging research. The record's 'the page does not state an institutional requirement, so an unaffiliated applicant should confirm' is resolved: unaffiliated entry qualifies. (2) The scope caveat the record flagged is now the decisive fact, and it is stricter than the record implies. This is a focused 'AI-Enabling Datasets' round - it wants high-dimensional measurements added to human studies, large-scale perturbation experiments in living organisms, tools for measuring biology in common samples like blood draws, and adaptive human trials - and it carries a hard condition that resulting data be open-source and formatted for immediate ingestion by major AI model architectures. Reviewers combine bio and AI experts. A binder-design proposal is out of scope unless reframed as dataset generation, and the open-source data mandate directly negates the IP-preservation rationale the record uses to justify the self-funded Adaptyv route.

checks.name: ACS Precision Chemistry - 'Precision Polypeptides' special issue
checks.correction: Call is live and accurately described on substance. Deadline confirmed verbatim: 'Submissions are welcome through November 30, 2026.' Journal is Precision Chemistry (ACS, fully open access, partner journal co-published with USTC). Article types Articles, Letters, Perspectives, Reviews. Listed topics include polypeptide library construction and screening and 'Specific Binding and Function modulation of Polypeptide to Target Biomolecules', so the fit is real. The record's AI-policy prediction is now confirmed at journal level: 'Artificial intelligence (AI) tools do not qualify for authorship', and 'The use of AI tools for text or image generation should be disclosed in the manuscript within the Acknowledgments section with a description of when and how the tools were used' - so budget a disclosure statement as planned. ONE CORRECTION, and it breaks the cost model: 'effectively $0 beyond writing' is wrong. Precision Chemistry is fully open access and levies an Article Publishing Charge on accepted manuscripts. Country discounts apply and authors at institutions with ACS Read + Publish agreements can have the APC covered - neither of which an unaffiliated entrant can rely on. I could not confirm the exact figure from ACS's own pages (the journal About page returns 403 and the APC sits behind an interactive calculator); third-party aggregators report roughly $3,500. An APC in the low thousands exceeds the sub-$2k POC ceiling by itself, before any assay spend. The timing problem the record identifies is confirmed: competition results publish 15 Dec, after the 30 Nov deadline, so a submission here must rest on self-funded assay data.

checks.name: Adaptyv Bio protein binding service (rolling self-funded verifier)
checks.correction: Service is live, rolling and open to any organisation - the strongest-verified target in the set. Confirmed: BLI (Gator Bio) and SPR (Carterra); readouts are binding yes/no, kinetic curves fitted from raw data, precise KD/kon/koff (Full Affinity Characterization only) and expression yields low/medium/high; Screening Mode uses 2 concentrations vs 4+ for Full Affinity; >90% expression success, thousands of proteins monthly; API at docs.adaptyvbio.com/api-reference; no publication requirement, data stays private, with an optional 20% discount for releasing results on Proteinbase - so the IP-preservation argument holds. THREE CORRECTIONS on cost and speed. (1) Turnaround: the '3 days in its fastest configuration' claim is unsupported. The page documents 3-4 weeks with an explicit 21-day breakdown (days 0-7 submission and prep, 8-9 expression, 10-15 kinetic measurements, 16-21 data review and release). Plan on 3-4 weeks, which means an order placed in October lands data in November - still ahead of the 30 Nov ACS deadline, but only just. (2) The price attribution is inverted/muddled. The site headlines 'from $99/protein', but the actual cost estimator on the binding page shows $169/protein at the T2 tier, and the public page does not state consistently which service level $169 buys - one reading labels it Basic Binding Screening, another Full Affinity Characterization. Materials are also extra: Adaptyv's own write-up quotes $99.00/sequence for the assay plus $17.49/sequence materials, i.e. ~$116/sequence at entry level. (3) No minimum order is published - that is an unresolved risk, not a confirmed yes. Nothing public states a minimum sequence count or order value, the estimator's worked example is 60 proteins at $10,140, and per-protein price is explicitly said to vary with protein count, so a 10-15 design order may not price at the headline rate. Real pricing sits behind the Experiment Configurator at beta.adaptyvbio.com. Net: the record's $1-2.5k envelope survives arithmetically (15 x $169 = $2,535; 15 x ~$116 = ~$1,750) but 'well inside' the sub-$2k ceiling depends on the unconfirmed $99 tier and ignores materials. Budget ~$2.5k for 15 designs, and confirm small-order pricing in the configurator before committing.

targets.name: Arc Institute Virtual Cell Challenge 2026: final entry (zero-shot CRISPRi response prediction)
targets.what: Predict single-cell transcriptomic responses to 300 CRISPRi knockdowns in each of 3 held-out cell lines, with no challenge training set. The only inputs are the non-targeting-control profiles and the target gene list. Validation phase (live now): 3 validation lines, 300 perturbations each, public leaderboard until 22 Oct 2026. Final phase: the test NTC profiles and perturbation list are released 22 Oct 2026. The submission is one .vcc file (prepared from an h5ad) of 360,000 cells x 18,533 genes in raw counts, 400 cells per perturbation. Sources: https://virtualcellchallenge.org/evaluation and https://arcinstitute.org/news/virtual-cell-challenge-2026
targets.reward_or_value: Prizes stated in the official rules (revised 16 Sep 2026). 1st: $100k = $50k cash + $50k NVIDIA Brev credits. 2nd: $50k = $25k cash + $25k credits. 3rd: $25k = $12.5k cash + $12.5k credits. Total cash is $87.5k. The credits expire 1 year after issuance, have no cash value, and are non-transferable. Team prizes are split equally among members. Finalists must submit a high-level method description, which Arc publishes. Code and weights need not be disclosed, which gives reputational value in computational biology. Winners are announced mid-to-late Nov 2026. Scale of the field: in 2025, over 1,200 teams submitted and about 300 made final submissions (per Arc's 2025 wrap-up); Arc reported over 1,800 sign-ups for 2026 at one point.
targets.deadline: Final entry due 5 Nov 2026, 23:59 UTC. Final test set released 22 Oct 2026. Leaderboard (validation) entries accepted until 22 Oct 2026. There is no registration deadline other than registering before your first submission.
targets.verifier: Automated scoring by cell-eval2 (MIT, pip install cell-eval2; https://github.com/ArcInstitute/cell-eval2) with the vcc2026 preset, against held-out measurements from Arc's lab. Six metrics are aggregated: pds_cosine, expr_mse_unbiased_capped_norm, de_wilcoxon_direction_fidelity_yield_raw, de_wilcoxon_direction_reach_raw, de_wilcoxon_sig_jaccard and de_wilcoxon_lfc_nmae. Each metric is reference-scaled so that 0 = cell-context mean and 1 = a real replicate experiment. The same scorer runs locally for free. Limits: 2 submissions per day in each phase. There is no final leaderboard between 22 Oct and 5 Nov, only the last final entry counts, and finalist scores are re-validated.
targets.eligibility: Must be 18 or older. Teams of 1-8 people, and one team per person. Open to individuals, academic labs, companies and independent research organizations. A team is either entirely personal-capacity, entirely employees of one organization, or entirely university representatives. Excluded: Arc and sponsor employees and interns (sponsors are NVIDIA, 10x Genomics and Ultima Genomics), people advised by Arc staff since Jan 2026, and Arc contractors. Also excluded: residents of Belarus, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, Crimea, Luhansk and Donetsk, and anyone on a US restricted-party list. No entry fee. Governed by California law, with an arbitration agreement.
targets.ai_policy: There is no restriction on AI-assisted development, and the official site actively supports coding agents. The evaluation page says that if you use a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini), 'vcc skill installs a skill that lets the agent drive this whole workflow for you'. The binding constraint is the 'Machine Learning Predictions Only' rule: entries must not contain experimental or literature results, and such results may not be used to revise model predictions, although they may be used to train or fine-tune. Any modelling strategy and any data you have rights to may be used, including the 2025 H1 hESC data. IP caveat: trained weights of Arc's State model carry a noncommercial license (https://huggingface.co/arcinstitute/ST-HVG-Tahoe/blob/main/MODEL_LICENSE.md), and the rules forbid using data or code you lack rights to use. A company-capacity entry should therefore avoid State weights or clear that license first.
targets.poc_cost: Estimate: Claude Max plus about $300-1,500 of GPU for training or fine-tuning on public Perturb-seq data (e.g. Replogle K562/RPE1, 2025 VCC H1) and generating predictions of 360k x 18.5k genes. Scoring is free (local cell-eval2 plus 2 leaderboard submissions per day). The clock is tight: about 3.5 weeks of leaderboard feedback remain, then a 14-day final window with no feedback.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the only live, cash-paying target in this domain with an automated, published scorer. It maps directly onto the factory's generator, critic-fixer and executor loop, with local cell-eval2 as an offline verifier. Realized-outcome evidence favours recombination plus strong baselines. In 2025 (a different task: H1 cells, narrower metrics), 3rd place used a purely statistical, summary-level model, and 1st place blended DEG-frequency statistics with protein-model embeddings. Arc's own 2025 wrap-up says purely AI approaches 'did not consistently outperform statistical baselines'. Caveat: 2025 winners partly exploited metric scale-sensitivity (L1-based PDS), and 2026 metrics were redesigned to resist this, so those findings transfer only partly. Arc reserves the right to alter scoring if it is manipulated. The factory must always run mean, additive and linear baselines. The mean baseline scores 0 by construction, so it is the floor to beat. Win odds are low given the field size, but the method write-up gives Arc-published reputation even without a prize.

targets.name: Virtual Embryo Challenge (NeurIPS 2026 competition), Agent Team track, Task 3 perturbation (plus Tasks 1-2 and the Generality Award)
targets.what: Three tasks on one mouse whole-embryo and heart single-cell/spatial atlas (~1M cells, 11 developmental stages), each with a hidden test set. T1: predict the gene-expression distribution (a set of cells) at a future stage. T2: forecast expression plus 3D location. T3: predict Gata4 and beta-catenin knockout effects at E8.75 from wild-type development data (expression plus 3D coordinates). The virtual-cell perturbation pack transfers most directly to T3. Teams can enter 1-3 tasks. Current phase is P2: validation leaderboard live, starter kit and baselines out. Phase P3 starts 20 Oct 2026, when validation answers are released and the test leaderboard opens. In P3, each board allows only 2 official test submissions in total, and they are locked once made.
targets.reward_or_value: $112K total in prizes and awards (per https://virtualembryo.ai/challenge/prizes), with separate, equal pools per track. Per track ($27K): one $8K 1st prize, two $5K 2nd prizes, three $3K 3rd prizes. Also an $8K Generality Award, a single award across both tracks for one shared architecture answering more than one task. Payment appears to be cash; the rules speak of taxes and payment info and mention no credits. Places with too few eligible entries are not awarded. Winners are announced at NeurIPS on 11 Dec 2026 and invited to co-author the joint challenge report, which has publication value. Entrants keep ownership of their methods, code and models. Funded by a Laude Institute Moonshots Seed Grant.
targets.deadline: Final submissions due 2 Dec 2026, per rules section 17 and the timeline page. Test phase opens 20 Oct 2026, official evaluation starts 4 Dec, winners are announced 11 Dec 2026.
targets.verifier: An automated metric panel scores against hidden test sets. Each metric is rescaled so that 50 = floor model (copy_last, or wt_identity for T3) and 100 = attainable ceiling, estimated by scoring half the held-out target against its other half. Cell types are assigned by a frozen organizer classifier. The starter kit includes the exact evaluation code and a standalone scorer, so offline verification is free. To be eligible for a prize, a team must score above the floor on its boards, and its result must be reproducible.
targets.eligibility: The captain must be at least 18 (or of legal age where higher). Teams of up to 10, one team per person, one track per team. Switching track retires all scores. Open to academic, industry and independent entrants, and the affiliation may be 'Independent researcher'. The same capacity rules apply as at VCC: no mixing employee and personal capacity within a team. Excluded: the Qiu Lab (Stanford) and Neil Chi's group (UCSD), people they have advised since Jan 2026, contractors, and anyone legally barred. No blanket country list is published.
targets.ai_policy: There is an explicit Agent Team track for 'coding agents / LLM-driven recursive systems'. Humans may do anything before the 'configuration lock' (prompts, harness, model, tools, budget). After the lock, no human may read intermediate results and steer, change the configuration, or pick among the run's outputs. The agent must write the prediction file itself. Humans may launch many locked runs and choose which completed run to submit. Every submission needs at least 2 evidence types, one of them the trajectory (at most 200 MB per file, 600 MB per team). It must also declare the framework and model string, and it may be audited or re-run. Prizes require the trajectory, the prompts and the harness. External public data, pretrained models and code are allowed if licensed and disclosed. Held-out stages and genotypes are banned by any route, including via pretrained models or datasets whose data is close in stage. Inverting scores or differencing them across submissions to recover targets is banned. The data is unpublished: any publication using it needs prior approval from Neil Chi's team.
targets.poc_cost: Estimate: Claude Max for the agent runs plus about $200-1,000 of GPU (a 1M-cell atlas, plus generative or flow models for T3). Scoring is free (local scorer plus daily validation submissions). The evidence logging the factory's outcome ledger already needs costs nothing extra. Check that long unattended agent runs fit within Claude Max usage limits.
targets.why_factory_fits: This is the closest match found to OptiLex's architecture. Its Agent Team track rewards exactly what the factory is: a locked, autonomous generator, critic-fixer and executor pipeline with full trajectory logging. Prize money is set aside for agents, so OptiLex never competes against human-designed methods for the same prize. The agent track is probably much thinner than the 1,200-team VCC field (no participation numbers were published, so this is an inference). Agent prizes can fall to fewer eligible entrants, but places with too few entries are not awarded. The Generality Award rewards one architecture across tasks, which matches a domain-agnostic engine. The perturbation pack from VCC work can be reused for T3 (knockout prediction). The agent evidence doubles as a published, audited record of the factory's capability. Risks: prizes are modest ($8K top per track). The stage-proximity data rules are intricate, and a leak means disqualification, so the factory needs a data-provenance gate. The T3 floor (wt_identity) is a strong trivial baseline to beat.

targets.name: Virtual Embryo Challenge Community Contribution Award
targets.what: Paid awards for tutorials, notebooks, tools, documentation and fixes that help other people compete in the Virtual Embryo Challenge. Awards do not depend on leaderboard rank.
targets.reward_or_value: Up to $200 per contribution from a $20K pool, which grows with any unawarded placement money. One person may receive several awards. Paid after the challenge closes, together with the leaderboard prizes. The value is small; the main return is visibility with the organizers and NeurIPS attendees.
targets.deadline: Runs while the challenge is open. The prizes page gives no separate cutoff; assume the challenge close (final submissions 2 Dec 2026) and confirm via the 'How to apply' link.
targets.verifier: Organizer judgement of usefulness to other competitors. This is weaker than an automated score, but contributions that can be executed (working loaders, baselines, scorer fixes) are checkable.
targets.eligibility: Open to non-competitors as well as teams, per the prizes page. The general challenge exclusions (organizing labs, etc.) presumably apply.
targets.ai_policy: The prizes page states no specific rule. The challenge itself is agent-friendly (Agent Team track), and the rules require disclosure and licence-compliant use of external code. Disclosing AI assistance in contributed notebooks is the prudent default.
targets.poc_cost: About $0-50 beyond Claude Max: CPU notebooks, documentation and tooling.
targets.why_factory_fits: A cheap, low-risk calibration channel with realized payouts. The factory's executor already produces baselines, data loaders and verified notebooks as by-products of targets 1-2. Submitting them converts sunk work into small cash, early feedback from organizers and credibility, at almost no extra cost. Its value comes only in combination with targets 1-2; alone it is not worth pursuing.

targets.name: CZI Virtual Cells Platform: model submission and cz-benchmarks Perturbation Expression Prediction task
targets.what: A rolling submission of an open virtual-cell or perturbation model to CZI's Virtual Cells Platform (https://virtualcellmodels.cziscience.com/), where suitable models are benchmarked with the open cz-benchmarks suite. The relevant task, contributed by NVIDIA (https://virtualcellmodels.cziscience.com/benchmark-task/perturbation), predicts the expression of masked genes in CRISPRi-perturbed cells from the unmasked genes and scores the predicted versus experimental log fold changes on DE genes. Accepted domains include single-cell transcriptomics and perturbation prediction.
targets.reward_or_value: No cash. Value: CZI-hosted listing and benchmarking (reputational and distribution), an independent verification of a VCC-derived model, and a route to visibility in CZI and Biohub's $500M Virtual Biology Initiative (announced 29 Apr 2026). That initiative has no open external call; its contact is virtualbiology@biohub.org. All 28 CZI science RFAs are currently listed as closed, so this is not a grant channel today.
targets.deadline: Rolling. Initial decision within 4 weeks, publication about 2 weeks after acceptance, up to 6 weeks in total.
targets.verifier: The open-source cz-benchmarks package (multi-metric, runnable locally) plus CZI's review for novelty, utility, performance, accessibility and responsible AI. Possible outcomes are Accepted & Benchmarked, Accepted (not benchmarked) or Not accepted. The public perturbation-task page currently shows no listed datasets, metrics or models, so the leaderboard appears thin or under construction.
targets.eligibility: The guide says 'anyone can submit a model for consideration'. The model must use a permissive open-source license (MIT, Apache 2.0 or BSD-3) and ship a model card and a quickstart notebook; a tutorial is encouraged. CZI prefers published research.
targets.ai_policy: None stated for AI-assisted development. Requirements concern licensing, documentation and responsible-AI principles. Open weights and code are required, which conflicts with keeping a VCC method proprietary for licensing.
targets.poc_cost: About $0-200 beyond the VCC or Virtual Embryo work, mainly packaging, documentation and running cz-benchmarks locally.
targets.why_factory_fits: Reuses factory outputs as a second, independent verifier with no deadline pressure. Useful as an outcome-ledger anchor, because it checks whether a model that scores well on VCC generalizes to a different perturbation benchmark, which guards against overfitting to one metric. Low direct value: pursue it only after a VCC entry exists, and only if OptiLex is willing to open-source the model.

targets.name: OpenProblems living benchmarks: geneRNIB GRN inference (perturbation-scored) and single-cell perturbation_prediction
targets.what: Community 'living' benchmarks with fixed input/output contracts, gold-standard datasets and automated re-runs. geneRNIB (active; repo updated Jun 2026) ranks gene-regulatory-network inference methods across 10 datasets (2 multiomics, 8 transcriptomics). Its evaluation uses perturbation data (CRISPR knockouts, overexpression, chemical treatments, and observational data), ranked by per-dataset normalization, percentile ranking and modality-balanced aggregation (https://genernib-documentation.readthedocs.io/en/latest/leaderboard.html). task_perturbation_prediction covers small-molecule responses in PBMCs, from the NeurIPS 2023 Kaggle competition. It is MIT-licensed but dormant: its last commit was Jan 2025.
targets.reward_or_value: No cash. Value: an inclusion on a peer-reviewed-style public leaderboard and a citable method contribution. A strong GRN prior or perturbation model is also a reusable component for VCC-style zero-shot prediction.
targets.deadline: Rolling: methods are added by pull request following the repository's add-a-method flow. No deadline.
targets.verifier: Automated, version-controlled pipelines (Viash plus Docker or Singularity) that re-run every method on fixed datasets with published metrics. Contributions are community-reviewed.
targets.eligibility: Open to anyone via GitHub pull request, with code under an open license.
targets.ai_policy: Actively agent-friendly. The geneRNIB README ships an agent instructions file (agentic/AGENT.md) so AI agents can run inference and evaluation and add new methods. There is no prohibition on AI-assisted methods.
targets.poc_cost: About $0-300: CPU or modest GPU. The Singularity images for advanced baselines are about 48 GB.
targets.why_factory_fits: A free, always-open offline verifier for the virtual-cell domain pack, and a reasonable calibration step between the LM-training proxy and paid challenges. The factory can test whether its recombined ideas beat established methods on fixed data, independently of any single competition metric. Weakest value channel of the set (reputation only). The perturbation_prediction task is stale and covers a different modality (chemical, PBMC), so prioritize geneRNIB or use perturbation_prediction purely as a sanity-check verifier.

checks.name: Arc Institute Virtual Cell Challenge 2026: final entry (zero-shot CRISPRi response prediction)
checks.correction: The official rules match the brief on almost every point. The rules are effective 4 Aug 2026 and revised 16 Sep 2026. Prizes are $50k/$25k/$12.5k cash plus the same amount again in NVIDIA Brev credits; the credits expire after 1 year, have no cash value and cannot be transferred. The final test set is released 22 Oct, the final entry is due 5 Nov 2026 at 23:59 UTC, and each phase allows 2 submissions per day. Only the last final entry counts, finalist scores are re-validated, and a finalist must submit a method description that Arc publishes (no code or weights). Other points that match: ages 18+, teams of 1-8, the same capacity rules, the same country and restricted-party exclusions, no entry fee, California law and arbitration. The 'Machine Learning Predictions Only' wording matches the 16 Sep revision. The evaluation page does say that if you use a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini), the 'vcc skill' lets the agent drive the workflow. The cell-eval2 repo (MIT, vcc2026 preset) lists exactly the six metrics given in the brief, each scaled 0 = mean baseline, 1 = replicate. The page confirms the 360,000-cell x 18,533-gene shape. CORRECTIONS: (1) Winner timing: the brief says mid-to-late Nov, but the FAQ says 'late November' and the evaluation page says winners are announced 'in early December'. Plan for late Nov to early Dec. (2) The exclusion list is broader than the brief says. It also excludes former Arc employees who left after April 2026, students in Arc Core Investigator labs, and students or employees in Arc Innovation Investigator labs. Entrants also may not use help from any excluded person. (3) There is a practical file-size cap on non-zeros: about 13,200 per cell at the 360k shape. A dense 360k x 18,533 array is 1.40x the cap, so predictions must be stored sparse, without explicit zeros. The 2025 stats and method descriptions are confirmed by Arc's 2025 wrap-up: 1,200+ teams submitted and 300+ made final submissions. 1st place (BioMap) used DEG frequency plus protein embeddings, 3rd place (Outlier) used a summary-level statistical model, and the wrap-up says 'Purely AI-based approaches did not consistently outperform statistical baselines'. The 1,800 sign-ups figure for 2026 was not verified. Sponsor names appear on the site but the sponsor list was not checked item by item.

checks.name: Virtual Embryo Challenge (NeurIPS 2026 competition), Agent Team track, Task 3 perturbation (plus Tasks 1-2 and the Generality Award)
checks.correction: The rules, prizes page and timeline page match the brief on almost every point. Prizes total $112K. Each track pays $8K x1, $5K x2 and $3K x3 ($27K), plus one $8K Generality Award shared across tracks. Dates match: P2 opened 15 Aug, P3 starts 20 Oct, final submissions are due 2 Dec, evaluation starts 4 Dec and winners are announced at NeurIPS on 11 Dec. The captain must be 18 or the local age of majority; teams have up to 10 members, one team per person, and no mixing of capacities. Switching track retires all scores. The configuration-lock rules match, including that humans may launch many locked runs and pick a completed one. At least 2 evidence types are required, capped at 200 MB per file and 600 MB per team. The framework and model string must be declared, and entries may be audited or re-run. External data must be licensed and disclosed. Using held-out stages or genotypes by any route is banned, and nearness to a stage counts, not just its label. Score inversion and differencing are banned. Terms clause 14 does require prior approval from Dr. Neil Chi's team for any publication using the data. The Qiu Lab is at Stanford. CORRECTIONS: (1) The method write-up is mandatory for a prize, not just an invitation to co-author. Winners must deliver a written report on how the method works within 14 days of notification, and it is published alongside the results; code is not published but may be requested privately. (2) The floor rule applies to total standing: the team must beat the floor summed across all boards it entered (above 150 for all three tasks). Boards not attempted count as zero toward overall standing. (3) Unawarded places and an unclaimed Generality Award go to the Community Contribution pool, not the other track. (4) Development-phase quotas are 20 scored submissions per day for Task 1 and 8 for Task 2. A single prediction file may not exceed 1,200 MB. (5) Only the captain has an age minimum; other members do not. The atlas size (about 1M cells, 11 stages) was not checked.

checks.name: Virtual Embryo Challenge Community Contribution Award
checks.correction: Confirmed: a $20K pool, up to $200 per contribution, and no cap per person. Awards are committed on acceptance and paid after the Challenge closes, together with the leaderboard prizes. The award is open to anyone, including people who are not competing. It is judged on usefulness, quality, reach, openness and impact. CORRECTIONS: (1) The deadline is not 2 Dec. Contributions are rolling and reviewed as they arrive, until the fund is committed or the Challenge closes on 11 Dec 2026, whichever comes first. Filing early matters. (2) How to apply: sign in (no team registration needed) and file a public link through the form at https://virtualembryo.ai/challenge/community. All filings are listed publicly on Community resources. When two contributions overlap, the one filed first is weighted more. Standalone public repos count, as does work published before the award was announced. (3) Eligibility is stated as 'Anyone' with an account; the page does not repeat the general exclusions. (4) The pool can grow from unawarded placement prizes and an unclaimed Generality Award.

checks.name: CZI Virtual Cells Platform: model submission and cz-benchmarks Perturbation Expression Prediction task
checks.correction: Confirmed on the contribute_model page. Anyone can submit. A model card and a quickstart notebook are required, and a tutorial is strongly encouraged. Model code must carry a permissive open-source license (MIT, Apache 2.0 or BSD-3), and descriptive materials are published under CC-BY. Review looks at value with a preprint or publication, responsible AI and fitness for research use. Outcomes are Accepted & Benchmarked, Accepted (not benchmarked) or Not accepted, with resubmission allowed. The first decision comes within 4 weeks and publication about 2 weeks later, up to 6 weeks in total; expedited review is available on request. The perturbation task page confirms the task is NVIDIA-contributed (Michelle Gill, Polina Binder) and scores masked-gene LFC. It currently shows 0 datasets, 0 metrics and no models, so the leaderboard is thin. Nuance: the Biohub Virtual Biology Initiative page (29 Apr 2026, $500M) says $100M is committed 'to fund external research' for data generation and gives virtualbiology@biohub.org as the contact. No application process is posted there, so 'no open external call' holds for now, but this is a live funding line worth watching. I did not check the claim that all 28 CZI RFAs are closed.

checks.name: OpenProblems living benchmarks: geneRNIB GRN inference (perturbation-scored) and single-cell perturbation_prediction
checks.correction: Confirmed: the geneRNIB repo (task_grn_inference) is MIT-licensed and active, last pushed 12 Jun 2026. It ships agentic/AGENT.md and a know_how folder, and methods are added as Viash/Nextflow components under src/methods. The ranking uses per-dataset normalization, then percentile ranking, then a modality-balanced mean of per-modality medians. task_perturbation_prediction is MIT-licensed and dormant: its last main-branch commit was 28 Jan 2025. CORRECTIONS: (1) The dataset count is 11, not 10: 2 multiomics (OPSCA, MSCIC) and 9 transcriptomics (Nakatake, Norman, Replogle, 300BCG, ParseBioscience, Xaira HEK293T, Xaira HCT116, SoundLife, SoundLife Vaccine), per the README and the leaderboard page. The leaderboard page's own header says '10 transcriptomics' but lists 9. (2) The perturbation types are drug/chemical, TF overexpression, CRISPRa and CRISPRi, cytokine stimulation, and longitudinal observational data including flu vaccination. The CRISPR data is CRISPRi and CRISPRa screens (Replogle, Norman, Xaira), not strictly 'CRISPR knockouts'.
